UI pattern catalogue ### 43.1 Skip link - **Use when:** repeated header or navigation content precedes the main content (WCAG 2.4.1). - **Markup:** ```html Skip to main content …
…
``` - **Keyboard:** it's the first Tab stop; it becomes visible on focus, and Enter moves to main. - ❌ Hidden with `display:none` (then it can never be focused), or targeting an element that can't take focus, so the next Tab starts from the top again in some browsers ⚠ verify. - **Test:** CK-KEY (first Tab = skip link), CK-FOCUS (focus lands in main), CK-DOM (target exists). ### 43.2 Breadcrumb - **Markup:** ```html
  1. Home
  2. Guides
  3. Forms
``` - **Why `ol`:** the order is meaningful and screen readers announce the item count. - **ARIA:** `aria-current="page"` marks the current page. Separators belong in CSS (`::before`), not in the text content. - ❌ Separators as text ("Home > Guides > Forms" in one paragraph): they're read aloud and there's no list structure. ### 43.3 Pagination - **Markup:** `
` + list of links; the current page link has `aria-current="page"`. Previous/next links get descriptive text ("Previous page"). - ❌ Links labeled only "‹" or "›" without an accessible name. Button-only pagination that can't be bookmarked. - ⚡ Use real URLs (`?page=3`) so pages can be shared, the back button works and server rendering is possible. ### 43.4 Site navigation with dropdowns (disclosure navigation) - **Markup:** `nav` > `ul` > `li` > either a link, or a `` followed by a nested `ul id="sub1" hidden`. - **Keyboard:** Tab moves through items; Enter/Space toggles a submenu; Escape closes it and returns focus to the button. - ❌ `role="menu"`/`menuitem` for **site navigation**. Those roles are meant for application menus (like a desktop menu bar) and change how screen readers expect keys to work ⚠ verify (S23). - ❌ Opening submenus on hover only (WCAG 2.1.1, 1.4.13). - ⚡ `popover` + `popovertarget` gives light-dismiss submenus `[support-unverified]`. Keep `aria-expanded` in sync, or rely on the native popover state mapping ⚠ verify. ### 43.5 Mobile navigation toggle ("hamburger") - **Markup:** `` + `
`. - ✅ Give it a visible text label, or an icon with an accessible name. Keep the button **before** the nav in the DOM order. - ❌ An `` with a click handler, or a checkbox hack that has no announced state. - ⚡ If the panel covers the page like a modal, use `` with `showModal()` so focus can't escape. ### 43.6 Tabs - **First question:** do you need tabs at all? Headings with sections, or `details`, are often simpler and fully native. - **Markup (APG tabs, ⚠ verify S23):** ```html

…

Activation is automatic or manual (Enter/Space), by design choice. - ❌ Tabs that are really page navigation. ## 3. Classification conventions (apply to every record)

Each `source_claims` entry and each explanatory statement carries one of these labels:

| Label | Meaning | Example of a claim type (not yet sourced) |
|---|---|---|
| `normative-author` | An authoring conformance requirement in S01 | an attribute's allowed values |
| `normative-ua` | A user-agent processing requirement in S01 | parser repair behavior, entry-list construction |
| `normative-wcag` | A WCAG 2.2 success criterion | 1.3.1 Info and Relationships |
| `browser-default` | Behavior from a UA stylesheet or rendering default (S01 §15 or engine) | default display of an element |
| `implementation` | Engine-specific behavior that has been observed | only allowed with recorded execution evidence |
| `convention` | Widely used but optional practice | |
| `pedagogical` | A teaching recommendation | "start with native elements" |

Feature status labels: `stable`, `deprecated`, `obsolete-but-conforming` and `non-conforming` (from S01 §16), and `support-unverified`. The last one is the default for any feature not checked against S14.

---

## 4. Scope

### 4.1 In scope
- Inventory areas A–L from the brief, taught from the Living Standard as observed on 2026-10-16.
- Accessibility applied throughout, using native semantics first. ARIA is taught only where native HTML is not enough, and only once S05–S08 have been read.
- Browser practice exercises with fixed, minimal CSS and read-only JavaScript used only for observation.

### 4.2 Explicit exclusions

| Excluded | Reason / boundary |
|---|---|
| CSS authoring | Covered by a separate `css` subject. HTML exercises ship fixed, read-only CSS. |
| JavaScript programming | The learner never writes JS for a basic HTML exercise. Scripts supplied for observation or progressive enhancement are read-only and named in each exercise. |
| Full Web APIs: canvas (§4.12.5), workers (§10), storage (§12), server-sent events and messaging (§9), Navigation API (§7.2.6), drag and drop (§6.11) | Outside the HTML-markup scope; area H allows only a few marked extensions |
| Custom elements and shadow DOM (§4.13), `template`/`slot` | Deferred as a future extension; not required coverage |
| Microdata (§5), MathML and SVG authoring, image maps (§4.8.12–14) | Not in the required inventory |
| Server-side form processing | Exercises only observe the submitted payload; there is no server-side validation code |
| SEO ranking claims | Metadata is taught with explicit limits; no claim that markup guarantees ranking |
| WCAG conformance certification | Automated tools plus manual review produce evidence, not a conformance claim |
| Curriculum order, prices, subscriptions, rewards | Application decisions. Difficulty labels describe task depth only, and `prerequisite_ids` record concept dependencies, not a learning path. |
| HTML4/XHTML 1.x authoring | Mentioned only for parse differences and obsolete-feature labels |
| Framework or templating syntax (JSX and similar) | Not HTML |

A technical curriculum for front-end engineers, instructors and AI mentors

1 Scope, learning routes and evidence
CSS describes presentation; HTML describes structure and meaning; JavaScript coordinates behavior. Sass is a
build-time language that emits CSS. Bootstrap is a collection of CSS conventions, Sass sources, components and
JavaScript plugins. Understanding their separate responsibilities is essential to using them together. A working page is
the output of the entire system, including browser algorithms, assets, fonts, input devices and user preferences.
This guide follows the earlier HTML curriculum's format: mental model, precise reference, concrete example, common
mistake, practice and evidence. It has four main subject areas: CSS fundamentals and architecture, Sass/SCSS,
Bootstrap 5, and their runtime integration with the DOM and Web APIs. The reference appendices supply property
metadata and additional inventories so that the narrative remains teachable rather than becoming an unstructured list
of names.
Version boundary. CSS3 is a historical umbrella name. Modern CSS consists of independently versioned modules.
The CSS property appendix covers every non-vendor property record in the retrieved W3C Webref package, including
advanced, SVG, print, speech and experimental proposals. Records in the CSS Snapshot 2025 property index are
identified; inclusion in either source is not a browser-support guarantee. The Snapshot index itself includes historical
names. Draft-only entries are research references, not blanket production recommendations. Vendor compatibility
aliases and historical aural properties receive separate treatment. Custom properties are an open-ended family.
The package versions and source hashes are recorded in the verification appendix. Bootstrap examples target 5.3.8.
Sass examples use Dart Sass 1.105.2. Living specifications and versioned package sources can differ: a new grammar
alternative in a draft may be unsupported by all target browsers. Feature detection proves only the specific condition
tested. A valid declaration can still be ineffective in the current layout context.
Accessibility boundary. The examples use semantic controls, visible labels, keyboard paths, contrast-conscious
colors, responsive reflow and motion preferences. The target is WCAG 2.2 AA, including applicable A criteria. An
isolated stylesheet or an automated scan cannot certify an entire experience as WCAG compliant. The verification
record states which compilation, browser and automated accessibility checks were actually run; manual screen-reader,
zoom, forced-color and cross-engine testing remain explicit acceptance work. Small syntax examples are complete
rules or complete functions; the integrated labs supply runnable documents and their actual dependencies.

Common curriculum, different entry points
• Foundations: learn cascade, computed values, boxes, normal flow and source order before layout abstractions.
• Layout: practice intrinsic sizing, Flexbox and Grid, then responsive constraints and component queries.
• Maintainability: introduce tokens, layers, naming, Sass modules and generated utilities after the plain CSS behavior is
  understood.
• Framework use: map Bootstrap classes to the CSS they emit, then study component state and plugin ownership.
• Runtime integration: connect DOM state and browser APIs to style changes with cleanup, fallbacks and measured
   performance.
• Assessment: explain a failure, predict the computed result, inspect evidence, repair the cause and test a
   counterexample. Do not award mastery for matching a screenshot alone.

Fourteen teaching lenses
For every lesson ask: what is the mental model; how is the rule created; how is its target selected; what changes its
value; how do nodes enter or leave; what is the traversal order; what establishes identity; what orders competing rules;
what transforms specified values; what work does the renderer perform; what happens at boundaries; which alternative
fits; which reusable pattern emerges; and which observation proves the claim? Apply these to CSS rather than
inventing algorithmic complexity claims for a selector or framework class.

2 CSS grammar, values and the cascade
Rules and parsing
A qualified rule combines a selector list with a declaration block. A declaration contains a property, colon, value and
optional importance flag. An at-rule has a name, prelude and either a semicolon or a block. Comments are removed
during tokenization. Unrecognized declarations are generally discarded individually; an invalid selector can invalidate
an ordinary selector list. Forgiving selector lists have specifically defined recovery behavior. Parsing recovery is not a
guarantee that an intended design survives.

  /* Complete stylesheet fragment. */
  .notice {
    color: #172b4d;
    background-color: #fff;
    padding: 1rem;
    border: 0.125rem solid currentColor;
  }
  @media (width >= 48rem) {
    .notice { padding: 1.5rem; }
  }

Browser devtools distinguishes a rule that never matched, a matched declaration that lost the cascade, an invalid value
and a winning value with no visible effect. Debug in that order. Do not respond to every unexpected result by adding
!important.

https://drafts.csswg.org/css-syntax-3/

Grammar notation and acceptable value types
In the property appendix, | means choose one alternative; || permits one or more alternatives in any order; && requires
every component in any order; juxtaposition requires sequence. Square brackets group grammar, not literal brackets. ?
means optional, * zero or more, + one or more, # a comma-separated list, and {m,n} a repetition range. Quoted
property references such as <'margin-top'> mean use that property's value grammar. Angle-bracket names refer to
defined types, not literal markup. Ranges such as <number [0,1]> constrain the value. Consult the defining module for
computed-value restrictions and newer syntax.
An identifier is not automatically a string; an unquoted family name can have different parsing rules from a quoted font
name. <custom-ident> excludes reserved identifiers in its context. <dashed-ident> starts with two hyphens. Strings use
quotes and escapes. URLs use URL syntax and must still satisfy application security policy. Images include raster
resources, gradients and supported generated images. Colors include named values, hex, rgb/hsl and modern color
spaces where supported. currentColor connects many paint values to the element's color.
Numbers can be unitless or have dimensions. Lengths include px, em, rem, ch, ex, lh, rlh, viewport units and container
query units. A CSS pixel is a reference unit, not necessarily a physical device pixel. em in font-size relates to the parent;
in many other properties it relates to the element's font size. rem uses the root font size. ch measures a font's zero
advance and is useful for approximate line lengths, not exact character counts. Angles include deg, rad, grad and turn;
times include s and ms; resolutions include dppx and dpi. Zero-length unit omission is contextual and must not be
transferred to time or arbitrary typed values.
Percentages resolve against a property-specific reference. Width, height, padding, transforms, backgrounds and gaps
do not share one universal percentage base. An indefinite containing size can change how a percentage participates in
layout. fr is a Grid flexible track unit, not a general length. auto, normal, none, initial and zero are not
interchangeable.
calc() combines compatible dimensions. min() and max() choose bounds; clamp() constrains a preferred value. Keep
spaces around binary plus/minus in calc expressions. Multiplication/division support depends on the CSS Values level;
do not assume Sass arithmetic and browser arithmetic have the same rules. Intrinsic keywords such as min-content,
max-content, fit-content and stretch are context-sensitive sizing requests.

The fluid font retains rem bounds. Test browser text scaling; a viewport-only size can defeat the intended enlargement.
Small/large/dynamic viewport units address different mobile viewport states; dynamic units can change while browser
chrome moves. Container units require a suitable query container, and fallback behavior must be understood before
using them.
https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-4/

Cascade precedence, specificity and source order
First determine relevance: selector match, media condition, feature condition, scope and tree. Cascade origin and
importance then outrank layer order and specificity. In ascending priority the broad origin order is normal user-agent
rules, normal user rules, normal author rules, keyframe animation values, important author rules, important user rules,
important user-agent rules and active transition values. Encapsulation contexts and inline declarations add defined
tie-breaks. Within the same cascade level, normal unlayered author rules outrank normal layered rules; later normal
layers outrank earlier ones. Important layer order reverses, so early important layers outrank later ones, and layered
important declarations outrank unlayered important declarations. Use importance sparingly and account for user
overrides.
Specificity is a tuple: IDs; classes/attributes/pseudo-classes; types/pseudo-elements. Compare left to right, never by a
decimal score. Combinators and the universal selector add no weight. :where() has zero specificity including its
arguments. :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument. :nth-child(... of S) adds
its pseudo-class weight and the most specific selector in S. Inline styles occupy a separate precedence position, not a
magical ID score. After specificity ties, scope proximity can matter before source order under @scope rules.
Examples: .card a is (0,1,1); [aria-expanded="true"] is (0,1,0); #app .card is (1,1,0); :where(#app) .card is (0,1,0);
:is(.card, #special) button is (1,0,1). Putting an ID in an unused branch of :is can still raise the rule's specificity.

  @layer reset, vendor, tokens, base, components, utilities;
  @layer base {
    :where(button, input, select, textarea) { font: inherit; }
  }
  @layer components {
    .action { border: 0.125rem solid currentColor; }
    .action:focus-visible { outline: 0.1875rem solid #111; outline-offset: 0.2rem; }
  }

A framework loaded unlayered will outrank these normal layered declarations regardless of their selector weight. Load
the framework into the vendor layer deliberately or maintain a separate, documented override strategy. CSS imports
must obey placement rules; importing with layer(vendor) is different from copying Sass source into a layer block.
https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade-6/

https://drafts.csswg.org/selectors-4/

Inheritance, defaults and value processing
A declaration produces a specified value after cascade and defaulting; computation resolves dependencies; layout
determines used values; rendering may approximate actual values. getComputedStyle() returns resolved values, which
can be used values for some properties. It does not reproduce authored shorthand text or prove that a layout is
accessible.
Inherited properties normally take the parent's computed value when no declaration wins. Non-inherited properties
normally take their initial value. Initial is the specification default, not the browser's HTML stylesheet choice: display
initially is inline even though div commonly displays as block. inherit explicitly takes the parent's computed value.

initial resets to the specification initial. unset chooses inherit or initial based on normal inheritance. revert rolls back
the current origin; revert-layer rolls back the current cascade layer according to its rules.
Shorthands set multiple longhands together and can reset omitted components. Background can reset
background-color; font resets multiple font settings; border resets border-image. Later longhands can override
individual parts. A shorthand containing var() may defer parsing, then become invalid at computed-value time. The
browser does not necessarily revive an earlier declaration when that happens.
Custom properties usually inherit and preserve token streams; var() substitutes tokens in consuming declarations. A
fallback is used when substitution needs it, not whenever the substituted value is invalid for the consuming property.
--size: red; width: var(--size, 10rem) does not make 10rem win. Registration through @property supplies syntax,
inheritance and an initial value under its constraints. Application token names remain open-ended.

  @property --progress {
    syntax: "<number>";
    inherits: false;
    initial-value: 0;
  }
  :root { --space-2: 0.5rem; --surface: #fff; --ink: #172b4d; }
  .panel { padding: var(--space-2); background: var(--surface); color: var(--ink); }

Practice: predict the winning color across two layers, an inline declaration and a user important declaration. Then
inspect each contender. Separately test an invalid custom-property substitution; explain why cascade selection and
computed-value validation are distinct stages.

3 Selectors, DOM relationships and state
Type, class, ID, universal and namespace selectors select by different identifiers. Attribute selectors test presence or
exact, whitespace-token, language-prefix, prefix, suffix and substring matches: [x], [x="y"], [x~="y"], [x|="en"],
[x^="y"], [x$="y"], [x*="y"]. The i flag requests ASCII case-insensitive matching; s requests case-sensitive
matching where supported. HTML attribute-name matching and attribute-value matching are not one rule. Escape
dynamic identifiers with CSS.escape when constructing a selector; prefer stable references over constructing selectors
from untrusted text.
The descendant combinator follows ancestry; > means a direct child; + means adjacent following sibling; ~ means later
siblings. The column combinator belongs to a specialized selector model and needs implementation verification.
Selector lists are unions, not sequential operations. A relational :has selector tests relative selectors against its subject;
it does not move the selected node to the descendant.
Structural pseudo-classes include :root, :empty, :first-child, :last-child, :only-child, :nth-child, :nth-last-child and their
of-type variants. Counting follows the relevant element sibling list; :nth-child(2 of .item) differs from
.item:nth-child(2). Whitespace handling for :empty has specification and implementation history; do not use a fragile
emptiness selector as the sole source of application truth.
State pseudo-classes include :hover, :active, :focus, :focus-visible, :focus-within, :checked, :indeterminate, :disabled,
:enabled, :required, :optional, :valid, :invalid, :user-valid, :user-invalid, :in-range, :out-of-range, :read-only, :read-write,
:placeholder-shown and :autofill. Match the correct native state. [checked] tests a content attribute; :checked tests
current checkedness. [aria-disabled="true"] does not disable a control. :visited has deliberate privacy restrictions.
:target reflects URL targeting, not generic component selection.
Language and direction selectors use :lang and :dir rather than assuming a lang/dir attribute exists on every
descendant. :is, :where, :not and :has provide logical composition. :defined can distinguish upgraded custom elements;
:host and :host-context have shadow-tree-specific rules and support constraints. Emerging states such as :state(),
:modal and :popover-open are tied to their defining APIs. Treat the complete selector appendix as a source inventory,
not a promise every browser implements every selector.
Pseudo-elements select generated or specialized parts: ::before, ::after, ::first-line, ::first-letter, ::marker, ::selection,
::placeholder, ::file-selector-button, ::backdrop, ::part(), ::slotted() and the view-transition pseudo-element tree.
Generated content is not a dependable place for essential instructions or interactive controls. ::slotted selects assigned
elements under specific restrictions; it does not become an unrestricted descendant selector into light DOM.

  .field:focus-within { border-color: #1b4d8a; }
  input:checked + label { font-weight: 700; }
  button:disabled { opacity: 0.7; cursor: not-allowed; }
  button:focus-visible { outline: 0.1875rem solid #111; outline-offset: 0.2rem; }
  @supports selector(:has(*)) {
    .field:has(input:user-invalid) { border-color: #9b1c20; }
  }

A class alone never supplies a label. For the adjacent-selector example, input and associated label must actually be
siblings in that order. Validation messages must exist as text and be connected to the control; a red border is
insufficient. Practice: implement a disabled submit button and explain how keyboard activation differs from a styled
aria-disabled link.

4 Boxes, normal flow and positioning
The box model and intrinsic sizing
The content box is surrounded by padding, border and margin. With content-box, declared width describes content;
with border-box it includes padding and border. Margin remains outside both. Minimum and maximum sizes constrain
preferred sizes, and intrinsic contributions constrain layout even when percentages or flexible tracks are used. Set
border-box consistently on elements and pseudo-elements rather than assuming it is inherited automatically.

  *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
  img, video { max-inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto; }
  .prose { max-inline-size: 70ch; overflow-wrap: anywhere; }

width: 100% plus padding can overflow under content-box. min-inline-size: 0 can allow a flex or grid child to shrink
below its automatic minimum; it should be applied to the actual constrained child, not scattered through the whole
application. overflow-wrap: anywhere affects intrinsic sizing differently from legacy break-word behavior. A fixed height
is rarely a good answer to varying text, translation or zoom.
Margins can be negative and vertical margins can collapse in ordinary block flow under defined conditions. Padding
cannot be negative and does not collapse. A new block formatting context, including flow-root, changes float interaction
and margin behavior. Inline formatting has line boxes and baselines; vertical margins on non-replaced inline boxes do
not create block spacing. Replaced elements have intrinsic dimensions and aspect ratios. Tables and ruby have
specialized rules.
Logical properties express block/inline directions from writing-mode and direction. Use margin-inline-start,
padding-block, inline-size and inset-inline-end where the intention is logical. Top/right/bottom/left remain physical. If
physical and logical declarations map to the same side, cascade and mapping determine the result; writing both is not
automatically a useful fallback.

Display, overflow and hiding
Display has outer and inner behavior: block versus inline participation, and flow/flex/grid/table layout within.
inline-flex is inline outside and flex inside. Display none removes boxes; visibility hidden generally retains layout
space; opacity zero still allows focus and hit testing unless other state changes intervene. content-visibility can skip
rendering work subject to containment, and requires care around intrinsic sizes and offscreen content. display:
contents removes the principal box but has accessibility and context-specific consequences; test rather than assuming
it preserves all semantics identically.
Overflow visible, hidden, clip, scroll and auto differ in clipping and scroll-container behavior. Hidden can still allow
programmatic scrolling; clip does not establish the same scroll container. Changing one overflow axis can change
computed behavior of the other. A sticky element can attach to an unexpected scrolling ancestor. Reserve necessary
scrollbar space with scrollbar-gutter where supported. Do not hide overflow simply to conceal a layout bug or crop
focus indicators.

Positioning and paint order
Static participates in normal flow. Relative retains its place and offsets its box. Absolute is removed from normal flow
and positions against a containing block determined by layout rules. Fixed is often viewport-relative, but transformed or
containing ancestors can establish another containing block. Sticky participates in flow until constrained by the relevant
scroll container and inset; it needs room to move. Insets, opposing constraints, auto margins and intrinsic sizing interact
differently for each positioning mode.
A stacking context isolates descendant z-index ordering. Positioned elements with non-auto z-index, certain flex/grid
items, opacity, transforms, isolation and other effects can create contexts. A child with z-index 9999 cannot escape its
ancestor's stacking context. The browser top layer used by native dialogs and popovers is a different mechanism.
Transform changes visual geometry and can create containing blocks without changing the normal-flow allocation.

5 Flexbox in depth
Flexbox distributes items along one main axis, with an orthogonal cross axis. Direction maps row/column through
writing mode; row-reverse changes visual order, not DOM reading order. Flex-wrap creates independent lines. A
wrapped flex layout is not a two-dimensional grid with aligned tracks across rows.
The container controls display, flex-direction, flex-wrap, justify-content, align-items, align-content and gap. flex-flow
combines direction and wrapping. Justify-content distributes main-axis free space after flex sizing and auto margins;
align-items supplies cross-axis alignment defaults; align-self overrides an item; align-content distributes multiple lines
when there is cross-axis free space. Gap creates gutters between items and lines, not outer container padding.
The item controls order, flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, align-self and its minimum/maximum sizes. Flex basis
supplies the initial main-size input; auto can take the main-size property or content sizing. Grow factors distribute
positive free space, not a direct percentage width. Shrink factors are weighted by flex base sizes, so equal shrink
factors do not necessarily remove equal pixels. Constraints freeze items during the algorithm; inspect the resulting
sizes rather than relying on a one-step ratio.
flex: 1 commonly expands to grow 1, shrink 1 and a zero-percent basis in browsers; specification expansion details
matter when the container's size is indefinite. Use explicit flex: 1 1 0 when that basis is intended. flex: auto means
1 1 auto; flex: none means 0 0 auto. Automatic minimum sizes can prevent shrinking long tokens. An auto margin can
absorb free space before alignment distribution, making it useful for pushing an action group to the end.

  .toolbar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 0.75rem; }
  .toolbar__title { margin: 0; flex: 1 1 16rem; min-inline-size: 0; }
  .toolbar__actions { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem; margin-inline-start: auto; }

Real use cases: toolbars, wrapping action groups, media objects, one-dimensional navigation, and a page shell with
flexible main content. Avoid flex order for a logical sequence that differs between keyboard and visual traversal.
Align-items stretch does not force identical heights if item constraints prevent it. Percentage flex bases, min-content
and aspect ratio can interact in surprising ways.
Practice: build three cards with long URLs and different text lengths. Measure widths before and after min-inline-size:0.
Explain why gap is still present when justify-content changes and why align-content may have no visible effect on a
single line.
https://drafts.csswg.org/css-flexbox-1/

6 CSS Grid in depth
Grid defines two-dimensional tracks, lines, areas and gaps. Explicit tracks come from grid-template-columns/rows;
implicit tracks come from auto placement and grid-auto-columns/rows. Grid-template-areas names rectangular areas;
each named area must form a rectangle. A period marks an empty cell. Line names can repeat and line numbers can
be positive or negative relative to the explicit grid.
A track can use fixed lengths, percentages, intrinsic min-content/max-content, flexible fr units, minmax() and
fit-content(). repeat() compresses repeated track syntax; auto-fill retains empty repeated tracks while auto-fit collapses
appropriate empty tracks after placement. A flexible track's automatic minimum can preserve min-content width.
minmax(0, 1fr) removes that automatic track minimum, but the item may still need its own min-inline-size correction.

Grid-column and grid-row combine start/end lines. Grid-area can refer to a named area or four line positions. Spans
describe track counts or named-line relationships. Grid-auto-flow controls row/column placement and optional dense
packing. Dense packing can visually move later items into earlier holes; do not use it where the meaning depends on
source order. Overlap is legal and needs deliberate paint order.
The grid shorthand combines explicit/implicit settings and resets properties, so prefer longhands while learning. Gap
and alignment are separate: justify-items/align-items position items inside areas, justify-content/align-content position
the track collection inside the container. Self properties override item alignment. Auto margins can absorb space before
self-alignment. Baseline alignment depends on available baselines.

  .workbench { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr); gap: 1.5rem; }
  .workbench > * { min-inline-size: 0; }
  @media (width >= 60rem) {
    .workbench { grid-template-columns: minmax(15rem, 1fr) minmax(0, 3fr); }
  }
  .card-list {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr));
    gap: 1rem;
  }

Subgrid allows a nested grid to use its parent's track sizing in an axis; it is not ordinary inheritance of the grid-template
declaration. A subgrid needs to span the intended parent tracks and can retain its own gap behavior. Newer
masonry-like grid proposals have changed names and algorithms; do not equate a draft keyword in an index with a
stable production layout.
Practice: create a two-column workbench whose right panel contains a long code sample. Explain which track and item
minimums prevent page-wide overflow. Then compare a nested ordinary grid with subgrid for aligning card titles and
actions. Preserve DOM order at every viewport.
https://drafts.csswg.org/css-grid-2/

7 Responsive design, typography and visual systems
Constraints before breakpoints
Start with a usable narrow layout. Use intrinsic sizes, wrapping, max-inline-size, auto-fit, minmax and fluid spacing
before adding viewport conditions. Choose breakpoints where content needs a different arrangement, not by a list of
device brands. Media queries can test width, height, aspect ratio, orientation, resolution, hover, pointer, color scheme,
forced colors, reduced motion and print. Range syntax expresses bounds directly. Screen pixels, layout viewport, visual
viewport and device scale are distinct measurements.
Container queries respond to an ancestor query container rather than the whole page. Set container-type:inline-size on
a suitable wrapper; query a descendant. The queried element cannot freely query its own size to create a circular sizing
dependency. Name containers to avoid accidental ancestor selection. Size containment affects intrinsic sizing, so do
not add container-type everywhere.

  .module-host { container: learning-module / inline-size; }
  .module { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }
  @container learning-module (width >= 36rem) {
    .module { grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 2fr) minmax(0, 1fr); }
  }

A container query must have a useful base layout when unsupported. Style queries and scroll-state queries have their
own support and syntax boundaries. The property inventory includes their related names without treating them as a
universal baseline.

Typography and internationalization
Choose a robust font stack with a generic fallback. Font-family, size, weight, style, stretch/width, line-height and variant
features describe different dimensions. Variable-font axis settings are low-level; prefer high-level properties when they
express the requirement. Optical sizing depends on the font and feature. Font display is an @font-face descriptor, not
an element property. Font loading can change metrics and cause layout shifts; reserve space where appropriate and
use a deliberate fallback strategy.
Unitless line-height scales with the descendant's own font size when inherited. A computed length may inherit as that
length. Letter-spacing and word-spacing affect text fit and can impair scripts if applied indiscriminately. Use real
language metadata for hyphenation and language-sensitive line breaking. White-space, white-space-collapse,
text-wrap and overflow-wrap solve different problems. Text-overflow:ellipsis needs a constrained box and appropriate
overflow/white-space behavior; it does not expose the missing content to every user.
Support text resizing, 320 CSS-pixel reflow where applicable, user text spacing and long translations. Horizontal
scrolling can be appropriate for a code region or data table, but should not become page-wide scrolling for ordinary
content. Direction and writing-mode change logical axes, not the text's language. Do not use bidi controls or visual
order to falsify meaningful reading order.

Color, surfaces and states
Create semantic tokens for ink, surfaces, borders, focus, success, warning and error. A palette name alone does not
establish contrast. WCAG AA normally requires 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text; relevant non-text
component boundaries and indicators generally need 3:1 under the applicable criterion. Disabled/inactive controls have
exceptions, but must still be understandable. Alpha colors must be evaluated after compositing against actual surfaces.
Color contrast tools for sRGB are not enough to reason blindly about every wide-gamut composition.
Use color-scheme to communicate supported native-control modes when the page actually supports them.
prefers-color-scheme can provide an initial choice; an explicit user choice should persist according to product policy.
Test both schemes. In forced-colors mode, system colors and user-agent adjustments may override authored paint;
avoid disabling forced-color-adjust without a strong, tested reason.

delay, easing and behavior form coordinated lists; keyframe animations additionally have names, iteration counts,
direction, fill mode, play state, composition and timelines. Negative delays start partway through an effect; fill mode can
retain animated values outside the active interval. A zero duration does not make every animation event/lifecycle
assumption disappear.

rendering pipeline, paint effects and layer state determine cost. Avoid transition:all in components where unrelated
changes should be immediate. will-change is a temporary resource hint, not a universal optimization. Remove
long-lived hints when no longer needed. Respect prefers-reduced-motion and keep essential state changes
understandable without animation.

8 CSS architecture and production debugging
A stylesheet needs ownership rules. Tokens describe shared decisions; base styles cover low-specificity semantic
defaults; components own local appearance; utilities express intentional single-purpose overrides; state belongs to
actual DOM/API state. BEM is one naming convention, CSS Modules provide build-time naming isolation, and Shadow
DOM provides tree-scoped styling. None removes the need for accessible markup or a clear theme contract.
Use cascade layers to make override order explicit. A reset should be small and understood; a universal all:unset reset
can remove useful native behavior. Keep selectors shallow and stable. Avoid binding styles to incidental DOM depth or
database IDs. Scope tokens: public component custom properties are an API, while internal variables can be private by
convention but remain observable CSS. Document default values, valid types, inheritance and fallback behavior.
Adopt a spacing scale and semantic color system, but do not generate every possible class and variant. Keep layout
primitives reusable: stack, cluster, switcher and grid are compositions of standard layout rules rather than magic
framework features. Separate content-specific exceptions from shared primitives so a one-off page fix does not change
every card.
Build pipeline: pin compiler and framework versions; resolve modules; compile Sass; apply the chosen CSS
transformations and prefix strategy; minify; generate source maps according to deployment policy; hash assets; and
verify the actual shipped CSS. A Sass compiler does not automatically add vendor prefixes. A prefixer does not polyfill
Grid, container queries or a JavaScript API. CSS purging must understand dynamically generated class names and
state selectors; test the production bundle rather than only development output.
Debug a failure through six observations: authored source, matched rules, winning declarations, computed/resolved
values, layout geometry and actual interaction. In performance work, measure style recalculation, layout, paint and
compositing. Reading geometry after writing style can force synchronous layout; collect reads, compute once and batch
writes. A requestAnimationFrame callback alone does not eliminate forced layout if it alternates reads and writes
internally.
Acceptance exercises: diagnose a selector defeated by an unlayered framework; locate an automatic minimum causing
overflow; repair focus clipped by overflow; compare live state to a stale attribute; explain a transform-created fixed
containing block; and remove a DOM-order mismatch introduced with Grid placement. For each exercise, include a
deliberately broken variant and an observable test that fails before the repair.

9 Sass and SCSS: build-time programming for styles
Syntax, compilation and the runtime boundary
Sass names the language and tool ecosystem. SCSS uses braces and semicolons and largely follows CSS syntax; the
indented .sass syntax uses indentation and omits many delimiters. Both compile to CSS. Browsers do not execute
Sass variables, mixins, loops or module loading. A compiled stylesheet remains subject to ordinary CSS cascade,
inheritance, layout and browser support. Sass abstraction can improve maintenance, but it can also multiply selectors
and output size.
The examples target Dart Sass. LibSass, Node Sass and Ruby Sass are not appropriate baselines for new
module-based application code. Use the modern JavaScript API, compile/compileAsync or
compileString/compileStringAsync, rather than render/renderSync. Pin versions and retain a lockfile. Build errors
should fail CI; warnings need an owner and migration plan rather than permanent blanket suppression.
A standalone SCSS file is a compilation unit. Partials conventionally start with underscore and are loaded through
another entry point. A partial does not imply runtime lazy loading. Sass can emit expanded CSS for review and
compressed CSS for deployment. Source maps connect output back to source; expose them publicly only under a
deliberate deployment policy.

  // Input: spacing.scss
  $space: 0.75rem;
  .notice {
    padding: $space;
    margin-block-end: $space * 2;
  }

  /* Expanded compiled output */
  .notice {
    padding: 0.75rem;
    margin-block-end: 1.5rem;
  }

This eliminates duplicated source literals; it does not make the runtime CSS inherently faster. Changing $space
requires rebuilding. Changing a CSS custom property can affect the running page through the cascade.

Variables, scope and configuration
Sass variables hold typed compile-time values and are imperative: earlier declarations use the value that existed when
evaluated. Hyphens and underscores in Sass identifiers are treated equivalently in many names; avoid treating
$space-small and $space_small as separate public variables. Names are case-sensitive. Local lexical scope controls
availability; flow-control assignment has special scope behavior that should be tested when accumulating results.
!default assigns only when a variable is undefined or null, making it useful for library configuration. !global assigns a
global variable and has restrictions; it should not become the normal mechanism for communicating between modules.
A module configured with @use ... with must expose configurable !default variables, and configuration must occur
before that module's first load. A module is evaluated once per compilation under the module system.

  // _tokens.scss
  $space: 0.75rem !default;
  $ink: #172b4d !default;

  // app.scss: a separate file compiled with _tokens.scss present
  @use "tokens" with ($space: 1rem);
  .panel { padding: tokens.$space; color: tokens.$ink; }

and multiplying can produce compound units that cannot be emitted as an ordinary CSS length. Use math.div for
compile-time division. A slash can be a CSS separator, especially for grid lines and font size/line-height, so legacy /

Strings may be quoted or unquoted, and interpolation can remove quoting in ways that change emitted CSS meaning.
Lists have separators and optional brackets; a one-item list and its item may behave similarly in some contexts, but an
empty list and a map have special relationships. Maps associate keys with values and preserve the language's
collection rules. Null often omits a declaration or list contribution; false is a real boolean. All values except false and null
are truthy in Sass conditions, including zero and an empty string. Do not import JavaScript truthiness assumptions.

color.mix, color.channel and color.to-space with explicit intent. Older global lighten/darken or red/green/blue workflows

compositing. Functions and mixins can be first-class values through sass:meta; selectors can be manipulated through
sass:selector. Calculations can remain CSS calculation values rather than being reduced immediately.

compilation; @warn emits a warning without automatically failing; @debug prints diagnostic values. Production builds
should not depend on parsing debug text. Use the modern logger API when collecting diagnostics in tooling.

copying. Placeholder selectors beginning with % emit no selector until extended. Extension has scope rules across

can create unexpected combinations and move the apparent cascade effect to the extended rule's location.

for an exclusive upper bound. @each iterates lists or map key/value pairs and can destructure entries. @while repeats

10 Sass modules, built-ins and scalable architecture
@use, @forward and partials
@use loads a stylesheet once and exposes names under a namespace. It must obey ordering rules and precede
ordinary style rules, with allowed configuration declarations handled as defined. @forward re-exports a public API and
can show/hide members or add a prefix. Forwarding does not itself make members available locally; add @use if the
forwarding file also consumes them. Public module paths are part of a library's API. Leading underscore/hyphen
members are private under module rules.

  // abstracts/_tokens.scss
  $space: 1rem !default;

  // abstracts/_index.scss
  @forward "tokens";

  // components/_card.scss
  @use "../abstracts" as design;
  .card { padding: design.$space; }

  // app.scss
  @use "abstracts" with ($space: 1.25rem);
  @use "components/card";

  .card { padding: 1.25rem; }

Configure the tokens before any component indirectly loads them. A second @use with a different configuration is not
an independent module instance. Avoid CSS output in pure token modules so importing a dependency does not
unexpectedly emit base rules. Use package importers and documented load paths rather than fragile chains of
parent-directory traversal in published libraries.

The 7-1 pattern and alternatives
The 7-1 pattern places seven concerns under one entry point: abstracts, vendors, base, layout, components, pages
and themes. Abstracts contain non-emitting tokens/functions/mixins. Vendors contain adapters and integration entry
points rather than edited upstream source. Base contains resets and semantic defaults. Layout contains shared
arrangements. Components contain local UI styling. Pages contain real route-specific exceptions. Themes contain
deliberate theme contracts. The final entry point establishes order.
This is a convention, not a Sass feature. A small application can use fewer folders. A large design system may organize
by component package instead. Modern @use loading order and CSS cascade layers must be designed together;
folder names do not control runtime precedence. Runtime themes often belong in custom properties and data attributes
rather than separate compiled copies of every component.

  // main.scss; each referenced partial is an actual project dependency.
  @use "abstracts";
  @use "vendors";
  @use "base";
  @use "layout";
  @use "components";
  @use "pages";
  @use "themes";

This entry-point contract is illustrated fully in the accompanying module lab. Do not create empty architecture folders
solely to satisfy a diagram. A useful review asks which files emit CSS, which expose API and which may depend on
which others. Cyclic modules are architectural errors, not something to fix with repeated imports.

Built-in module map
• sass:math: numerical bounds, rounding, trigonometry, logarithms, random values, unit inspection and compatible-unit
   operations. Random compile-time values produce unstable output unless deliberately controlled outside Sass; avoid
   them for deterministic design tokens.
• sass:color: color-space-aware channel inspection, adjustment, scaling, mixing and conversion. Distinguish an
   absolute channel change from proportional scaling and verify rendered contrast.
• sass:string: quoting/unquoting, insertion, slicing, replacement through composition, indexing and identifiers. Sass
   indexing conventions differ from JavaScript's zero-based string APIs; inspect the specific function contract.
• sass:list: length, nth, set-nth, append, join, zip, index, separator and bracket inspection. A list's comma/space/slash
   separator affects emitted CSS.
• sass:map: get, has-key, keys, values, merge, remove, set and nested map operations, including deep operations
   where provided. Merging a map does not update derived maps that were already computed elsewhere.
• sass:selector: append, nest, extend, replace, unify, parse and superselector checks. Selector values are structured
   Sass lists; string concatenation is not a substitute for unification.
• sass:meta: type inspection, inspect, feature/tool introspection, function/mixin lookup and invocation, module member
   discovery and load-css. load-css emits CSS; it does not replace a clear @use public API or create access to private
   members.

What the framework provides
Bootstrap 5 combines Reboot defaults, typography/content styles, a responsive Flexbox grid, utilities, helpers, forms,
components and optional JavaScript plugins. It is utility-rich and component-oriented; calling it purely utility-first hides
the component selectors and runtime plugins that are central to the system. Bootstrap Icons is a separate project.

the non-bundle build needs the required dependency supplied separately.

CDN dependency. If using a CDN in a product, verify the exact URL and integrity hash together, include the appropriate
crossorigin setting and define the application's CSP. An integrity hash from a different version breaks loading. A
framework stylesheet does not supply HTML labels, meaningful content, server validation or a screen-reader-tested
interaction by itself.

bundled copy of the same plugins. Framework data APIs and a React/Vue state layer can conflict if both mutate the
same classes, attributes or children. Either let Bootstrap own its documented component lifecycle through a wrapper, or

larger widths until overridden. Breakpoints are configuration, not device detection.
.container provides width 100% with responsive max-widths: 540, 720, 960, 1140 and 1320px from sm through xxl.
.container-fluid remains 100% wide. .container-md, for example, is fluid below md, then uses responsive max-width
behavior from md upward. Container padding and gutters still matter; a max-width is not the final width of all nested
content. Custom Sass can change these values, so verify a customized build rather than assuming defaults.
Bootstrap's .container class is not a CSS query-container declaration. Its breakpoints are viewport media queries. For
a component that appears in a sidebar and a main panel, native container queries may express its layout more
accurately than adding more Bootstrap viewport classes.

The grid relationship is container, row, columns, then content. Rows use flex wrapping and gutter compensation;
columns provide padding. .col shares remaining space; .col-auto sizes to content; .col-1 through .col-12 allocate
fractions of the 12-column width. .col-12.col-md-6.col-xl-4 means full width, then half width, then one third.
.row-cols-1.row-cols-md-2 sets a default number of columns per row. A nested grid needs its own row inside an
existing column.

panel IDs; headings must remain meaningful. Alerts communicate messages; dismissible alerts need a labeled close

numbers the sole accessible name. Breadcrumbs use navigation labeling, a list and aria-current for the current item.
Buttons should be button elements for actions and anchors for navigation. Outline variants still require contrast checks.

headings, links, images and landmarks based on their actual content. Close buttons need an accessible label and
sufficient target area. List groups can be lists, navigation or actionable controls; mixing these arbitrarily changes
keyboard and screen-reader expectations.

anchor unless its behavior and focus are handled. Placeholders represent loading presentation and should not create
fake operable controls or repeated meaningless announcements. Progress markup in 5.3 puts progressbar semantics
and value attributes on the documented outer progress element; include a label and useful min/max/current values.
Spinners need a meaningful status strategy and reduced-motion consideration. Repeated decorative spinners should
not each announce the same loading state.

with component-specific methods. Configuration comes from defaults, data attributes and explicit options under the

as sanitization settings are restricted. Data attributes use the bs prefix and kebab-case. Do not assume an option
supported by one component exists on another.

shown.bs.modal or hidden.bs.offcanvas when completion matters. A call during an active transition can be ignored
according to the plugin contract. The show/hide events are often cancelable; shown/hidden report completion. Event

15 Symbiotic ecosystem: from source files to a running
interface
The lifecycle and ownership model
At build time, application SCSS loads modules, evaluates variables/functions/loops and emits CSS. Bootstrap Sass
can participate in that build or arrive as a precompiled dependency. At request time, HTML parsing creates DOM nodes
while linked CSS is fetched and parsed into stylesheets. Script execution can affect both trees. Style resolution
matches selectors, runs cascade/defaulting and computes values. Layout resolves geometry, paint produces drawing
commands and compositing combines relevant layers. Resource and font completion, viewport changes, user input
and DOM mutations can invalidate work. A rendering engine can optimize this pipeline, so the phases are a conceptual
model rather than a promise every mutation runs every phase.
A component has at least four representations: semantic DOM and native control state, application state, CSS state
and geometry, and accessibility exposure. A reliable implementation keeps them aligned. SCSS cannot observe
runtime DOM changes. A utility class cannot authorize a server operation. A JavaScript property change does not
always rewrite the corresponding HTML attribute. A visual state alone does not establish an accessible name or an
evaluation result. Animate theme paint cautiously: changing foreground immediately while a background slowly
transitions can create a low-contrast intermediate state. The lab changes foreground and background together.
Consider a practice-card disclosure. HTML supplies a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls and a region with
hidden. JavaScript owns opening and closing, updating the two states together. CSS derives its arrow presentation
from aria-expanded. A live region can announce a meaningful result if the workflow needs it. Sass can generate the
shared styles, and Bootstrap could supply a different collapse controller, but both controllers should not own the same
region simultaneously.

HTML attributes, pseudo-classes and custom properties
Use native attributes such as disabled, required, checked and hidden when their semantics match the intended
behavior. Boolean attributes are true by presence: disabled="false" remains disabled. Attribute selectors test serialized
content; pseudo-classes can test current native state. A checkbox's checked property can differ from its checked
attribute after user interaction. :checked follows current state. A data attribute is an application-defined string, not a
browser-enforced permission. CSS custom properties carry style tokens and normally inherit; they are not private
storage.
ARIA state may be a useful style hook when application behavior keeps it truthful. [aria-expanded="true"] is
appropriate for styling an actual expanded control; it does not expand a region itself. aria-hidden does not automatically
remove focusability and can create a hidden-but-focusable interface. The hidden attribute and display rules interact;
author CSS that overrides [hidden] can accidentally reveal content. The integrated labs explicitly keep [hidden] {
display:none !important; } as a narrowly owned application rule.

ClassList manages tokens without replacing unrelated classes. Toggle with an explicit boolean rather than inverting
uncertain state repeatedly. Use style.setProperty for an intentional custom-property update; do not replace the entire
style attribute. Keep untrusted strings out of CSS URLs, selectors and declarations. CSS.escape escapes identifiers for
selector construction; it is not a universal CSS sanitizer.

CSSOM, resolved style and geometry
Document.styleSheets and CSSStyleSheet expose stylesheet objects, subject to origin restrictions. Reading cssRules
from a cross-origin sheet can fail. element.style sees inline declarations, not all matching styles. getComputedStyle
returns resolved values after cascade; it can require pending style/layout work. getBoundingClientRect reports a
viewport-relative rectangle including transforms and may be fractional. offsetWidth and clientWidth measure different
boxes and round differently. Scroll sizes describe scrollable overflow, not semantic content completeness.

polling
ResizeObserver reports observed element box sizes, including changes caused by layout or content rather than a
window resize. Choose content-box, border-box or device-pixel-content-box where supported and appropriate.
ResizeObserverEntry exposes different measurements; box-size collections can represent fragments. inlineSize and

fragment as a total across all fragments without declaring that assumption.

observation and a loop warning. requestAnimationFrame can move work to a later frame but does not resolve an
unstable feedback equation by itself. Prefer observing a container and updating a non-sizing output, or compute an
idempotent bounded result. Disconnect when the component is no longer owned; unobserve individual targets when
appropriate.

  // Complete controller; output is a separate non-sizing text node in the page.
  function reportWidth(target, output) {
    if (typeof globalThis.ResizeObserver !== 'function') {
      output.textContent = 'Automatic measurement is unavailable.';
      return () => {};
    }
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
      const entry = entries.find(item => item.target === target);
      if (!entry) return;
      const text = `${Math.round(entry.contentRect.width)} CSS px wide`;
      if (output.textContent !== text) output.textContent = text;
    });
    observer.observe(target, { box: 'content-box' });
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }

should handle presentational layout changes; an observer is justified when application logic needs actual
measurement, canvas backing size or integration with a non-CSS system.

Attribute filters reduce noise; old-value options preserve selected prior values. It does not directly observe every form
property change, computed style change, layout change or stylesheet-driven visual transition. An input.value
assignment can occur without a value-attribute mutation. A media query can change appearance with no DOM
mutation.
Callbacks are delivered asynchronously through the specified microtask machinery and can contain multiple records.
Treat records as evidence of mutations, then read the current relevant state; do not assume every record is a complete
historical application state. Avoid observing an attribute and rewriting it unconditionally in the same callback.
Disconnect before teardown, and use takeRecords deliberately when queued records matter.

  // Complete observer utility for third-party markup integration.
  function watchExpanded(button, onState) {
    const read = () => onState(button.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true');
    const observer = new MutationObserver(read);
    observer.observe(button, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['aria-expanded'] });
    read();
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }

When your application already owns the state, update the dependent state directly rather than creating an observer to
rediscover your own writes. This utility is useful at a genuine integration boundary. Native input/change events,
ResizeObserver, font-loading events and transition/animation events answer different questions. Select the observation
based on the fact needed, not based on familiarity with one API.
Practice: change a class that changes width, assign input.value and append a child. Predict which mutation records
exist and which visible changes need another source of evidence. Include a test that would fail if the observer were

19 View Transitions API: preserving the update
contract
A same-document view transition captures visual states around a DOM update callback, builds a transition
pseudo-element tree and animates the change where supported. Cross-document transitions use a different opt-in and
navigation lifecycle. A view-transition-name pairs elements and must meet uniqueness rules within the relevant
capture. The generated pseudo-elements include root, group, image-pair, old and new layers. Styling them is different
from styling the live element itself.
The application update must work when the API is absent, capture is skipped, names conflict or the user prefers
reduced motion. Distinguish updateCallbackDone, ready and finished promises; a visual transition can fail while the
DOM update succeeds. Do not run a mutating update twice in a catch handler after it already ran. Track whether the
update began before deciding on a fallback.

  // Complete helper for a synchronous, idempotent DOM update.
  async function updateView(update) {
    const reduced = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
    if (!document.startViewTransition || reduced) {
      update();
      return;
    }
    let began = false;
    let transition;
    try {
      transition = document.startViewTransition(() => {
        began = true;
        update();
      });
    } catch (error) {
      if (!began) update();
      else throw error;
      return;
    }
    // Consume capture failures separately from the application's update result.
    transition.ready.catch(() => {});
    const finished = transition.finished.catch(() => {});
    await transition.updateCallbackDone;
    await finished;
  }

The helper's update must be synchronous and should not perform a network mutation; the lab uses it only to toggle a
local presentation theme. If update throws, the caller receives the rejection and must report the actual application
failure. An API fallback must not swallow server errors and pretend an action succeeded. Focus and announcements
need their own policy; a transition screenshot is not a new accessible document.

  ::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) {
    animation-duration: 150ms;
  }
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    ::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) { animation: none; }
  }

Practice: test absent API, reduced motion, duplicate element names and a rejected update callback. Assert one
application update, correct final state and no unhandled rejection. Then test keyboard focus before and after the
transition independently of the animation.

20 Custom Elements, Shadow DOM and style contracts
Custom elements define a lifecycle for valid hyphenated element names. Construction, connection, disconnection,
observed attribute changes, adoption and supported state-preserving moves have distinct roles. A constructor should
initialize its own structure without assuming attributes/children are already fully parsed. connectedCallback can run
more than once; guard initialization and make resource setup repeatable. disconnectedCallback releases listeners,
observers, timers and other resources. A reconnection should restore needed resources without duplicating the
shadow tree.
Shadow DOM scopes selectors and retargets events under defined rules. It is not a security boundary for hostile code.
A closed shadow root changes access conventions; it does not isolate an attacker's script. A host remains part of the
outer tree; inherited values and custom properties can cross into shadow content through inheritance. Global selectors
do not simply reach internal buttons. Use :host, ::part and documented custom properties for a deliberate public styling
API.
A slot projects light-DOM children without moving their ownership into the shadow tree. ::slotted applies to assigned
elements under its limited selector model; it cannot arbitrarily select deeply nested projected descendants. slotchange
reports assignment changes, not every mutation inside an already assigned node. Shared constructable stylesheets
and adoptedStyleSheets can reduce repeated sheet creation where supported; a shared stylesheet mutation affects
every adopter, so ownership and fallback handling matter.
The integrated learning-panel element exposes a named title slot and a panel part, accepts a tone attribute, and
reads --panel-accent as a theme token. Its internal button is a real button with aria-expanded and a controlled hidden
region. It uses an AbortController for connection-owned listeners, disconnects its observer on removal and restores
resources on reconnection. Unsupported APIs leave a usable basic disclosure or slot content rather than blocking the
whole page.
Form-associated custom elements require explicit ElementInternals participation, form value/validity and accessibility
design. Merely naming a tag input-like does not make it submit. CustomStateSet/:state can express supported custom
states; it is separate from defining an aria attribute. Avoid duplicating native controls unless the design requirement
justifies the additional keyboard, form and accessibility work.

21 High-performance interaction and accessible
runtime behavior
Batch geometry reads before style writes. Cache results only for a known validity window; font loading, zoom, content
changes and container changes can invalidate them. requestAnimationFrame schedules work near rendering, but it
does not make an expensive read-write loop free. Avoid observing every element with every API merely because the
APIs are available.
Use CSS for declarative layout and known visual states; use JavaScript for state transitions and facts CSS cannot
express. Prefer a single state owner. A server result can update a status region, but visual success styling must not
precede actual success. Respect pending/error/empty states. Fetch cancellation does not undo a completed server
mutation; idempotency and authorization belong to the receiver.
Separate geometry from semantics: a ResizeObserver can choose a canvas resolution but does not decide an
accessible name. A MutationObserver can report a changed attribute but does not prove the intended state transition
occurred. A CSS transitionend event can be absent when duration is zero, a property does not transition, the node is
removed or the transition is canceled. Do not make essential cleanup depend exclusively on an event that may never
arrive; use the component's authoritative lifecycle and bounded fallbacks.
IntersectionObserver can defer nonessential work until visibility conditions are met, but it is not proof that a human read
content. FontFaceSet readiness can help coordinate measurements, but fonts can be loaded later. matchMedia
change listeners can follow user preference changes and need removal during teardown. The Web Animations API
exposes animation objects and promises, with cancellation behavior that differs from simply removing a CSS class.
CSS.supports is a parsing/capability check, not a browser bug detector or accessibility test.
Performance exercise: append 100 practice rows in a fragment, then apply a class once. Compare with a loop that
reads each row's geometry immediately after inserting it. Record actual browser trace durations on representative
hardware; do not assert a fixed speedup. Use content-visibility only after verifying search, keyboard navigation, scroll
position and placeholder sizing in the target engines.

The complete lab sources follow in the document. They use local Bootstrap assets and compile-time Sass

viewport, title and semantic document structure. API demonstrations use progressive enhancement. Small snippets

imaginary endpoints.

Lab A: responsive learning workbench
Build a semantic page with a skip link, header, main content, a filter form, a result list and a help disclosure. Use Grid
for the page and card list, Flexbox for action clusters, logical properties, intrinsic constraints and rem-based bounds.
Keep labels visible and update an existing status node after explicit filtering. Test 320, 768 and 1280 CSS-pixel widths,
long labels and zero results. Verify source order and keyboard behavior before visual polish.

Lab B: Bootstrap review flow
Use the pinned full Bootstrap CSS and bundle, a responsive container/row/column layout, cards, a native validation
form, an accordion and a review modal. The modal displays a local summary and performs no payment or account
operation. Verify its label, focus entry, close action, Escape and focus return. Keep dark-mode support explicit. Test

then disconnect and reconnect the host. A theme button uses the guarded view-transition helper. Typed OM is
attempted only where available with a string fallback. Verify cleanup by reconnecting and ensuring one listener
response per click. Rendering should remain usable without the advanced APIs.

Lab D: Sass source-to-output workshop
Compile independent examples for variables, nesting, mixins/content, functions, placeholders, loops, interpolation,
maps and module configuration. Assert generated selectors and selected declarations, then test deliberate invalid
argument cases. Compile a selected Bootstrap customization build and inspect the generated utility family and theme
class. Keep dependency deprecations visible in the evidence report.

Score semantic correctness, state correctness, layout robustness, maintainability, performance evidence and
accessibility evidence separately. A learner who chooses Grid rather than Flexbox can be correct if the requirements
and observable behavior hold. A screenshot match with incorrect reading order is not a passing solution. A successful
compile says nothing about whether the UI is usable with a keyboard.

Production acceptance sequence
1. Confirm requirements: content order, devices/input modes, supported engines, languages, themes and WCAG
target. 2. Build reproducibly: lock dependencies, compile all entries, review warnings, inspect output size and
production asset loading. 3. Validate semantics: headings, regions, labels, unique IDs, real control states, meaningful
alternatives and actual form payloads. 4. Verify layout: narrow viewport, zoom/reflow, long text, localization, RTL,
missing assets, fonts and overflow boundaries. 5. Verify interactions: keyboard paths, focus visibility, modal cleanup,
repeated actions, pending/error states and teardown/reconnection. 6. Verify accessibility: automated rules plus manual
screen-reader, contrast, focus, target-size, reduced-motion and forced-color checks appropriate to the product. 7.
Measure performance: representative content/hardware, trace style/layout/paint, investigate long tasks and check
layout shifts. 8. Record evidence: exact source/package versions, source hashes, test commands, observed results,
untested conditions and accepted tradeoffs. Retest after material changes.

contrast, resize/reflow, text spacing, non-text contrast, keyboard operation, focus order/visibility/not-obscured, target
size, labels/instructions, error identification, name/role/value and status messages. Additional criteria can apply to the
actual product; this list is a training map rather than a complete conformance audit.

BOOTSTRAP 5 4 Boxes, normal flow and positioning The box model and intrinsic sizing The content box is surrounded by padding, border and margin. With content-box, declared width describes content; with border-box it includes padding and border. Margin remains outside both. Minimum and maximum sizes constrain preferred sizes, and intrinsic contributions constrain layout even when percentages or flexible tracks are used. Set border-box consistently on elements and pseudo-elements rather than assuming it is inherited automatically. *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } img, video { max-inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto; } .prose { max-inline-size: 70ch; overflow-wrap: anywhere; } width: 100% plus padding can overflow under content-box. min-inline-size: 0 can allow a flex or grid child to shrink below its automatic minimum; it should be applied to the actual constrained child, not scattered through the whole application. overflow-wrap: anywhere affects intrinsic sizing differently from legacy break-word behavior. A fixed height is rarely a good answer to varying text, translation or zoom. Margins can be negative and vertical margins can collapse in ordinary block flow under defined conditions. Padding cannot be negative and does not collapse. A new block formatting context, including flow-root, changes float interaction and margin behavior. Inline formatting has line boxes and baselines; vertical margins on non-replaced inline boxes do not create block spacing. Replaced elements have intrinsic dimensions and aspect ratios. Tables and ruby have specialized rules. Logical properties express block/inline directions from writing-mode and direction. Use margin-inline-start, padding-block, inline-size and inset-inline-end where the intention is logical.

Display, overflow and hiding Display has outer and inner behavior: block versus inline participation, and flow/flex/grid/table layout within. inline-flex is inline outside and flex inside. Display none removes boxes; visibility hidden generally retains layout space; opacity zero still allows focus and hit testing unless other state changes intervene. content-visibility can skip rendering work subject to containment, and requires care around intrinsic sizes and offscreen content. display: contents removes the principal box but has accessibility and context-specific consequences; test rather than assuming it preserves all semantics identically. Overflow visible, hidden, clip, scroll and auto differ in clipping and scroll-container behavior. Hidden can still allow programmatic scrolling; clip does not establish the same scroll container. Changing one overflow axis can change computed behavior of the other. A sticky element can attach to an unexpected scrolling ancestor. Reserve necessary scrollbar space with scrollbar-gutter where supported. Do not hide overflow simply to conceal a layout bug or crop focus indicators. Absolute is removed from normal flow and positions against a containing block determined by layout rules. Cascade origin and importance then outrank layer order and specificity. In ascending priority the broad origin order is normal user-agent rules, normal user rules, normal author rules, keyframe animation values, important author rules, important user rules, important user-agent rules and active transition values. Encapsulation contexts and inline declarations add defined tie-breaks. Within the same cascade level, normal unlayered author rules outrank normal layered rules; later normal layers outrank earlier ones. Important layer order reverses, so early important layers outrank later ones, and layered important declarations outrank unlayered important declarations. Use importance sparingly and account for user overrides. Specificity is a tuple: IDs; classes/attributes/pseudo-classes; types/pseudo-elements. Compare left to right, never by a decimal score. Combinators and the universal selector add no weight. :where() has zero specificity including its arguments. :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument. :nth-child(... of S) adds its pseudo-class weight and the most specific selector in S. Inline styles occupy a separate precedence position, not a magical ID score. After specificity ties, scope proximity can matter before source order under @scope rules. Historical Snapshot names outside the current property records
The following names occur in the Snapshot index but have no current non-vendor property record in this retrieved Webref dataset.
They are retained for audit and migration, not assigned invented current grammar or browser support. Historical CSS2 aural names
are particularly unsuitable as a way to control a modern screen reader.
• azimuth: Historical aural source direction; specialized speech output has a different modern voice model. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-azimuth
• elevation: Historical aural source elevation; not a visual transform or current universal speech setting. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-elevation
• pitch: Historical aural pitch; compare voice-pitch in the modern speech module. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-pitch
• pitch-range: Historical aural pitch variation; compare voice-range where a speech renderer implements it. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-pitch-range
• play-during: Historical aural background sound; use explicit user-controlled media rather than assuming this is a browser audio
API. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-play-during
• property-name: An index placeholder rather than a concrete authoring property; do not write property-name as a universal
configurable setting. Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#propdef-property-name
• richness: Historical aural voice richness; no ordinary screen-reader styling guarantee. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-richness
• speak-header: Historical aural table-header repetition; actual table semantics and assistive technology behavior remain essential.
Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-header
• speak-numeral: Historical aural number pronunciation; do not depend on it for accessible mathematical content. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-numeral
• speak-punctuation: Historical aural punctuation pronunciation; document semantics and AT preferences control real reading
behavior. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-punctuation
• speech-rate: Historical aural rate; compare voice-rate only in a verified speech-CSS environment. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speech-rate
• stress: Historical aural stress setting; not a text-decoration control. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-stress
• volume: Historical aural volume; actual HTMLMediaElement volume and user controls are separate. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-volume

@use loads a module; @forward re-exports an API; @mixin/@include declare and invoke emitting abstractions; @function/@return
compute values; @extend unifies selector relationships; @if/@else choose branches; @each/@for/@while generate bounded
output; @at-root controls nesting context; @debug/@warn/@error report diagnostics. @content inserts a caller block and can pass
arguments to using. Sass @import is a deprecated dependency mechanism with legacy scope behavior; a preserved CSS @import
has different browser/network behavior. CSS at-rules such as @media, @supports, @layer, @container, @keyframes and
@font-face are emitted according to Sass nesting/interpolation and CSS parsing rules. Silent // comments disappear; block
comments can survive according to output mode and preservation rules.
Private module members, configuration, rest/keyword arguments, list/map destructuring, parent-selector values, placeholder
selectors, interpolation, calculations, built-in modules and the modern importer/function/logger APIs complete the major
language/tooling surface taught here. A public library should document argument names because callers can use keyword
arguments. Passing an argument list can preserve keywords; meta.keywords can inspect them. @content using makes argument
transfer explicit.
