29 Complete runnable lab source
Create the files under one lab directory, preserving the filenames shown below. Use Node.js 22.18 or a compatible
maintained Node runtime. Install the pinned Sass and Bootstrap dependencies locally. Copy Bootstrap distribution
assets into vendor as shown; its license is retained with the copied assets. Launch a local static server and open the
named HTML files. The labs have no remote data endpoint and perform no account, payment or persistent server
mutation.
The Markdown is the canonical source for copying code. The PDF visually wraps long lines to fit the page; do not treat
a printed line wrap inside a string as a required source newline. Bootstrap minified distribution files are installed, not
reproduced as thousands of opaque lines. All authored lab source is included.

  npm init -y
  npm install --save-exact sass@1.105.2 bootstrap@5.3.8
  mkdir -p vendor
  cp node_modules/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css vendor/bootstrap.min.css
  cp node_modules/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js vendor/bootstrap.bundle.min.js
  cp node_modules/bootstrap/LICENSE vendor/BOOTSTRAP-LICENSE.txt
  npx sass --load-path=node_modules bootstrap-custom.scss bootstrap-custom.css
  python3 -m http.server 8080

Visit http://localhost:8080/workbench.html, http://localhost:8080/bootstrap.html and http://localhost:8080/apis.html. The
local server is a development convenience; deploy through the application's actual secure asset pipeline. The selected
custom Bootstrap stylesheet is a separate compilation exercise and is not a replacement for the full framework CSS
used by the component lab.

record.document:
Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: embedded-python; runtime: micropython
Python (embedded) · pin interrupts on MicroPython boards · creation · L2
Concept: Bind the loop variable with a default argument when you create handlers in a loop
Misconception: A lambda created in a loop remembers the value the variable had at that moment.
Explanation: A closure captures the variable and not its value, so after the loop every handler sees the last value. A default argument is evaluated when the lambda is created, so lambda p, i=i: freezes the current index. The same applies to callbacks given to Timer and to asyncio tasks.
Incorrect:
from machine import Pin
hits_bad = []
pins_bad = [Pin(20 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
    pins_bad[i].irq(lambda p: hits_bad.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
from machine import Pin
hits = []
pins = [Pin(30 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
    pins[i].irq(lambda p, i=i: hits.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Complexity: O(n)

Separate framework sections share a common foundation, practice model and verification register. 1 Purpose, boundaries and learning routes This curriculum follows the earlier HTML and CSS/Sass/Bootstrap material: mental model first, mechanism second, complete implementation third, then failure diagnosis and evidence. It teaches how to reason about a framework rather than memorize attractive snippets. Readers should already understand semantic HTML, the cascade, flex/grid, JavaScript events and basic React before the React-specific chapters. Tailwind CSS is a utility compiler and design-token interface. Bulma is a CSS component and layout framework whose interaction code belongs to the application. shadcn/ui distributes source-owned components and supporting tooling; its behavioral dependencies and chosen primitive base remain essential. Calling all three interchangeable CSS libraries obscures these differences. “Comprehensive” here means a structured treatment of the major shipped concepts, utility families, Bulma modules and shadcn component categories, with focused API records and working labs. Arbitrary values, generated permutations, third-party registries, commercial products and future releases cannot form a finite exhaustive list. The catalogue explains their grammar and extension points. Verify the installed source before accepting an unlisted prop or class. A complete beginner follows chapters in order after the HTML/CSS prerequisites. A framework switcher starts with the comparison and reproduces the same study dashboard in each system. An experienced interview candidate completes the debugging cases and explains the underlying CSS/DOM behavior without relying on framework vocabulary. All routes use the same acceptance criteria; experience changes pacing, not correctness. Each topic should be learned through fourteen lenses: purpose, mental model, setup, syntax, composition, state, layout, responsive behavior, tokens, accessibility, performance, failure modes, appropriate use and verification. A visual match alone cannot demonstrate a correct component. This is candidate reference and practice material. It has not been ingested into the application or approved as an automatically graded curriculum. Tested examples are explicitly separated from conceptual exercises. Browser checks cover the recorded Chrome environment; manual screen-reader and cross-browser checks remain necessary. A technical curriculum for front-end engineers, instructors and AI mentors
1 Scope, learning routes and evidence
CSS describes presentation; HTML describes structure and meaning; JavaScript coordinates behavior. Sass is a
build-time language that emits CSS. Bootstrap is a collection of CSS conventions, Sass sources, components and
JavaScript plugins. Understanding their separate responsibilities is essential to using them together. A working page is
the output of the entire system, including browser algorithms, assets, fonts, input devices and user preferences.
This guide follows the earlier HTML curriculum's format: mental model, precise reference, concrete example, common
mistake, practice and evidence. It has four main subject areas: CSS fundamentals and architecture, Sass/SCSS,
Bootstrap 5, and their runtime integration with the DOM and Web APIs. The reference appendices supply property
metadata and additional inventories so that the narrative remains teachable rather than becoming an unstructured list
of names.
Version boundary. CSS3 is a historical umbrella name. Modern CSS consists of independently versioned modules.
The CSS property appendix covers every non-vendor property record in the retrieved W3C Webref package, including
advanced, SVG, print, speech and experimental proposals. Records in the CSS Snapshot 2025 property index are
identified; inclusion in either source is not a browser-support guarantee. The Snapshot index itself includes historical
names. Draft-only entries are research references, not blanket production recommendations. Vendor compatibility
aliases and historical aural properties receive separate treatment. Custom properties are an open-ended family.
The package versions and source hashes are recorded in the verification appendix. Bootstrap examples target 5.3.8.
Sass examples use Dart Sass 1.105.2. Living specifications and versioned package sources can differ: a new grammar
alternative in a draft may be unsupported by all target browsers. Feature detection proves only the specific condition
tested. A valid declaration can still be ineffective in the current layout context.
Accessibility boundary. The examples use semantic controls, visible labels, keyboard paths, contrast-conscious
colors, responsive reflow and motion preferences. The target is WCAG 2.2 AA, including applicable A criteria. An
isolated stylesheet or an automated scan cannot certify an entire experience as WCAG compliant. The verification
record states which compilation, browser and automated accessibility checks were actually run; manual screen-reader,
zoom, forced-color and cross-engine testing remain explicit acceptance work. Small syntax examples are complete
rules or complete functions; the integrated labs supply runnable documents and their actual dependencies.
Common curriculum, different entry points
 • Foundations: learn cascade, computed values, boxes, normal flow and source order before layout abstractions.
 • Layout: practice intrinsic sizing, Flexbox and Grid, then responsive constraints and component queries.
 • Maintainability: introduce tokens, layers, naming, Sass modules and generated utilities after the plain CSS behavior is
 understood.
• Framework use: map Bootstrap classes to the CSS they emit, then study component state and plugin ownership.
 • Runtime integration: connect DOM state and browser APIs to style changes with cleanup, fallbacks and measured
 performance.
• Assessment: explain a failure, predict the computed result, inspect evidence, repair the cause and test a
 counterexample. Do not award mastery for matching a screenshot alone.
Fourteen teaching lenses
For every lesson ask: what is the mental model; how is the rule created; how is its target selected; what changes its
value; how do nodes enter or leave; what is the traversal order; what establishes identity; what orders competing rules;
what transforms specified values; what work does the renderer perform; what happens at boundaries; which alternative
fits; which reusable pattern emerges; and which observation proves the claim? Apply these to CSS rather than
inventing algorithmic complexity claims for a selector or framework class.

2 CSS grammar, values and the cascade
Rules and parsing
A qualified rule combines a selector list with a declaration block. A declaration contains a property, colon, value and
optional importance flag. An at-rule has a name, prelude and either a semicolon or a block. Comments are removed
during tokenization. Unrecognized declarations are generally discarded individually; an invalid selector can invalidate
an ordinary selector list. Forgiving selector lists have specifically defined recovery behavior. Parsing recovery is not a
guarantee that an intended design survives.
/* Complete stylesheet fragment. */
.notice {
  color: #172b4d;
  background-color: #fff;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 0.125rem solid currentColor;
}
@media (width >= 48rem) {
  .notice { padding: 1.5rem; }
}
Browser devtools distinguishes a rule that never matched, a matched declaration that lost the cascade, an invalid value
and a winning value with no visible effect. Debug in that order. Do not respond to every unexpected result by adding
!important.
https://drafts.csswg.org/css-syntax-3/
Grammar notation and acceptable value types
In the property appendix, | means choose one alternative; || permits one or more alternatives in any order; && requires
every component in any order; juxtaposition requires sequence. Square brackets group grammar, not literal brackets. ?
means optional, * zero or more, + one or more, # a comma-separated list, and {m,n} a repetition range. Quoted
property references such as <'margin-top'> mean use that property's value grammar. Angle-bracket names refer to
defined types, not literal markup. Ranges such as <number [0,1]> constrain the value. Consult the defining module for
computed-value restrictions and newer syntax.
An identifier is not automatically a string; an unquoted family name can have different parsing rules from a quoted font
name. <custom-ident> excludes reserved identifiers in its context. <dashed-ident> starts with two hyphens. Strings use
quotes and escapes. URLs use URL syntax and must still satisfy application security policy. Images include raster
resources, gradients and supported generated images. Colors include named values, hex, rgb/hsl and modern color
spaces where supported. currentColor connects many paint values to the element's color.
Numbers can be unitless or have dimensions. Lengths include px, em, rem, ch, ex, lh, rlh, viewport units and container
query units. A CSS pixel is a reference unit, not necessarily a physical device pixel. em in font-size relates to the parent;
in many other properties it relates to the element's font size. rem uses the root font size. ch measures a font's zero
advance and is useful for approximate line lengths, not exact character counts. Angles include deg, rad, grad and turn;
times include s and ms; resolutions include dppx and dpi. Zero-length unit omission is contextual and must not be
transferred to time or arbitrary typed values.
Percentages resolve against a property-specific reference. Width, height, padding, transforms, backgrounds and gaps
do not share one universal percentage base. An indefinite containing size can change how a percentage participates in
layout. fr is a Grid flexible track unit, not a general length. auto, normal, none, initial and zero are not
interchangeable.
calc() combines compatible dimensions. min() and max() choose bounds; clamp() constrains a preferred value. Keep
spaces around binary plus/minus in calc expressions. Multiplication/division support depends on the CSS Values level;
do not assume Sass arithmetic and browser arithmetic have the same rules. Intrinsic keywords such as min-content,
max-content, fit-content and stretch are context-sensitive sizing requests.

The fluid font retains rem bounds. Test browser text scaling; a viewport-only size can defeat the intended enlargement.
Small/large/dynamic viewport units address different mobile viewport states; dynamic units can change while browser

https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-4/
Cascade precedence, specificity and source order
First determine relevance: selector match, media condition, feature condition, scope and tree. Cascade origin and
importance then outrank layer order and specificity. In ascending priority the broad origin order is normal user-agent
rules, normal user rules, normal author rules, keyframe animation values, important author rules, important user rules,
important user-agent rules and active transition values. Encapsulation contexts and inline declarations add defined
tie-breaks. Within the same cascade level, normal unlayered author rules outrank normal layered rules; later normal
layers outrank earlier ones. Important layer order reverses, so early important layers outrank later ones, and layered
important declarations outrank unlayered important declarations. Use importance sparingly and account for user
overrides.
Specificity is a tuple: IDs; classes/attributes/pseudo-classes; types/pseudo-elements. Compare left to right, never by a
decimal score. Combinators and the universal selector add no weight. :where() has zero specificity including its
arguments. :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument. :nth-child(... of S) adds
its pseudo-class weight and the most specific selector in S. Inline styles occupy a separate precedence position, not a
magical ID score. After specificity ties, scope proximity can matter before source order under @scope rules.
Examples: .card a is (0,1,1); [aria-expanded="true"] is (0,1,0); #app .card is (1,1,0); :where(#app) .card is (0,1,0);
:is(.card, #special) button is (1,0,1). Putting an ID in an unused branch of :is can still raise the rule's specificity.
@layer reset, vendor, tokens, base, components, utilities;
@layer base {
  :where(button, input, select, textarea) { font: inherit; }
}

Mixins and content blocks
A mixin emits declarations or rules and can accept positional, named, default and rest arguments. Use @include to
invoke it. A function returns a value and should not emit unrelated rules. Content blocks let the caller provide rules at a
controlled insertion point. Arguments passed to @content require a matching using clause. A content block's lexical
scope belongs to its declaration site; it does not implicitly inherit every local variable from inside the mixin.
@mixin focus-ring($color: #111, $offset: 0.2rem) {
  &:focus-visible {
    outline: 0.1875rem solid $color;
    outline-offset: $offset;

  @media (min-width: $width) { @content; }
}

  display: grid;
  @include at-width(48rem) { grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; }
}

  outline: 0.1875rem solid #111;
  outline-offset: 0.2rem;

.layout { display: grid; }
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; }

semantic mixin name such as focus-ring conveys intent; a mixin that merely renames one property often adds little
value. Validate public parameters with @error so invalid configuration fails early.

Functions and diagnostics
User functions use @function and @return. Keep them deterministic with clear input types and units. @error aborts
compilation; @warn emits a warning without automatically failing; @debug prints diagnostic values. Production builds
should not depend on parsing debug text. Use the modern logger API when collecting diagnostics in tooling.
@use "sass:math";
@function space($step, $unit: 0.25rem) {
  @if not math.is-unitless($step) { @error "space step must be unitless"; }
  @if $step < 0 { @error "space step must be nonnegative"; }
  @return $step * $unit;
}
.panel { padding: space(4); gap: space(3); }
.panel {
  padding: 1rem;
  gap: 0.75rem;
}
A numerical type check should precede arithmetic when exposing this to arbitrary library consumers; the example's
contract is a numeric step. For stronger public APIs use meta.type-of and math.is-unitless together. The complete lab
includes that validation. Sass does not perform unit conversion between arbitrary relative units such as em and rem,
because their runtime bases can differ.
@extend and placeholders
@extend unifies selectors so the extending selector matches rules associated with an existing selector. It is not textual
copying. Placeholder selectors beginning with % emit no selector until extended. Extension has scope rules across
modules and at-rules; extending inside a media query cannot freely alter unrelated rules outside it. Selector unification
can create unexpected combinations and move the apparent cascade effect to the extended rule's location.
%surface {
  background: #fff;
  border: 0.0625rem solid #526170;
}
.card { @extend %surface; padding: 1rem; }
.notice { @extend %surface; padding: 0.75rem; }
.notice, .card {
  background: #fff;
  border: 0.0625rem solid #526170;
}
.card { padding: 1rem; }
.notice { padding: 0.75rem; }
Choose @extend for a real selector-level semantic relationship and inspect the resulting selector list. Choose a mixin
for parameterized output, a utility class for an explicit markup composition, and a custom property for runtime theming.
!optional can suppress an absent-target extension error, but it can also hide a broken dependency; it should not be a
blanket setting.
Control directives and bounded generation
@if/@else conditionally emit based on compile-time values. @for can use through for an inclusive upper bound or to
for an exclusive upper bound. @each iterates lists or map key/value pairs and can destructure entries. @while repeats
until a condition becomes false and needs an explicit terminating state change. These constructs run during
compilation, not when a user clicks.

10 Sass modules, built-ins and scalable architecture
@use, @forward and partials
@use loads a stylesheet once and exposes names under a namespace. It must obey ordering rules and precede
ordinary style rules, with allowed configuration declarations handled as defined. @forward re-exports a public API and
can show/hide members or add a prefix. Forwarding does not itself make members available locally; add @use if the
forwarding file also consumes them. Public module paths are part of a library's API. Leading underscore/hyphen
members are private under module rules.
// abstracts/_tokens.scss
$space: 1rem !default;
 
// abstracts/_index.scss
@forward "tokens";
 
// components/_card.scss
@use "../abstracts" as design;
.card { padding: design.$space; }
 
// app.scss
@use "abstracts" with ($space: 1.25rem);
@use "components/card";
.card { padding: 1.25rem; }
Configure the tokens before any component indirectly loads them. A second @use with a different configuration is not
an independent module instance. Avoid CSS output in pure token modules so importing a dependency does not
unexpectedly emit base rules. Use package importers and documented load paths rather than fragile chains of
parent-directory traversal in published libraries.
The 7-1 pattern and alternatives
The 7-1 pattern places seven concerns under one entry point: abstracts, vendors, base, layout, components, pages
and themes. Abstracts contain non-emitting tokens/functions/mixins. Vendors contain adapters and integration entry
points rather than edited upstream source. Base contains resets and semantic defaults. Layout contains shared
arrangements. Components contain local UI styling. Pages contain real route-specific exceptions. Themes contain
deliberate theme contracts. The final entry point establishes order.
This is a convention, not a Sass feature. A small application can use fewer folders. A large design system may organize
by component package instead. Modern @use loading order and CSS cascade layers must be designed together;
folder names do not control runtime precedence. Runtime themes often belong in custom properties and data attributes
rather than separate compiled copies of every component.
// main.scss; each referenced partial is an actual project dependency.
@use "abstracts";
@use "vendors";
@use "base";
@use "layout";
@use "components";
@use "pages";
@use "themes";
This entry-point contract is illustrated fully in the accompanying module lab. Do not create empty architecture folders
solely to satisfy a diagram. A useful review asks which files emit CSS, which expose API and which may depend on
which others. Cyclic modules are architectural errors, not something to fix with repeated imports.

Built-in module map
 • sass:math: numerical bounds, rounding, trigonometry, logarithms, random values, unit inspection and compatible-unit

them for deterministic design tokens.
• sass:color: color-space-aware channel inspection, adjustment, scaling, mixing and conversion. Distinguish an

• sass:list: length, nth, set-nth, append, join, zip, index, separator and bracket inspection. A list's comma/space/slash
 separator affects emitted CSS.
• sass:map: get, has-key, keys, values, merge, remove, set and nested map operations, including deep operations
 where provided. Merging a map does not update derived maps that were already computed elsewhere.
• sass:selector: append, nest, extend, replace, unify, parse and superselector checks. Selector values are structured
 Sass lists; string concatenation is not a substitute for unification.
• sass:meta: type inspection, inspect, feature/tool introspection, function/mixin lookup and invocation, module member
 discovery and load-css. load-css emits CSS; it does not replace a clear @use public API or create access to private
members.

Migration, compatibility and code quality
Sass @import and global built-in functions were deprecated beginning with Dart Sass 1.80.0. New application modules
should use @use/@forward and namespaced built-ins. Bootstrap 5.3 still uses the older import architecture, so its
integration is a deliberate compatibility exception. A mechanical replacement of @import with @use can break shared
scope, configurable variables and map ordering. Keep that exception at the vendor boundary and plan the migration
against the upstream framework version.
Other migration concerns include slash division, color function changes, mixed declarations after nested rules, the
legacy JavaScript API, invalid combinators, stricter argument handling and changes to conditional function syntax. Use
@if for clear control flow rather than writing new examples around a deprecated legacy if() function. Preserve plain
CSS functions when the browser should evaluate them. Run the official Sass migrator on a reviewable branch and
inspect compiled diffs; a successful migration command does not prove unchanged design behavior.
Production checks: compile every entry point; test functions against invalid units and types; compare expanded CSS
snapshots for deliberate output changes; enforce a selector-depth and output-size budget; verify source-map policy;
render component states; and run accessibility checks in the final CSS build. Separate owned-code warnings from
upstream dependency warnings. Record which warnings remain and why. Do not silently suppress a warning merely to
call a build pristine.

11 Bootstrap 5 ecosystem and layout
What the framework provides
Bootstrap 5 combines Reboot defaults, typography/content styles, a responsive Flexbox grid, utilities, helpers, forms,
components and optional JavaScript plugins. It is utility-rich and component-oriented; calling it purely utility-first hides
the component selectors and runtime plugins that are central to the system. Bootstrap Icons is a separate project.
Bootstrap 5 does not require jQuery. The bundled JavaScript includes Popper for components that need positioning;
the non-bundle build needs the required dependency supplied separately.
Pin CSS and JavaScript to the same version. The integrated lab uses local files from bootstrap@5.3.8, avoiding a live
CDN dependency. If using a CDN in a product, verify the exact URL and integrity hash together, include the appropriate
crossorigin setting and define the application's CSP. An integrity hash from a different version breaks loading. A
framework stylesheet does not supply HTML labels, meaningful content, server validation or a screen-reader-tested
interaction by itself.
Load exactly one owner for each interactive component. Do not load both a bundled UMD file and an independently
bundled copy of the same plugins. Framework data APIs and a React/Vue state layer can conflict if both mutate the
same classes, attributes or children. Either let Bootstrap own its documented component lifecycle through a wrapper, or
use a framework-native implementation with compatible styling and an explicitly different API.
https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/getting-started/introduction/
https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/getting-started/javascript/
Breakpoints and containers
The default tiers are xs below 576px, sm from 576px, md from 768px, lg from 992px, xl from 1200px and xxl from
1400px. There is no xs infix: .col-6 starts at the smallest tier. Most min-width responsive classes continue applying at
larger widths until overridden. Breakpoints are configuration, not device detection.
.container provides width 100% with responsive max-widths: 540, 720, 960, 1140 and 1320px from sm through xxl.
.container-fluid remains 100% wide. .container-md, for example, is fluid below md, then uses responsive max-width
behavior from md upward. Container padding and gutters still matter; a max-width is not the final width of all nested
content. Custom Sass can change these values, so verify a customized build rather than assuming defaults.
Bootstrap's .container class is not a CSS query-container declaration. Its breakpoints are viewport media queries. For
a component that appears in a sidebar and a main panel, native container queries may express its layout more
accurately than adding more Bootstrap viewport classes.
The 12-column grid
The grid relationship is container, row, columns, then content. Rows use flex wrapping and gutter compensation;
columns provide padding. .col shares remaining space; .col-auto sizes to content; .col-1 through .col-12 allocate
fractions of the 12-column width. .col-12.col-md-6.col-xl-4 means full width, then half width, then one third.
.row-cols-1.row-cols-md-2 sets a default number of columns per row. A nested grid needs its own row inside an
existing column.

12 Bootstrap utilities, content, helpers and forms
Utility grammar and coverage
A utility class maps to actual declarations. Many are generated with !important by default, so a later ordinary
component rule may not override them. Responsive and state variants are generated only for configured families; do
not invent a class because a naming pattern seems plausible. The utility appendix extracts every entry of the installed
$utilities Sass map and lists its CSS properties, class prefix, values, responsive setting, print setting and generated
states. That is the exact build-source contract, not a list remembered from another Bootstrap version.
Spacing uses {property}{sides}-{breakpoint?}-{size}: m/p for margin/padding; t/b/s/e/x/y or no side; optional sm
through xxl; and default scale 0,1,2,3,4,5 with values 0,0.25,0.5,1,1.5,3rem. Auto belongs to margin where generated.
s/e are logical start/end conventions processed by the appropriate LTR/RTL build; loading LTR CSS and expecting
every direction-sensitive utility to flip automatically is insufficient. Negative margins are opt-in through Sass and should
not be assumed present. Gap utilities follow their configured families.
Display includes none, inline, inline-block, block, grid, inline-grid, table forms, flex and inline-flex with responsive/print
variants where configured. Flex families cover direction, wrapping, fill, grow/shrink, alignment and order. Sizing
provides selected percentage/auto values, viewport-relative helpers and min/max helpers; arbitrary values such as
.w-37 are not generated by default. Position utilities cover static/relative/absolute/fixed/sticky and selected
edges/translations; responsive position variants are not universally available.
Other families cover background and text colors, opacity, borders and rounding, shadows, object fit, overflow, float,
vertical alignment, interaction, visibility, link opacity/underlines, font sizing/weight/style, line height, text
alignment/wrapping/transformation/decoration and small z-index values. .invisible retains layout space and differs
from .d-none. .text-truncate needs a suitable constrained formatting context. .pe-none disables pointer targeting, not
keyboard focus or programmatic activation. .user-select-none should not be used to obstruct normal text use.
Content and helper layer
Reboot normalizes selected element defaults using box-sizing, typography, margins and native-control adjustments. It
is global CSS; assess it before importing into an existing site. Heading utility classes such as h1/h5 change appearance
but do not change heading semantics. Use the correct HTML heading level. .lead, .small, .mark, list-unstyled and
list-inline are presentational conventions, not substitutes for meaning.
Images can use .img-fluid, .img-thumbnail, rounded utilities and figure classes; they still need appropriate
alternatives and actual width/height information. Tables use .table with contextual, striped, hover, bordered,
borderless, size and responsive wrappers. A .table-responsive wrapper enables horizontal overflow and can clip
floating content; preserve header associations and consider how keyboard users reach an overflowing region.
Helpers include clearfix, color/background helpers, colored links, focus-ring, icon-link, fixed/sticky positioning, ratio,
hstack/vstack, stretched-link, text-truncation, vertical-rule and visually-hidden. .visually-hidden keeps content
available to assistive technology while hiding it visually; .visually-hidden-focusable is useful for a skip link that
appears on focus. A stretched link overlays an anchor's click area and can conflict with other controls; keep its
containing block and interaction boundaries deliberate. A ratio helper creates geometry, not an accessible media title.

.form-control styles text-like inputs and textareas; .form-select styles selects; .form-check, .form-check-input,
.form-check-label and .form-switch structure choices; .form-range styles range controls. .input-group groups
controls and visible add-ons, but add-ons do not automatically become labels. Floating labels require the documented
order and placeholder relationship; a floating placeholder is not a substitute for the real label element.

text with aria-describedby where appropriate. Reflect actual error state with aria-invalid and provide an understandable
error message after validation. A red border or icon is insufficient. Do not display errors for untouched fields

13 Bootstrap component mastery and lifecycle
Static components and semantic contracts
Accordion combines collapse state with heading/button structure. Use real buttons with matching aria-controls and
panel IDs; headings must remain meaningful. Alerts communicate messages; dismissible alerts need a labeled close
button and a plan for focus when the alert disappears. Badges supplement labels and should not make unexplained
numbers the sole accessible name. Breadcrumbs use navigation labeling, a list and aria-current for the current item.
Buttons should be button elements for actions and anchors for navigation. Outline variants still require contrast checks.
Button groups need a useful group label and appropriate control semantics. Cards are visual containers; select
headings, links, images and landmarks based on their actual content. Close buttons need an accessible label and
sufficient target area. List groups can be lists, navigation or actionable controls; mixing these arbitrarily changes
keyboard and screen-reader expectations.
Pagination uses navigation, descriptive labels and aria-current; an anchor with a disabled-looking class is still an
anchor unless its behavior and focus are handled. Placeholders represent loading presentation and should not create
fake operable controls or repeated meaningless announcements. Progress markup in 5.3 puts progressbar semantics
and value attributes on the documented outer progress element; include a label and useful min/max/current values.
Spinners need a meaningful status strategy and reduced-motion consideration. Repeated decorative spinners should
not each announce the same loading state.
Interactive plugins: API contract
Bootstrap plugins generally expose getInstance(element), getOrCreateInstance(element, options) and dispose(),
with component-specific methods. Configuration comes from defaults, data attributes and explicit options under the
documented precedence. data-bs-config can hold supported JSON configuration, but security-sensitive options such
as sanitization settings are restricted. Data attributes use the bs prefix and kebab-case. Do not assume an option
supported by one component exists on another.
Methods that start transitions generally return before the transition finishes. Listen for lifecycle events such as
shown.bs.modal or hidden.bs.offcanvas when completion matters. A call during an active transition can be ignored
according to the plugin contract. The show/hide events are often cancelable; shown/hidden report completion. Event
names and payloads differ by component. The appendix extracts the exact default option names, default values and
declared types from all 12 JavaScript plugin constructors in the pinned UMD bundle.
Component-by-component behavior
 • Accordion/collapse: methods show, hide and toggle; events show/shown/hide/hidden.bs.collapse. parent enables
 grouped behavior. toggle affects construction. It does not automatically implement every optional ARIA accordion
keyboard pattern; decide which keyboard model is required and test it. Keep triggers operable when transitions are
disabled.
• Alert: close removes the alert after its transition; close/closed.bs.alert describe the lifecycle. Move focus to a
 meaningful surviving control if dismissal removes the focused close button. A nonurgent message may fit role=status
rather than an interruptive alert.
• Button: toggle manages the plugin's active state; a toggle button needs an accurate pressed state and a label that
 makes sense in both states. Do not use the plugin's class as a substitute for a real checkbox when a form value is
needed.

15 Symbiotic ecosystem: from source files to a running
interface
The lifecycle and ownership model
At build time, application SCSS loads modules, evaluates variables/functions/loops and emits CSS. Bootstrap Sass
can participate in that build or arrive as a precompiled dependency. At request time, HTML parsing creates DOM nodes
while linked CSS is fetched and parsed into stylesheets. Script execution can affect both trees. Style resolution
matches selectors, runs cascade/defaulting and computes values. Layout resolves geometry, paint produces drawing
commands and compositing combines relevant layers. Resource and font completion, viewport changes, user input
and DOM mutations can invalidate work. A rendering engine can optimize this pipeline, so the phases are a conceptual
model rather than a promise every mutation runs every phase.
A component has at least four representations: semantic DOM and native control state, application state, CSS state
and geometry, and accessibility exposure. A reliable implementation keeps them aligned. SCSS cannot observe
runtime DOM changes. A utility class cannot authorize a server operation. A JavaScript property change does not
always rewrite the corresponding HTML attribute. A visual state alone does not establish an accessible name or an
evaluation result. Animate theme paint cautiously: changing foreground immediately while a background slowly
transitions can create a low-contrast intermediate state. The lab changes foreground and background together.
Consider a practice-card disclosure. HTML supplies a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls and a region with
hidden. JavaScript owns opening and closing, updating the two states together. CSS derives its arrow presentation
from aria-expanded. A live region can announce a meaningful result if the workflow needs it. Sass can generate the
shared styles, and Bootstrap could supply a different collapse controller, but both controllers should not own the same
region simultaneously.
HTML attributes, pseudo-classes and custom properties
Use native attributes such as disabled, required, checked and hidden when their semantics match the intended
behavior. Boolean attributes are true by presence: disabled="false" remains disabled. Attribute selectors test serialized
content; pseudo-classes can test current native state. A checkbox's checked property can differ from its checked
attribute after user interaction. :checked follows current state. A data attribute is an application-defined string, not a
browser-enforced permission. CSS custom properties carry style tokens and normally inherit; they are not private
storage.
ARIA state may be a useful style hook when application behavior keeps it truthful. [aria-expanded="true"] is
appropriate for styling an actual expanded control; it does not expand a region itself. aria-hidden does not automatically
remove focusability and can create a hidden-but-focusable interface. The hidden attribute and display rules interact;
author CSS that overrides [hidden] can accidentally reveal content. The integrated labs explicitly keep [hidden] {
display:none !important; } as a narrowly owned application rule.
ClassList manages tokens without replacing unrelated classes. Toggle with an explicit boolean rather than inverting
uncertain state repeatedly. Use style.setProperty for an intentional custom-property update; do not replace the entire
style attribute. Keep untrusted strings out of CSS URLs, selectors and declarations. CSS.escape escapes identifiers for
selector construction; it is not a universal CSS sanitizer.
CSSOM, resolved style and geometry
Document.styleSheets and CSSStyleSheet expose stylesheet objects, subject to origin restrictions. Reading cssRules
from a cross-origin sheet can fail. element.style sees inline declarations, not all matching styles. getComputedStyle
returns resolved values after cascade; it can require pending style/layout work. getBoundingClientRect reports a
viewport-relative rectangle including transforms and may be fractional. offsetWidth and clientWidth measure different
boxes and round differently. Scroll sizes describe scrollable overflow, not semantic content completeness.

16 CSS Typed OM and Houdini boundaries
CSS Typed OM replaces some string-based access with typed CSS values. attributeStyleMap addresses inline
declarations; computedStyleMap addresses computed style values where supported. CSSUnitValue holds a value and
unit; CSS.px(), CSS.percent() and related factories construct values; CSSKeywordValue represents keywords;
CSSMathValue subclasses represent calculations; CSSTransformValue and transform components represent
supported transforms. CSSStyleValue.parse can parse supported property values. Custom property values can appear
as CSSUnparsedValue rather than a fully typed numeric object.

unsupported-property errors. A resolved auto is not a number to divide by two. Converting incompatible units is invalid;
converting relative lengths can need context that a detached numerical value does not contain. Typed OM coverage is
not universal. Feature detection must check the exact API and use a string-based fallback.
// Complete function; call with an existing HTMLElement and a finite pixel value.
function setInlineMeasure(element, pixels) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(pixels) || pixels < 0) {
    throw new TypeError('pixels must be a finite nonnegative number');
  }
  if (element.attributeStyleMap && globalThis.CSS?.px) {
    try {
      element.attributeStyleMap.set('width', CSS.px(pixels));
      return 'typed';
    } catch {
      // A supported interface may still reject this property/value combination.
    }
  }
  element.style.width = `${pixels}px`;
  return 'string';
}

intrinsic CSS layout first. A registered @property or CSS.registerProperty can define a custom property's syntax,
inheritance and initial value; registration can enable typed interpolation under its rules. Registration is distinct from
Typed OM access and from a worklet. The CSS Painting API and other Houdini worklets are separate capabilities with
their own lifecycle, support and security considerations.

17 ResizeObserver: geometry changes without window
polling
ResizeObserver reports observed element box sizes, including changes caused by layout or content rather than a
window resize. Choose content-box, border-box or device-pixel-content-box where supported and appropriate.
ResizeObserverEntry exposes different measurements; box-size collections can represent fragments. inlineSize and
blockSize follow writing mode, whereas contentRect width/height are physical dimensions. Do not quietly treat the first
fragment as a total across all fragments without declaring that assumption.
Callbacks run during the rendering lifecycle. Writing a size that changes the observed element can trigger another
observation and a loop warning. requestAnimationFrame can move work to a later frame but does not resolve an
unstable feedback equation by itself. Prefer observing a container and updating a non-sizing output, or compute an
idempotent bounded result. Disconnect when the component is no longer owned; unobserve individual targets when
appropriate.
// Complete controller; output is a separate non-sizing text node in the page.
function reportWidth(target, output) {
  if (typeof globalThis.ResizeObserver !== 'function') {
    output.textContent = 'Automatic measurement is unavailable.';
    return () => {};
  }
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
    const entry = entries.find(item => item.target === target);
    if (!entry) return;
    const text = `${Math.round(entry.contentRect.width)} CSS px wide`;
    if (output.textContent !== text) output.textContent = text;
  });
  observer.observe(target, { box: 'content-box' });
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

a user. Provide an explicit measurement request or a quiet visible readout when needed. Native container queries
should handle presentational layout changes; an observer is justified when application logic needs actual
measurement, canvas backing size or integration with a non-CSS system.
For canvas, set its backing pixel dimensions separately from its CSS size and account for device scale. Changing
width/height resets drawing state. Avoid reading pixel data or exporting a tainted cross-origin canvas. A chart also
needs accessible text or table content; sharp pixels do not expose data relationships.

18 MutationObserver: structural evidence, not visual
truth
MutationObserver observes configured changes to attributes, child lists and character data within a chosen subtree.
Attribute filters reduce noise; old-value options preserve selected prior values. It does not directly observe every form
property change, computed style change, layout change or stylesheet-driven visual transition. An input.value
assignment can occur without a value-attribute mutation. A media query can change appearance with no DOM
mutation.
Callbacks are delivered asynchronously through the specified microtask machinery and can contain multiple records.
Treat records as evidence of mutations, then read the current relevant state; do not assume every record is a complete
historical application state. Avoid observing an attribute and rewriting it unconditionally in the same callback.
Disconnect before teardown, and use takeRecords deliberately when queued records matter.
// Complete observer utility for third-party markup integration.
function watchExpanded(button, onState) {
  const read = () => onState(button.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true');
  const observer = new MutationObserver(read);
  observer.observe(button, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['aria-expanded'] });
  read();
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

rediscover your own writes. This utility is useful at a genuine integration boundary. Native input/change events,
ResizeObserver, font-loading events and transition/animation events answer different questions. Select the observation
based on the fact needed, not based on familiarity with one API.

19 View Transitions API: preserving the update
contract
A same-document view transition captures visual states around a DOM update callback, builds a transition
pseudo-element tree and animates the change where supported. Cross-document transitions use a different opt-in and
navigation lifecycle. A view-transition-name pairs elements and must meet uniqueness rules within the relevant
capture. The generated pseudo-elements include root, group, image-pair, old and new layers. Styling them is different
from styling the live element itself.
The application update must work when the API is absent, capture is skipped, names conflict or the user prefers
reduced motion. Distinguish updateCallbackDone, ready and finished promises; a visual transition can fail while the
DOM update succeeds. Do not run a mutating update twice in a catch handler after it already ran. Track whether the
update began before deciding on a fallback.
// Complete helper for a synchronous, idempotent DOM update.
async function updateView(update) {
  const reduced = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
  if (!document.startViewTransition || reduced) {
    update();
    return;
  }
  let began = false;
  let transition;
  try {
    transition = document.startViewTransition(() => {
      began = true;
      update();
    });
  } catch (error) {
    if (!began) update();
    else throw error;
    return;
  }
  // Consume capture failures separately from the application's update result.
  transition.ready.catch(() => {});
  const finished = transition.finished.catch(() => {});
  await transition.updateCallbackDone;
  await finished;
}
The helper's update must be synchronous and should not perform a network mutation; the lab uses it only to toggle a
local presentation theme. If update throws, the caller receives the rejection and must report the actual application
failure. An API fallback must not swallow server errors and pretend an action succeeded. Focus and announcements
need their own policy; a transition screenshot is not a new accessible document.
::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation-duration: 150ms;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) { animation: none; }
}

application update, correct final state and no unhandled rejection. Then test keyboard focus before and after the
transition independently of the animation.

20 Custom Elements, Shadow DOM and style contracts
Custom elements define a lifecycle for valid hyphenated element names. Construction, connection, disconnection,
observed attribute changes, adoption and supported state-preserving moves have distinct roles. A constructor should
initialize its own structure without assuming attributes/children are already fully parsed. connectedCallback can run
more than once; guard initialization and make resource setup repeatable. disconnectedCallback releases listeners,
observers, timers and other resources. A reconnection should restore needed resources without duplicating the
shadow tree.
Shadow DOM scopes selectors and retargets events under defined rules. It is not a security boundary for hostile code.
A closed shadow root changes access conventions; it does not isolate an attacker's script. A host remains part of the
outer tree; inherited values and custom properties can cross into shadow content through inheritance. Global selectors
do not simply reach internal buttons. Use :host, ::part and documented custom properties for a deliberate public styling
API.
A slot projects light-DOM children without moving their ownership into the shadow tree. ::slotted applies to assigned
elements under its limited selector model; it cannot arbitrarily select deeply nested projected descendants. slotchange
reports assignment changes, not every mutation inside an already assigned node. Shared constructable stylesheets
and adoptedStyleSheets can reduce repeated sheet creation where supported; a shared stylesheet mutation affects
every adopter, so ownership and fallback handling matter.

design. Merely naming a tag input-like does not make it submit. CustomStateSet/:state can express supported custom
states; it is separate from defining an aria attribute. Avoid duplicating native controls unless the design requirement

runtime behavior
Batch geometry reads before style writes. Cache results only for a known validity window; font loading, zoom, content
changes and container changes can invalidate them. requestAnimationFrame schedules work near rendering, but it
does not make an expensive read-write loop free. Avoid observing every element with every API merely because the

express. Prefer a single state owner. A server result can update a status region, but visual success styling must not
precede actual success. Respect pending/error/empty states. Fetch cancellation does not undo a completed server
mutation; idempotency and authorization belong to the receiver.

accessible name. A MutationObserver can report a changed attribute but does not prove the intended state transition
occurred. A CSS transitionend event can be absent when duration is zero, a property does not transition, the node is
removed or the transition is canceled. Do not make essential cleanup depend exclusively on an event that may never
arrive; use the component's authoritative lifecycle and bounded fallbacks.
IntersectionObserver can defer nonessential work until visibility conditions are met, but it is not proof that a human read
content. FontFaceSet readiness can help coordinate measurements, but fonts can be loaded later. matchMedia
change listeners can follow user preference changes and need removal during teardown. The Web Animations API
exposes animation objects and promises, with cancellation behavior that differs from simply removing a CSS class.
CSS.supports is a parsing/capability check, not a browser bug detector or accessibility test.

Historical Snapshot names outside the current property records
The following names occur in the Snapshot index but have no current non-vendor property record in this retrieved Webref dataset.
They are retained for audit and migration, not assigned invented current grammar or browser support. Historical CSS2 aural names
are particularly unsuitable as a way to control a modern screen reader.
• azimuth: Historical aural source direction; specialized speech output has a different modern voice model. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-azimuth
• elevation: Historical aural source elevation; not a visual transform or current universal speech setting. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-elevation
• pitch: Historical aural pitch; compare voice-pitch in the modern speech module. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-pitch
• pitch-range: Historical aural pitch variation; compare voice-range where a speech renderer implements it. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-pitch-range
• play-during: Historical aural background sound; use explicit user-controlled media rather than assuming this is a browser audio
API. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-play-during
• property-name: An index placeholder rather than a concrete authoring property; do not write property-name as a universal
configurable setting. Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#propdef-property-name
• richness: Historical aural voice richness; no ordinary screen-reader styling guarantee. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-richness
• speak-header: Historical aural table-header repetition; actual table semantics and assistive technology behavior remain essential.
Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-header
• speak-numeral: Historical aural number pronunciation; do not depend on it for accessible mathematical content. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-numeral
• speak-punctuation: Historical aural punctuation pronunciation; document semantics and AT preferences control real reading
behavior. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speak-punctuation
• speech-rate: Historical aural rate; compare voice-rate only in a verified speech-CSS environment. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-speech-rate
• stress: Historical aural stress setting; not a text-decoration control. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-stress
• volume: Historical aural volume; actual HTMLMediaElement volume and user controls are separate. Source:
https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/aural.html#propdef-volume

Complete Sass statement map
@use loads a module; @forward re-exports an API; @mixin/@include declare and invoke emitting abstractions; @function/@return
compute values; @extend unifies selector relationships; @if/@else choose branches; @each/@for/@while generate bounded
output; @at-root controls nesting context; @debug/@warn/@error report diagnostics. @content inserts a caller block and can pass
arguments to using. Sass @import is a deprecated dependency mechanism with legacy scope behavior; a preserved CSS @import
has different browser/network behavior. CSS at-rules such as @media, @supports, @layer, @container, @keyframes and
@font-face are emitted according to Sass nesting/interpolation and CSS parsing rules. Silent // comments disappear; block
comments can survive according to output mode and preservation rules.
Private module members, configuration, rest/keyword arguments, list/map destructuring, parent-selector values, placeholder
selectors, interpolation, calculations, built-in modules and the modern importer/function/logger APIs complete the major
language/tooling surface taught here. A public library should document argument names because callers can use keyword
arguments. Passing an argument list can preserve keywords; meta.keywords can inspect them. @content using makes argument
transfer explicit.

function setInlineMeasure(element, pixels) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(pixels) || pixels < 0) {
    throw new TypeError('pixels must be a finite nonnegative number');
  }
  if (element.attributeStyleMap && globalThis.CSS?.px) {
    try {

// Complete controller; output is a separate non-sizing text node in the page.
function reportWidth(target, output) {
  if (typeof globalThis.ResizeObserver !== 'function') {
    output.textContent = 'Automatic measurement is unavailable.';
    return () => {};
  }
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
    const entry = entries.find(item => item.target === target);
    if (!entry) return;
    const text = `${Math.round(entry.contentRect.width)} CSS px wide`;
    if (output.textContent !== text) output.textContent = text;
  });
  observer.observe(target, { box: 'content-box' });
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

resets to the specification initial. unset chooses inherit or initial based on normal inheritance. revert rolls back the current origin; revert-layer rolls back the current cascade layer according to its rules. Shorthands set multiple longhands together and can reset omitted components. Background can reset background-color; font resets multiple font settings; border resets border-image. Later longhands can override individual parts. A shorthand containing var() may defer parsing, then become invalid at computed-value time. The browser does not necessarily revive an earlier declaration when that happens. Custom properties usually inherit and preserve token streams; var() substitutes tokens in consuming declarations. A fallback is used when substitution needs it, not whenever the substituted value is invalid for the consuming property. --size: red; width: var(--size, 10rem) does not make 10rem win. Registration through @property supplies syntax, inheritance and an initial value under its constraints. Application token names remain open-ended. @property --progress { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; } :root { --space-2: 0.5rem; --surface: #fff; --ink: #172b4d; } .panel { padding: var(--space-2); background: var(--surface); color: var(--ink); } Practice: predict the winning color across two layers, an inline declaration and a user important declaration. Then inspect each contender. Separately test an invalid custom-property substitution; explain why cascade selection and computed-value validation are distinct stages. 2. Mental model, representation, and construction
Linear nodes with next pointer only.
C++ representation: custom Node{T value; Node* next;} or unique_ptr-owned next links.
Canonical operations
push front/back
insert after
erase after
reverse
find
Canonical C++ sketch
struct Node{int v; Node* next;}; Node* reverse(Node* h){Node* p=nullptr; while(h){auto*n=h->next;h->next=p;p=h;h=n;}return p;}
Construction questions
What owns the storage or nodes?
What is fixed at compile time versus runtime?
Which initialization forms value-initialize versus leave primitive storage indeterminate?
Can construction allocate or throw?
What copy/move behavior should the learner expect?

C++ Prim MST — Algorithm Training Blueprint
Standalone DSA/RAG training unit · algorithm-specific curriculum
Grows an MST from a starting component by repeatedly taking cheapest edge crossing the cut.
Field
Value
Type
Algorithm / Technique
Primary category
06 Graph
C++ baseline
C++17/20 idioms; note version-specific APIs where relevant
Goal
Learn, practice, interview, and RAG retrieval
Teaching contract: the learner must recognize the problem shape, derive the algorithm from an invariant, write an idiomatic C++ implementation, prove correctness at interview depth, state complexity precisely, and know when a different technique is required.

1. The algorithm lenses
#
Lens
Question
1
Problem shape
What wording/constraints should trigger this technique?
2
Preconditions
What assumptions must hold?
3
State / representation
What variables/data structures encode progress?
4
Invariant
What remains true after each step?
5
Transition / movement
How does one step reduce the unsolved region/state?
6
Termination
Why must it stop?
7
Correctness
Why can no discarded alternative beat the retained answer?
8
Complexity
Time, space, amortized/output-sensitive bounds?
9
Failure conditions
When do assumptions break?
10
Alternatives
Which neighboring algorithms compete?
11
C++ implementation
Which STL types/comparators/lifetime details matter?
12
Edge cases
Which inputs expose boundary errors?
13
Variants
What common interview mutations exist?
14
Testing
How do we compare against brute force?
15
Explanation
Can the learner defend it without memorized code?

2. Mental model and mechanism
Grows an MST from a starting component by repeatedly taking cheapest edge crossing the cut.
Core mechanism: Mark start; min-heap crossing edges; pop cheapest to unseen vertex; add and push its outgoing edges.
Canonical C++ skeleton
// min-heap of (weight,to); skip if visited; add weight; push neighbors.
What the learner should narrate while coding
What state means before the loop/recursion starts.
Why the chosen operation/movement is safe.
What part of the search space is permanently discarded.
How the invariant is restored after an update.
What exactly makes the algorithm terminate.

3. Invariant and correctness reasoning
heap contains candidate cut edges
accepted vertices form one growing tree per run
Proof checkpoint
Question
Initialization
Why is the invariant true before the first step?
Maintenance
Why does one transition preserve it?
Progress
What strictly decreases/increases so the algorithm cannot loop forever?
Termination
How does the invariant imply the returned result is correct?
Counterexample test
What minimal input would break a wrong pointer move/state transition?

4. Complexity and implementation costs
Dimension
Bound
time with adjacency list heap
O(E log V)
space
O(V+E)
Count total pointer/index/edge/state movements rather than only visible nesting.
Include sorting, heap operations, hashing, recursion stack, and output size when they dominate.
In C++, mention copying versus references, container invalidation, comparator cost, and integer-width/overflow where relevant.
For randomized or average-case algorithms, distinguish guarantees from expectations.

5. Recognition signals, best fit, and rejection signals
Recognition signals
MST with adjacency list
dense variant with O(V^2)
Best use
graph naturally adjacency-based
Avoid / reject when
global edge sort simpler
Alternatives
Kruskal
Required pre-code exercise: identify at least two signals from the prompt and one condition that would invalidate this technique.

6. Gotchas, boundary failures, and debugging
Failure mode
Learner drill
stale edges to already visited nodes
Construct a failing input, trace the state, and repair the implementation while preserving the invariant.
disconnected graph
Construct a failing input, trace the state, and repair the implementation while preserving the invariant.
Run tiny hand traces before large tests.
Compare random small inputs with brute force/reference solver.
Enable sanitizers for pointer/index-heavy custom code.
Use assertions for monotonicity, heap/tree/DSU invariants, or distance bounds when appropriate.

7. Variants, patterns, and canonical problems
Related patterns
greedy cut property
Problem mapping
Min Cost to Connect Points
Approach tier
Training objective
Brute force
Write the obvious correct solution and state the bottleneck.
Observation
Identify repeated work or exploitable order/monotonicity/state overlap.
Optimized
Derive this algorithm from that observation rather than recalling code.
Variant
Modify one assumption: duplicates, weights, sortedness, memory, online updates, reconstruction.
Alternative comparison
Solve or outline with the closest competing technique and compare tradeoffs.

8. Curriculum levels and exit checks
Level
Exit check
L0 Foundations
Define Prim MST, draw/trace a tiny instance, and state the fundamental invariant.
L1 C++ Fluency
Construct, access, mutate, iterate, and destroy/use Prim MST idiomatically in C++.
L2 Handling Mechanics
Master indices, pointers, iterators, nodes, ranges, or states that Prim MST requires.
L3 Cost Awareness
Know operation costs and identify hidden allocations, copies, rehashes, shifts, or traversals.
L4 Pattern Application
Solve canonical interview problems where Prim MST is the natural tool.
L5 Recognition
Given a new prompt, justify whether Prim MST should be considered before coding.
L6 Constraint Flips
Adapt when input becomes huge, immutable, streamed, duplicated, weighted, or memory-limited.
L7 Optimization
Reduce constant factors and choose representation details without changing correctness.
L8 Interview Defense
Explain invariant, correctness, complexity, alternatives, and failure conditions clearly.
L9 Production / Internals
Understand implementation-defined details, allocator/lifetime behavior, and debugging tools relevant to Prim MST.
Algorithm promotion gate: code correctness alone is insufficient. The learner must state the invariant and explain why the asymptotic improvement occurs.

9. Exercise formats and interview simulator
Predict the result of a short Prim MST operation sequence and explain every state change.
Spot the bug in a deliberately incorrect Prim MST implementation.
Complete a trace table showing the key position/pointer/iterator/state after every step.
Implement the minimal Prim MST interface from scratch without copying a library implementation.
Give three adversarial inputs that stress the most important edge cases.
Explain the core invariant in two sentences, then show where a buggy implementation violates it.
Compare Prim MST against its two closest alternatives under time, space, stability, and implementation complexity.
Constraint flip: solve the same task after removing extra memory or after making updates frequent.
Complexity audit: identify hidden linear or logarithmic work inside a loop.
Interview mode: derive the approach aloud before writing code.
Refactor a correct-but-fragile solution into idiomatic modern C++.
Write randomized differential tests against a slower reference implementation where practical.

Tutor behavior
Clarify
Ask learner for input constraints and required output.
Baseline
Require brute-force approach and complexity.
Optimize
Ask what repeated work/property can be exploited.
Invariant
Require one-sentence invariant before code.
Implement
Allow code; give only graduated hints.
Test
Ask learner to generate edge cases and trace one.
Defend
Ask why this algorithm beats one alternative and when it would fail.

Partition-based divide-and-conquer sort placing elements around a pivot then recursing on partitions.

Goal

Teaching contract: the learner must recognize the problem shape, derive the algorithm from an invariant, write an idiomatic C++ implementation, prove correctness at interview depth, state complexity precisely, and know when a different technique is required.

1. The algorithm lenses

Explanation

2. Mental model and mechanism
Partition-based divide-and-conquer sort placing elements around a pivot then recursing on partitions.
Core mechanism: Choose pivot; partition; recursively sort left/right; production std::sort uses introspective strategy rather than naive quicksort mandate.
Canonical C++ skeleton
// Hoare/Lomuto partition, recurse on resulting ranges.
What the learner should narrate while coding
What state means before the loop/recursion starts.
Why the chosen operation/movement is safe.
What part of the search space is permanently discarded.
How the invariant is restored after an update.
What exactly makes the algorithm terminate.

For randomized or average-case algorithms, distinguish guarantees from expectations.

7. Variants, patterns, and canonical problems

partition

Approach tier
Training objective
Brute force
Write the obvious correct solution and state the bottleneck.
Observation
Identify repeated work or exploitable order/monotonicity/state overlap.
Optimized
Derive this algorithm from that observation rather than recalling code.
Variant
Modify one assumption: duplicates, weights, sortedness, memory, online updates, reconstruction.
Alternative comparison
Solve or outline with the closest competing technique and compare tradeoffs.

8. Curriculum levels and exit checks
Level
Exit check
L0 Foundations
Define Quick Sort, draw/trace a tiny instance, and state the fundamental invariant.
L1 C++ Fluency
Construct, access, mutate, iterate, and destroy/use Quick Sort idiomatically in C++.
L2 Handling Mechanics
Master indices, pointers, iterators, nodes, ranges, or states that Quick Sort requires.
L3 Cost Awareness
Know operation costs and identify hidden allocations, copies, rehashes, shifts, or traversals.
L4 Pattern Application
Solve canonical interview problems where Quick Sort is the natural tool.
L5 Recognition
Given a new prompt, justify whether Quick Sort should be considered before coding.
L6 Constraint Flips
Adapt when input becomes huge, immutable, streamed, duplicated, weighted, or memory-limited.
L7 Optimization
Reduce constant factors and choose representation details without changing correctness.
L8 Interview Defense
Explain invariant, correctness, complexity, alternatives, and failure conditions clearly.
L9 Production / Internals
Understand implementation-defined details, allocator/lifetime behavior, and debugging tools relevant to Quick Sort.
Algorithm promotion gate: code correctness alone is insufficient. The learner must state the invariant and explain why the asymptotic improvement occurs.

9. Exercise formats and interview simulator
Predict the result of a short Quick Sort operation sequence and explain every state change.
Spot the bug in a deliberately incorrect Quick Sort implementation.
Complete a trace table showing the key position/pointer/iterator/state after every step.
Implement the minimal Quick Sort interface from scratch without copying a library implementation.
Give three adversarial inputs that stress the most important edge cases.
Explain the core invariant in two sentences, then show where a buggy implementation violates it.
Compare Quick Sort against its two closest alternatives under time, space, stability, and implementation complexity.
Constraint flip: solve the same task after removing extra memory or after making updates frequent.
Complexity audit: identify hidden linear or logarithmic work inside a loop.
Interview mode: derive the approach aloud before writing code.
Refactor a correct-but-fragile solution into idiomatic modern C++.
Write randomized differential tests against a slower reference implementation where practical.
Interview phase
Tutor behavior
Clarify
Ask learner for input constraints and required output.
Baseline
Require brute-force approach and complexity.
Optimize
Ask what repeated work/property can be exploited.
Invariant
Require one-sentence invariant before code.
Implement
Allow code; give only graduated hints.
Test
Ask learner to generate edge cases and trace one.
Defend
Ask why this algorithm beats one alternative and when it would fail.

1. Mental model and hardware contract
Mechanical switch bounce, time-based debounce, integrator/state-machine debounce, interrupt-assisted designs, and latency tradeoffs.
Key vocabulary
debounce: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
edge: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
integrator: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
timestamp: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
hysteresis: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
Core invariant
The firmware must preserve the documented hardware/software contract for Button Debouncing: every state transition, buffer ownership change, register update, or timing assumption must be explicit and bounded.
Recognition signals
A requirement directly mentions one of: debounce, edge, integrator, timestamp.
Timing, memory, or power constraints make a naive blocking implementation unsafe.
The same data crosses foreground/ISR, DMA/CPU, or task boundaries and therefore needs an ownership/synchronization rule.
When not to reach for it
When a simpler peripheral/library primitive already provides the required guarantee.
When the hardware does not implement the assumed feature; select a valid peripheral or external component instead.
When correctness requires stronger synchronization or protocol guarantees than the technique provides.

2. Register, timing, and state model
Teach the learner to move from the datasheet block diagram to a small explicit state model. Avoid memorizing register names across MCU families; instead identify the repeated roles: clock/reset gate, configuration, status, data, interrupt enable, interrupt flags, and DMA request plumbing.
Hardware concern
Question to ask
Typical evidence
Failure if ignored
Clock/reset
Is the peripheral clocked and released from reset?
clock tree + enable bit
register writes appear ineffective
Configuration
Are mode/width/polarity/timing fields correct?
reference manual + datasheet
silent misbehavior or bus errors
Status/flags
Which flags are level, edge, sticky, read-to-clear, or write-one-to-clear?
status-register semantics
lost or repeated events
Data path
Who owns the buffer/register now: CPU, ISR, DMA, task, peripheral?
state diagram / ownership table
races, corruption, stale data
Timing
What is the maximum service latency and jitter?
datasheet timing + measured budget
overrun, protocol violation
Timing arithmetic
Use integer-safe formulas with explicit units. Derive timer, baud, sampling, PWM, and protocol timing from the actual peripheral clock rather than from the CPU headline frequency. Always document rounding error and acceptable tolerance.

3. Canonical C implementation pattern
// Canonical embedded-C pattern// 1) validate preconditions// 2) update only owned state/register fields// 3) keep bounded execution time// 4) return explicit status rather than hiding failureint operation(context_t *ctx) {    if (ctx == NULL) return ERR_ARG;    /* hardware/platform-specific work */    return OK;}
Implementation rules
Use <stdint.h> widths for registers, wire formats, counters, and masks.
Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.
Separate mechanism (register/HAL transport) from policy (retries, parsing, scheduling, application behavior).
Make buffer ownership transitions visible in names, state, or API contracts.
Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

4. Platform implementation matrix
platform
training emphasis
STM32_HAL
STM32 Cortex-M using STM32Cube HAL/LL and CMSIS concepts. Teach HAL APIs first, then show LL/register mapping and CMSIS/NVIC concepts where useful.
RP2040_SDK
RP2040 Cortex-M0+ using Pico SDK, PIO, DMA, and multicore-aware patterns. Emphasize Pico SDK APIs, dual-core implications, DMA, and PIO when timing-sensitive I/O applies.
ESP_IDF
ESP32-class targets using ESP-IDF; classic ESP32 is Xtensa, family variants may differ. Use driver/event/task-oriented ESP-IDF concepts; networking topics should account for FreeRTOS/lwIP integration.
AVR_Bare_Metal
ATmega/AVR register-level C with avr-libc style headers. Favor datasheet/register-driven examples, interrupt vectors, small RAM budgets, and 8-bit atomicity concerns.
Arduino_C
Arduino-style embedded development; sketches are compiled as C++ but this track emphasizes C-like embedded patterns. Use Arduino APIs as an approachable layer, while explaining the underlying timer/register/interrupt cost. Note that Arduino sketches are compiled as C++.
hardware_verified: false. These records teach portable reasoning and representative API/register patterns. Board-specific register addresses, alternate-function mappings, pin capabilities, DMA routing, peripheral instances, clock constraints, and electrical limits must be verified against the exact MCU/board reference manual before deployment.

5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
Questions the learner must answer
Can this code run from foreground, ISR, DMA completion, RTOS task, or multiple contexts?
Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?
Safe design pattern
Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

6. Reliability, failure modes, and common gotchas
delay in ISR: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
double events: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
too-long debounce window: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
Forgetting volatile on a register or ISR-shared flag can let the optimizer reuse a stale value; adding volatile alone does not make compound operations atomic.
Pointer arithmetic scales by pointed-to type, not bytes; use uint8_t* when byte stepping is intended and preserve alignment requirements.
Never trust external lengths, counts, or frame fields without bounds checking before buffer access.
Avoid malloc/free in timing-critical or ISR paths unless the allocation strategy is explicitly designed and bounded.
Do not clear peripheral status flags using a guessed read-modify-write sequence; follow the documented clear semantics.
Test wraparound of tick counters, ring indices, sequence numbers, and timer capture values.
Debugging ladder
Confirm power/clock/reset and pin mux first.
Observe raw status/flags before blaming application logic.
Instrument timing with GPIO/SWO/trace or a logic analyzer when protocol/timing matters.
Reduce to a minimal register/HAL transaction.
Add deterministic fault counters and reset-cause logging.
