2. Overview and mental model: Segment tree
A segment tree stores an aggregate (sum, minimum, maximum, gcd) for every segment of an array, so any range
query and any point update take O(log n) after an O(n) build.
The recursive layout keeps node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and uses a 4n-slot Array. A bottom-up version with
leaves at n..2n-1 is shorter for associative operations. Lazy propagation adds O(log n) range updates.
Pick the identity of the operation for out-of-range segments: 0 for sum, Float::INFINITY for min.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
ruby-segmenttree-build   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-query. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.
The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself
forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots,
which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(arr, l, r)
  return arr[l] if l == r
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  attr_reader :tree, :size
  def initialize(arr)
    @size = arr.size
    @tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
    build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
  end
  def total
    @tree[1]
  end
  private
  def build(arr, node, l, r)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
    build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
ruby-segmenttree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-query. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-min. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old
value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only
one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def update_bad(t, node, l, r, i, v)
  if l == r
    t[node] = v
    return
  end
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  if i <= mid
    update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
  else
    update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
  end
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def update(i, v)
    update_at(1, 0, @size - 1, i, v)
    self
  end
  private
  def update_at(node, l, r, i, v)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    if i <= mid
      update_at(2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
    else
      update_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
    end
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A range query returns the identity for disjoint segments, the stored value for covered ones,
and combines otherwise
ruby-segmenttree-query   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-access
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-build. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-update. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A query can return the stored value whenever the segment is covered, and recurse
otherwise, without a disjoint case.
Without the disjoint check the recursion reaches leaves that lie outside the query and adds their values. For a sum
the identity is 0: return 0 when the node range does not intersect the query, return the stored sum when it is fully
inside, and otherwise add the answers from both children. At most about 2 log n nodes are expanded, so a query is
O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def query_bad(t, node, l, r, ql, qr)
  return t[node] if l == r || (ql <= l && r <= qr)
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  query_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) +
    query_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def query(ql, qr)
    query_at(1, 0, @size - 1, ql, qr)
  end
  private
  def query_at(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @tree[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    query_at(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + query_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Lazy propagation must push pending additions to the children before descending into them
ruby-segmenttree-lazy   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-min. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A pending range addition stored on a node can stay there until the whole node is queried.
A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent,
so they return stale values. Push the pending value down (apply it to both children and clear it) before recursing.
Then range add and range sum are both O(log n) instead of O(n) per update.

Correct:
 class LazySeg
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @sum = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    @lazy = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    build(1, 0, @n - 1, arr)
  end
  def add(l, r, v)
    range_add(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r, v)
  end
  def sum(l, r)
    range_sum(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r)
  end
  private
  def build(node, l, r, arr)
    if l == r
      @sum[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(2 * node, l, mid, arr)
    build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, arr)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def apply(node, l, r, v)
    @sum[node] += v * (r - l + 1)
    @lazy[node] += v
  end
  def push(node, l, r)
    return if @lazy[node].zero?
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    apply(2 * node, l, mid, @lazy[node])
    apply(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, @lazy[node])
    @lazy[node] = 0
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      apply(node, l, r, v)
      return
    end
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end

The identity element must match the operation: Float::INFINITY for minimum, not 0
ruby-segmenttree-min   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-update. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-lazy. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Starting the running result at 0 works for any combine operation.
Zero is the identity for sum, but for minimum any positive value is larger than 0, so every query returns 0. The identity
of min is Float::INFINITY and of max is -Float::INFINITY. This bottom-up version stores the leaves at n..2n-1 and
answers half-open ranges [l, r) by climbing; build is O(n) and query O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class MinSegBad
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, 0)
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| @t[@n + i] = v }
    (@n - 1).downto(1) { |i| @t[i] = [@t[2 * i], @t[2 * i + 1]].min }
  end
  def query(l, r)
    res = 0
    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r
      if l.odd?
        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1
        res = [res, @t[r]].min
      end
      l /= 2
      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end
end
Correct:
 class MinSegTree
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, Float::INFINITY)
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| @t[@n + i] = v }
    (@n - 1).downto(1) { |i| @t[i] = [@t[2 * i], @t[2 * i + 1]].min }
  end
  def query(l, r)
    res = Float::INFINITY
    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r
      if l.odd?
        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1
        res = [res, @t[r]].min
      end
      l /= 2
      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end
end

Prompt. Why is a recursive segment tree usually stored in an array of 4n slots?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The recursive layout puts the children of node i at 2i and 2i + 1 and splits
ranges in the middle, so for sizes that are not powers of two the tree is not complete and some indexes are skipped. The
deepest level can reach an index of almost 4n, so 4n slots are a simple safe upper bound. A power-of-two padded size of
2 * 2^ceil(log2 n) would also work.

2. Overview and mental model: Bloom filter
A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic set. add sets k bits chosen by hashing; include? returns false only if the item
was never added, and true if the item was added or by chance collides (a false positive). It never gives false
negatives.
In Ruby one arbitrarily large Integer can hold the whole bit array: set with |= 1 << i, read with bits[i]. Positions come
from double hashing with Zlib.crc32 and Digest::MD5; String#hash is randomised per process and must not be used.
Size it with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits and k = (m / n) ln 2 hashes. Standard filters cannot delete; use a counting filter
when removal is needed.
Toolbox

require "digest"
bf = BloomFilter.new(256, 3)
bf.add("apple")
bf.include?("apple")

Set a bit with OR, not addition; setting an already-set bit must change nothing
ruby-bloomfilter-bits   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ruby-bloomfilter-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-hash. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-query. Complexity: O(m/64).
 Common misconception. bits + (1 << i) sets bit i just like bits | (1 << i).
Addition carries: if bit i is already set, adding 1 << i clears it and sets bit i + 1, silently corrupting a neighbour. OR is
idempotent. Ruby Integers have arbitrary size, so one Integer can serve as the whole bit array, and Integer#[] reads a
bit (0 or 1). Integers are immutable, so store the new value back in the instance variable. Memory is m / 8 bytes.

end

end

end

Derive the k positions from stable hashes such as Zlib.crc32 and Digest::MD5, never from
String#hash
ruby-bloomfilter-hash   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-bloomfilter-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-bits. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. item.hash is a quick way to get the hash value for a Bloom filter.
String#hash is seeded randomly for every Ruby process, so the same string hashes differently after a restart. A filter
that was saved, shared or rebuilt elsewhere then answers wrongly. Use deterministic hashes: Zlib.crc32 and
Digest::MD5 give two independent values h1 and h2, and double hashing derives all k positions as (h1 + i * h2) % m.
Keep h2 non-zero so positions differ. Each add or lookup costs O(k).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

Correct:
 require "digest"
require "zlib"
class BloomFilter
  attr_reader :m, :k, :bits
  def initialize(m, k)
    @m = m
    @k = k
    @bits = 0
  end
  def positions(item)
    s = item.to_s
    h1 = Zlib.crc32(s)
    h2 = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(s).to_i(16) % (@m - 1) + 1
    Array.new(@k) { |i| (h1 + i * h2) % @m }
  end
  def add(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @bits |= 1 << i }
    self
  end
  def include?(item)
    positions(item).all? { |i| @bits[i] == 1 }
  end
end

A membership query needs all k bits set; one set bit is not enough
ruby-bloomfilter-query   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-bloomfilter-access
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-bits. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-size. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. If any one of the k bits is set the item is probably present.
Other items set bits too, so a single set bit is weak evidence. Requiring every one of the k bits makes a false positive
need all k positions covered by other items. The answer "no" is always right, because an added item set all of its bits,
while "yes" means probably. There are no false negatives unless bits are cleared.

require "zlib"
class BloomFilter
  attr_reader :m, :k, :bits
  def initialize(m, k)
    @m = m
    @k = k
    @bits = 0
  end
  def positions(item)
    s = item.to_s
    h1 = Zlib.crc32(s)
    h2 = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(s).to_i(16) % (@m - 1) + 1
    Array.new(@k) { |i| (h1 + i * h2) % @m }

  def add(item)

A Bloom filter cannot delete; clearing bits breaks other items, so use counters
ruby-bloomfilter-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-bloomfilter-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-size. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. Removing an item means clearing its k bits.
Those bits may also belong to other items, which would then be reported absent: false negatives, which a Bloom filter
must never produce. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter per position, increments on add and decrements
on remove, and treats a position as set when its counter is above zero. It uses several times the memory. Only
remove items that were added.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class BloomFilter
  def remove_bad(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @bits &= ~(1 << i) }
    self
  end
end
Correct:
 class CountingBloom < BloomFilter
  def initialize(m, k)
    super
    @counts = Array.new(m, 0)
  end
  def add(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @counts[i] += 1 }
    self
  end
  def include?(item)
    positions(item).all? { |i| @counts[i] > 0 }
  end
  def remove(item)
    return false unless include?(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @counts[i] -= 1 }
    true
  end
end
Size the filter with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 and k = (m / n) ln 2
ruby-bloomfilter-size   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: ruby-bloomfilter-complexity
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-query. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Take m = n * ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 for n items and a false-positive rate p.
For p < 1, ln(p) is negative, so the formula needs a minus sign or m comes out negative. The optimal number of hash
functions is (m / n) ln 2, rounded. For one thousand items at one percent this gives about 9586 bits and 7 hashes,
roughly 9.6 bits per item. Memory is independent of the size of the items.

Prompt. Why can a standard Bloom filter not remove items without creating false negatives?

2. Overview and mental model: Date, Time and DateTime
Date (require "date") models calendar days; Time models an instant with a time zone; DateTime is a legacy class that
the Ruby documentation discourages in favour of Time. Date arithmetic is O(1): + adds days, >> adds months with
clamping, and subtracting two dates gives a Rational number of days.
Date.new raises Date::Error for impossible dates; valid_date? checks first. wday is 0 for Sunday, cwday follows ISO
(Monday 1 to Sunday 7). Date.parse guesses the field order, so use strptime or Date.iso8601 for external text.
Time.utc(...) and Time.at(...).utc avoid dependence on the machine time zone. Time subtraction returns Float
seconds.

Date.new raises Date::Error for an impossible date; check with valid_date? first
ruby-datetime-invalid   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-datetime-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-month. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Date.new(2024, 2, 30) rolls over into March.
Date.new validates its arguments and raises Date::Error (invalid date) for February 30. Date.valid_date?(y, m, d)
returns false instead of raising, which suits user input. Leap years are handled by the calendar: 2024 has February
29, 2100 does not.

  Date.new(y, m, d)
end
Correct:
 require "date"
def make(y, m, d)
  return nil unless Date.valid_date?(y, m, d)
  Date.new(y, m, d)
end

date + n adds days, date >> n adds months and clamps to the month end
ruby-datetime-month   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-datetime-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-datetime-invalid. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-diff. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Adding 30 days is the same as adding one month.
Date#+ adds days, so Jan 31 + 30 is Mar 1 in a leap year. Date#>> adds months and clamps the day to the last day
of the target month: Jan 31 >> 1 is Feb 29 (2024). Use >> for calendar months and + for exact day counts. Both
return new objects and are O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "date"
def next_month_bad(d)
  d + 30
end
Correct:
 require "date"
def next_month(d)
  d >> 1
end
Subtracting two Dates gives a Rational number of days; call to_i for a whole count
ruby-datetime-diff   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-datetime-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-datetime-month. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-weekday. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. date2 - date1 is an Integer number of days.
Date#- returns a Rational, so (Date.new(2024,3,10) - Date.new(2024,3,5)) is (5/1). It prints as "5/1" in strings and
compares equal to 5, but arithmetic with it stays Rational. Convert with to_i when you want a plain count of days.

def days_bad(a, b)
  (b - a).to_s
end
Correct:
 require "date"
def days(a, b)

end

wday counts from Sunday = 0 while cwday follows ISO with Monday = 1 and Sunday = 7
ruby-datetime-weekday   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-datetime-access
Prerequisites: ruby-datetime-diff. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-parse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. wday numbers Monday as 1 and Sunday as 7.
Date#wday returns 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday. Date#cwday follows ISO 8601: Monday is 1 and Sunday is
7. Mixing them shifts a weekday check by one. Use cwday > 5 for a weekend test, or saturday? and sunday?.

def weekend_bad?(d)
  d.wday > 5
end
Correct:

def weekend?(d)
  d.cwday > 5
end

2. Overview and mental model: Matrix and Vector
Matrix and Vector (require "matrix", a bundled gem since Ruby 3.1) provide linear algebra on arrays of numbers.
They work with Integer, Rational and Float entries, and many operations are exact: the inverse of an integer matrix
has Rational entries.
Matrix[[1, 2], [3, 4]] builds from rows; rows must have equal length. * is the matrix product (O(n^3) for square
matrices), hadamard_product is element-wise, determinant and inverse are O(n^3), and ** uses repeated squaring.
Shapes must match: A * B needs A.column_count == B.row_count. Vector * Vector is undefined; use inner_product.
A 2D Array of Arrays is often enough for grids; use Matrix for algebra.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Matrix rows must have equal length; a ragged literal raises ErrDimensionMismatch
ruby-matrix-ragged   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-matrix-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-multiply. Complexity: O(r * c).
 Common misconception. Matrix[[1, 2], [3]] pads the short row with zeros.
Every row of a Matrix must have the same number of columns. A ragged row list raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Build matrices with Matrix[[...]], Matrix.build(rows, cols) { |r, c| ... },
Matrix.identity(n) or Matrix.zero(r, c). Matrix needs require "matrix" (a bundled gem since Ruby 3.1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def ragged_bad
  Matrix[[1, 2], [3]]
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def built
  Matrix.build(2, 2) { |r, c| r * 2 + c + 1 }
end

Page 5
* is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication
ruby-matrix-multiply   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-ragged. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-shape. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
* computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise
multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes
O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def square_bad(m)
  Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def square(m)
  m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
  m.hadamard_product(m)
end
Multiplying needs left columns equal to right rows; otherwise ErrDimensionMismatch is
raised
ruby-matrix-shape   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-multiply. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-inverse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any two matrices can be multiplied.
The product A * B requires A.column_count == B.row_count. A 1 x 2 matrix times a 1 x 2 matrix raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Check the shapes before multiplying, or transpose one operand: A *
B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def product_bad(a, b)
  a * b
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def product(a, b)
  return nil unless a.column_count == b.row_count
  a * b
end

Page 6
inverse of an integer matrix has Rational entries and a singular matrix raises ErrNotRegular
ruby-matrix-inverse   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-shape. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-fib. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. The inverse of an integer matrix is made of floats, and every square matrix has one.
Matrix#inverse uses exact arithmetic: integer input gives Rational entries such as (3/2). A matrix with determinant 0
has no inverse and raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrNotRegular. Test determinant.zero? first, or use rescue.
Determinant and inverse are O(n^3).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def invert_bad(m)
  m.inverse
end

2. Overview and mental model: Range
A Range represents an interval with a beginning and an end: 1..10 includes 10, 1...10 stops before it, and "a".."z"
works for anything with a successor and a comparison. Ranges are lazy: they store only the two ends.
A range can be endless (1..) or beginless (..5), which makes them useful as slice bounds (a[1..]) and with lazy
enumeration. cover? is O(1), while size and include? on non-numeric ranges may iterate.
Iteration needs a successor, so Float ranges use step. Range#bsearch does binary search over an integer range
when the block is monotone.

 Common misconception. (0..a.size) is the right range for visiting every index of an array.
The two-dot range includes its end, the three-dot range stops before it. The valid indexes of an array are 0...a.size, so
(0..a.size) visits one extra index, where a[i] is nil. (1..5).size is 5 and (1...5).size is 4. For simple loops prefer
each_index or each_with_index.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def doubled_bad(a)
  (0..a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end
Correct:
 def doubled(a)
  (0...a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end
An endless range cannot be turned into an array; take from it or use lazy
ruby-range-endless   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-range-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-range-exclusive. Follow-up: ruby-range-member. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (1..).to_a returns the numbers from 1 upwards.
An endless range (1..) has no last element, so to_a raises RangeError (cannot convert endless range to an array).
Use first(n), take_while, find, or lazy to consume only what you need. The same range works as a slice end: a[1..] is
the array without its first element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def first_squares_bad(n)
  (1..).to_a.first(n).map { |x| x * x }
end
Correct:
 def first_squares(n)
  (1..).lazy.map { |x| x * x }.first(n)
end

A Float range cannot be iterated with each; use step
ruby-range-float   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-range-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-range-member. Follow-up: ruby-range-bsearch. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (0.0..1.0).each walks the values with a step of 0.1.
Iteration needs a successor, and Float has none, so each on a Float range raises TypeError (can't iterate from Float).
Use (0.0..1.0).step(0.25) for evenly spaced values, or iterate over integers and scale. step is O(number of values).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  out = []
  (0.0..1.0).each { |x| out << x }
  out
end
Correct:

  (0.0..1.0).step(0.25).to_a
end
cover? tests the bounds, include? tests membership; they differ for string ranges
ruby-range-member   lens: equality   level: L3   family: ruby-range-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-range-endless. Follow-up: ruby-range-float. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. include? and cover? give the same answer for every range.
For numeric ranges both compare against the bounds. For a string range ("a".."z"), include? checks whether the
value is one of the generated elements, while cover? only checks begin <= value <= end by string comparison, so
"bb" is covered but not included. cover? is O(1); include? on a string range may iterate.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

end
Correct:
 def in_letters?(s)

end

Page 6
Range#bsearch needs a monotone block: false then true; testing == is not monotone
ruby-range-bsearch   lens: patterns   level: L4   family: ruby-range-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-range-float. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. bsearch { |x| x * x == n } finds the square root.
In find-minimum mode the block must be false for small values and true from some point on. The test x * x == n is
false again after the root, so it is not monotone and the search may return nil even though a root exists. Search for
the first x with x * x > n and subtract one to get the floor of the square root. Binary search over an integer range is
O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def isqrt_bad(n)
  (0..n).bsearch { |x| x * x == n }
end
Correct:
 def isqrt(n)
  (0..n + 1).bsearch { |x| x * x > n } - 1
end

Prompt. Why must a Range#bsearch block in find-minimum mode be monotone?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Binary search discards half of the range after each probe, assuming that
if the block is true at some x it stays true for every larger x, and false for every smaller one. A block such as x * x == n is
true at one point only, so a probe on the wrong side of it throws away the part that contains the answer. A condition like x
* x > n is false then true, so each probe is safe.

2. Overview and mental model: Red-Black tree
A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are colored so that the root is black, no red node has a red child
and every path to a nil leaf has the same number of black nodes. These rules bound the height by 2 log2(n + 1).
The left-leaning variant implemented here stores a 2-3 tree and needs only three fix-up rules (rotate left, rotate right,
flip colors). It supports insert and search in O(log n); deletion is more involved and is omitted.
Include Enumerable with an in-order each to get sort, min, max and friends. Production libraries typically use a
different red-black variant.

ruby-redblacktree-fixup   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-redblacktree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-redblacktree-rotate. Follow-up: ruby-redblacktree-height. Complexity: O(1).

A single insert can need several fixes on the same node: a right rotation can produce a node with two red children
that must then be flipped. With elsif the flip is skipped and two red children stay in the tree. Apply the three rules in
order with independent ifs: rotate left if only the right child is red, rotate right if two reds are in a row on the left, flip if

2. Overview and mental model: Queue
A queue is a first-in, first-out structure. Ruby's Array can act as one through push and shift, and shift is O(1)
amortised in CRuby. A custom queue shows what happens underneath and fixes capacity when needed.
enqueue and dequeue are O(1) in a linked queue, a ring buffer and an amortised two-stack queue. Typical uses are
breadth-first search, task scheduling and sliding windows.
Watch the empty-to-nonempty transitions: reset the tail in a linked queue, wrap indexes with modulo in a ring buffer,
and move between stacks only when the output side is empty.

A linked queue must reset its tail when the last node is dequeued
ruby-queue-linked   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-queue-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-queue-twostack. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue only needs to move the head pointer.
When the last node is removed the head becomes nil but the tail still points to the removed node. The next enqueue
then links the new node behind the dead node, and the queue looks empty or loses elements. Reset the tail to nil
whenever the head becomes nil. enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    @head = @tail = nil
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = [v, nil]
    if @tail
      @tail[1] = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head[0]
    @head = @head[1]
    v
  end
  def to_a
    out = []
    node = @head
    while node
      out << node[0]
      node = node[1]
    end
    out
  end
end

 class QNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value)
    @value = value

end
class LinkedQueue
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = QNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head.value
    @head = @head.next
    @tail = nil unless @head
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    @head && @head.value
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end

Breadth-first search marks a node as seen when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued
ruby-queue-bfs   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-ring. Follow-up: ruby-queue-movingavg. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. Marking a node visited when it is dequeued avoids repeats.
A node reachable by two paths is enqueued twice if it is only marked on dequeue, producing duplicates in the visiting
order and wasted work. Mark on enqueue so each node enters the queue once. An Array works as the queue
because shift is O(1) amortised in CRuby. BFS is O(V + E).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def bfs_bad(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = {}
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    seen[node] = true
    order << node
    graph[node].each { |n| queue.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Correct:
 def bfs(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = { start => true }
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node
    graph[node].each do |n|
      next if seen[n]
      seen[n] = true
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  order
end
A moving average keeps a queue of the window and divides by its current length
ruby-queue-movingavg   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-bfs. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Dividing the running sum by the window size is right from the first value.
Until the window fills, the queue holds fewer values than the window size, so dividing by the size understates the
average. Add the new value, subtract the value that leaves the queue, and divide by the queue length. fdiv avoids
integer division. Each update is O(1).

A ring buffer queue wraps its indexes with modulo so storage stays fixed
ruby-queue-ring   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-twostack. Follow-up: ruby-queue-bfs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Advancing head and tail with += 1 is enough for a fixed-size queue.
Without modulo the indexes grow forever, and assigning past the end of a Ruby Array silently extends it, so the
supposedly fixed buffer keeps growing. Wrap with (i + 1) % capacity. Track size separately to tell full from empty.
enqueue and dequeue are O(1) with constant memory.

Correct:
 class RingQueue
  def initialize(cap)
    @buf = Array.new(cap)
    @head = @tail = @size = 0
  end
  def slots
    @buf.size
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    return false if @size == @buf.size
    @buf[@tail] = v
    @tail = (@tail + 1) % @buf.size
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil if @size.zero?
    v = @buf[@head]
    @buf[@head] = nil
    @head = (@head + 1) % @buf.size
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def to_a
    Array.new(@size) { |i| @buf[(@head + i) % @buf.size] }
  end
end

A queue from two stacks moves items across only when the output stack is empty
ruby-queue-twostack   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-linked. Follow-up: ruby-queue-ring. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue can always move everything from the input stack to the output stack first.
Moving every time puts newer items on top of older ones that are still waiting in the output stack, so the order is
wrong. Transfer only when the output stack is empty. Each element moves at most once, so dequeue is O(1)
amortised.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
end
Correct:
 class TwoStackQueue
  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty? if @out.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
  def size
    @in.size + @out.size
  end
end

Prompt. Why is dequeue O(1) amortised in a queue built from two stacks even though one call can move many
elements?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output
stack at most once, and popped once. A single dequeue may transfer many elements, but the transfer only happens
when the output stack is empty, so across n operations the total number of moves is at most n. The cost spread over all
operations is constant per operation.

2. Overview and mental model: Doubly linked list
A doubly linked list stores prev and next links in every node. With head and tail sentinels, insertion and removal given
a node are O(1) with no special cases for the ends.
It is the structure behind LRU caches: a Hash maps keys to nodes and the list orders them by recency. Positional
access is O(n); use an Array when you index often.
Including Enumerable and defining each and reverse_each gives forward and backward traversal plus map, select,
sort and more.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Inserting between two nodes rewires four pointers, and sentinels remove the edge cases
ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Inserting after a node only needs node.next and the new node's prev.
A doubly linked list has two links per edge. Inserting between a and b must set the new node's prev and next and also
a.next and b.prev. Forgetting b.prev leaves the backward chain skipping the new node, so forward and backward
traversal disagree. Head and tail sentinel nodes mean every real node has both neighbours, so push_front,
push_back and middle inserts share one code path in O(1).

  fresh.next = node.next
  fresh.prev = node
  node.next = fresh
  fresh
end

 class DNode
  attr_accessor :value, :prev, :next
  def initialize(value = nil)
    @value = value
  end
end
class DList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = DNode.new
    @tail = DNode.new
    @head.next = @tail
    @tail.prev = @head
    @size = 0
  end
  def link_after(node, fresh)
    fresh.prev = node
    fresh.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = fresh
    node.next = fresh
    @size += 1
    fresh
  end
  def insert_after(node, v)
    link_after(node, DNode.new(v))
  end
  def push_front(v)
    insert_after(@head, v)
  end
  def push_back(v)
    insert_after(@tail.prev, v)
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head.next
    until node.equal?(@tail)
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
  def reverse_each
    return to_enum(:reverse_each) unless block_given?
    node = @tail.prev
    until node.equal?(@head)
      yield node.value
      node = node.prev
    end
  end
end

Index from the nearer end, and normalise negative indexes before walking
ruby-doublylinkedlist-at   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-access
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Walking i times from the head also handles negative indexes.
Integer#times does nothing for a negative count, so a negative index silently returns the first element. Normalise it by
adding the size, reject out-of-range values with nil, then walk from whichever end is closer, at most size/2 steps.
Access by position is still O(n); a list is not a replacement for an Array when you index a lot.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def at_bad(list, i)
  node = list.head.next
  i.times { node = node.next }
  node.value
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def at(i)
    i += @size if i < 0
    return nil unless i >= 0 && i < @size
    if i < @size / 2
      node = @head.next
      i.times { node = node.next }
    else
      node = @tail.prev
      (@size - 1 - i).times { node = node.prev }
    end
    node.value
  end
end
Removing a node you already hold is O(1) because it knows both neighbours
ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Unlinking a node only needs prev.next = node.next.
The node after the removed one still points back to it through prev unless node.next.prev is updated too. Backward
traversal then visits a node that forward traversal no longer sees. With both links fixed, removal given a node
reference is O(1); a singly linked list must first find the previous node in O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def remove_bad(node)
  node.prev.next = node.next
  node.value
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def remove(node)
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev
    @size -= 1
    node.value
  end
end

Reverse a doubly linked list by swapping prev and next in every node, sentinels included
ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-at. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. After swapping a node's links, node.next still leads to the next node to visit.
Once node.next and node.prev are swapped, node.next points to the old previous node, so advancing with it walks
backwards and stops at once. Save the old next first, swap, then move on. Swap the two sentinels too, then
exchange the head and tail references. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reverse_bad(list)
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
    node = node.next
  end
  list
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def reverse!
    node = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
      node = nxt
    end
    @head, @tail = @tail, @head
    self
  end
end
An LRU cache pairs a Hash for lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order
ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Hash alone can evict the least recently used key, even if get never refreshes it.
A Hash keeps insertion order, not usage order, so get must move the entry to the most recent end. A list gives O(1)
unlink and relink, and the Hash maps each key to its node, so get and put are both O(1). Evict the node before the tail
sentinel and delete its key from the Hash as well.

 class LRU
  def initialize(cap)
    @cap = cap
    @map = {}
    @list = DList.new
  end
  def get(k)
    node = @map[k]
    return nil unless node
    @list.remove(node)
    @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
    node.value[1]
  end
  def put(k, v)
    if (node = @map[k])
      @list.remove(node)
      @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
      node.value = [k, v]
      return v
    end
    if @map.size >= @cap
      old = @list.tail.prev
      @list.remove(old)
      @map.delete(old.value[0])
    end
    @map[k] = @list.push_front([k, v])
    v
  end
end

Prompt. Why do head and tail sentinel nodes simplify a doubly linked list?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). With sentinels every real node always has a previous and a next node,
so insert and remove never have to test for the first or last node or update separate head and tail references. push_front,
push_back and middle inserts all use the same four pointer updates, and an empty list is just two linked sentinels, which
removes a whole class of nil bugs.

2. Overview and mental model: Data
Data.define(:x, :y) (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class. Instances are frozen, have readers but no setters,
compare by value and have a stable hash. with(x: 5) returns a modified copy.
Construction is strict: every member is required (positionally or by keyword) and extra arguments raise
ArgumentError. Defaults come from overriding initialize with keyword defaults and calling super.
Immutability is shallow: mutable members such as arrays can still change unless you copy and freeze them. Use
Data for keys, set elements and values passed between layers; use Struct when you need mutation.

Data instances have no setters; use with to get a changed copy
ruby-data-immutable   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ruby-data-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-data-args. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Data object can be changed with a setter like a Struct.
Data.define(:x, :y) creates readers only, and instances are frozen. Assigning pt.x = 5 raises NoMethodError, and
instance_variable_set raises FrozenError. with(x: 5) returns a new object with the changed field and leaves the
original untouched.

Data defines ==, eql? and hash from its members, and instances cannot change, so their hash code stays valid in a

Purpose and mental model
Bubble sort as an adjacent-swap teaching algorithm, with early-exit optimization.
Why Rust changes this topic
The algorithmic idea is language-independent, but the implementation must make ownership, aliasing, mutation, failure, and allocation explicit. Prefer borrowing slices and references for read-only work, narrowly scoped &mut borrows for mutation, owned values when ownership transfer is the cleanest API, and smart pointers/interior mutability only when the data model genuinely requires shared topology.
Recognition vocabulary

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
fn sort<T: Ord>(a: &mut [T]) {    // Implement using indices/slice operations; avoid unnecessary Clone bounds.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Space. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
using in production: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
missing shrink bound: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
comparison overflow: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

Suggested Practice families
Arrays/strings: Two Sum, 3Sum, Product Except Self, Longest Substring, Minimum Window.
Linked/tree: Reverse Linked List, Cycle Detection, Merge Lists, Validate BST, Lowest Common Ancestor.
Graph: Number of Islands, Course Schedule, Network Delay, Redundant Connection.
DP/greedy: House Robber, Coin Change, LIS, LCS, Jump Game.
Heap/interval: Top K Frequent, Kth Largest, Merge Intervals, Meeting Rooms.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.
Unsafe code is justified only when implementing low-level abstractions that Safe Rust cannot express efficiently. The unsafe block must be smaller than the safe abstraction and its invariants must be documented and testable.

Purpose and mental model
Cell<T> for copy/replace-style interior mutation of small values without exposing references.
Why Rust changes this topic
The algorithmic idea is language-independent, but the implementation must make ownership, aliasing, mutation, failure, and allocation explicit. Prefer borrowing slices and references for read-only work, narrowly scoped &mut borrows for mutation, owned values when ownership transfer is the cleanest API, and smart pointers/interior mutability only when the data model genuinely requires shared topology.
Recognition vocabulary
Cell: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
get: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
set: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
replace: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
interior mutability: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.
Question
Rust-specific answer
Failure if ignored
Who owns each value?
Name owner, borrowers, and drop point.
moves, dangling design assumptions, clone-heavy code
Where can mutation occur?
One active &mut, or controlled interior mutability.
borrow conflicts or runtime RefCell panic
What represents absence/failure?
Option / Result, not magic sentinels.
invalid state and panics
What is identity?
Index, key, pointer identity, or value equality.
incorrect graph/list behavior
What must remain invariant?
Cell structural/algorithmic invariant.
silent wrong answers or unsound unsafe code

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
// Canonical Rust 2021 sketch for cellfn demo<T>(input: &[T]) {    let _n = input.len();    // Preserve ownership and borrowing invariants explicitly.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(1). Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
using for non-Copy reads: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
hidden shared mutation: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
confusing with RefCell: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

6. Exercises and Practice-equivalent practice
Exercise type
Prompt
Grading
Predict ownership
Mark every variable as moved, immutably borrowed, mutably borrowed, copied, or cloned after each statement.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Compiler diagnosis
Given a borrow-checker error, state the aliasing problem before changing code.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Implement
Implement Cell in Safe Rust without unnecessary Clone bounds.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Constraint flip
Return borrowed output instead of owned output, or remove allocation while preserving correctness.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Practice equivalent
Solve a canonical medium problem that exercises this pattern using Rust 2021 signatures.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Complexity defense
Defend O(1) and include allocation/refcount/hash costs that Big-O hides.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Unsafe review
If an unsafe version exists, list every safety invariant and show how the public API preserves it.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Suggested Practice families
Arrays/strings: Two Sum, 3Sum, Product Except Self, Longest Substring, Minimum Window.
Linked/tree: Reverse Linked List, Cycle Detection, Merge Lists, Validate BST, Lowest Common Ancestor.
Graph: Number of Islands, Course Schedule, Network Delay, Redundant Connection.
DP/greedy: House Robber, Coin Change, LIS, LCS, Jump Game.
Heap/interval: Top K Frequent, Kth Largest, Merge Intervals, Meeting Rooms.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Interior Mutability. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.
Unsafe code is justified only when implementing low-level abstractions that Safe Rust cannot express efficiently. The unsafe block must be smaller than the safe abstraction and its invariants must be documented and testable.

Curriculum progression
Beginner: syntax + ownership model + standard collections + simple loops.
Intermediate: slice-first APIs + HashMap/VecDeque/BinaryHeap + recursion + graph/DP patterns.
Advanced: custom pointer-based structures + interior mutability + custom traits/iterators + safe unsafe abstractions.
Retrieval guidance
Filter by track, rust_edition, safety_profile, level, record_type, and topic before semantic retrieval. When debugging a compiler error, retrieve the topic concept plus ownership/borrowing gotchas. When solving interview problems, retrieve the algorithm concept plus one reference guide and staged exercise hints rather than the final solution first.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(V^3) Time, O(V^2) Space. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

loop order wrong: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
overflow: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
quadratic memory: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.

Purpose and mental model

Why Rust changes this topic
The algorithmic idea is language-independent, but the implementation must make ownership, aliasing, mutation, failure, and allocation explicit. Prefer borrowing slices and references for read-only work, narrowly scoped &mut borrows for mutation, owned values when ownership transfer is the cleanest API, and smart pointers/interior mutability only when the data model genuinely requires shared topology.

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(E log V) typical; heuristic-dependent. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
inadmissible heuristic: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
wrong heap ordering: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
stale entries: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.
Unsafe code is justified only when implementing low-level abstractions that Safe Rust cannot express efficiently. The unsafe block must be smaller than the safe abstraction and its invariants must be documented and testable.

Purpose and mental model
VecDeque<T> as ring buffer/deque for BFS, sliding windows, scheduling, and avoiding Vec::remove(0).
Why Rust changes this topic
The algorithmic idea is language-independent, but the implementation must make ownership, aliasing, mutation, failure, and allocation explicit. Prefer borrowing slices and references for read-only work, narrowly scoped &mut borrows for mutation, owned values when ownership transfer is the cleanest API, and smart pointers/interior mutability only when the data model genuinely requires shared topology.
Recognition vocabulary
VecDeque: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
push_back: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
pop_front: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
ring buffer: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
BFS: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.

Where can mutation occur?
One active &mut, or controlled interior mutability.
borrow conflicts or runtime RefCell panic
What represents absence/failure?
Option / Result, not magic sentinels.
invalid state and panics
What is identity?
Index, key, pointer identity, or value equality.
incorrect graph/list behavior
What must remain invariant?
Vecdeque structural/algorithmic invariant.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
use std::collections::VecDeque;let mut q = VecDeque::from([0usize]);while let Some(u) = q.pop_front() {    // process u}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: push/pop both ends O(1) amortized. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
assuming contiguous storage: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
indexing across wrap: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
using Vec as queue: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

Return borrowed output instead of owned output, or remove allocation while preserving correctness.

Defend push/pop both ends O(1) amortized and include allocation/refcount/hash costs that Big-O hides.

Unsafe review
If an unsafe version exists, list every safety invariant and show how the public API preserves it.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
Suggested Practice families
Arrays/strings: Two Sum, 3Sum, Product Except Self, Longest Substring, Minimum Window.
Linked/tree: Reverse Linked List, Cycle Detection, Merge Lists, Validate BST, Lowest Common Ancestor.
Graph: Number of Islands, Course Schedule, Network Delay, Redundant Connection.
DP/greedy: House Robber, Coin Change, LIS, LCS, Jump Game.
Heap/interval: Top K Frequent, Kth Largest, Merge Intervals, Meeting Rooms.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.
Unsafe code is justified only when implementing low-level abstractions that Safe Rust cannot express efficiently. The unsafe block must be smaller than the safe abstraction and its invariants must be documented and testable.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: Closure-call overhead normally optimized away. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

wrong closure trait: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
moving captured state unexpectedly: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
borrow lasts through closure: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

Which lines only borrow?

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: State-dependent. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
borrow memo entry across recursive call: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
clone-heavy cached values: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
wrong key state: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

7. Trait and iterator integration
Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.
Use Iterator adapters for transformations when they clarify the invariant; use explicit loops when mutation, early exits, or state transitions are clearer.
Avoid unnecessary trait bounds. A read-only algorithm on &[T] should not require Clone unless it actually duplicates values.

8. Safe vs interior-mutability vs unsafe design
This unit defaults to safety_profile=Safe Rust. Safe Rust should remain the first choice.
Interior mutability is appropriate when the ownership model requires mutation through shared ownership; it moves some checking to runtime and must be deliberately scoped.
Unsafe code is justified only when implementing low-level abstractions that Safe Rust cannot express efficiently. The unsafe block must be smaller than the safe abstraction and its invariants must be documented and testable.

Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.

Where meaningful, expose iter()/iter_mut()/IntoIterator rather than forcing index-based access. Custom ordered elements must satisfy consistent Eq/Ord contracts.

Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.

Purpose and mental model
Choosing Copy, Clone, move, borrow, or ownership transfer in algorithms and custom containers.
Why Rust changes this topic

Copy: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
Clone: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.

clone_from: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.
ownership: learner should recognize and explain this term in a Rust implementation.

1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.

One active &mut, or controlled interior mutability.
borrow conflicts or runtime RefCell panic
What represents absence/failure?

invalid state and panics
What is identity?

incorrect graph/list behavior
What must remain invariant?
Copy Vs Clone structural/algorithmic invariant.

2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.

3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
// Canonical Rust 2021 sketch for copy-vs-clonefn demo<T>(input: &[T]) {    let _n = input.len();    // Preserve ownership and borrowing invariants explicitly.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?

4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: Copy O(1) for small values; Clone type-dependent. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

5. Common gotchas and compiler-guided debugging
cloning to silence borrow checker: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
assuming Clone is cheap: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Copy on large semantic objects: predict the compiler/runtime symptom, explain the violated invariant, then repair without reflexive cloning.
Rc cycles leak because reference counts never reach zero; use Weak for non-owning back-links.
RefCell borrow rules are checked at runtime; overlapping borrow_mut calls panic.
usize underflow/overflow and index math deserve explicit boundary reasoning.
String/&str indexing is byte-based at slicing boundaries; Unicode code points and grapheme clusters are different concepts.
sort_by comparator must define a coherent ordering; prefer cmp/then_with instead of arithmetic subtraction.

Return borrowed output instead of owned output, or remove allocation while preserving correctness.
correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity

correctness + Rust idioms + invariant + complexity
