4.4 Algorithm chunks
isSubsetOf tests membership of every element; comparing sizes is not a subset test
ts-set-subset   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-set-subset
Prerequisites: ts-set-algebra. Follow-up: ts-set-unique-by. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a is a subset of b whenever a.size <= b.size.
A smaller set need not be contained in the larger one. Use a.isSubsetOf(b), isSupersetOf or isDisjointFrom. Two sets
are equal when their sizes match and one is a subset of the other.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isSubsetBad(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): boolean {
  return a.size <= b.size;
}
Correct:
 function isSubset(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): boolean {
  return a.isSubsetOf(b);
}

TypeScript Set: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
union, intersection and difference return new Sets; hand-written loops often mutate an input
ts-set-algebra   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-set-methods
Prerequisites: ts-set-order. Follow-up: ts-set-subset. Complexity: O(min(n, m)).
 Common misconception. Removing items from a while iterating is a safe way to compute the intersection with b.
Deleting during iteration is legal, but it changes the input set, which surprises callers. The ES2025 methods
a.union(b), a.intersection(b), a.difference(b) and a.symmetricDifference(b) return new Sets and leave both inputs
alone. Check the runtime supports them (Node 22 does).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function commonBad(a: Set<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): Set<number> {
  for (const x of a) if (!b.has(x)) a.delete(x);
  return a;
}
Correct:
 function common(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): Set<number> {
  return a.intersection(b);
}
To keep the first item for each key, track seen keys in a Set; a Map built from pairs keeps the
last
ts-set-unique-by   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-set-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-set-subset. Follow-up: ts-set-readonly. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. new Map(items.map(i => [key(i), i])).values() keeps the first item per key.
When a Map is built from pairs, later pairs overwrite earlier ones, so it keeps the last item for each key. A filter with a
Set of seen keys keeps the first and preserves the original order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function uniqueByBad<T>(xs: readonly T[], key: (x: T) => string): T[] {
  return [...new Map(xs.map((x) => [key(x), x] as const)).values()];
}
Correct:
 function uniqueBy<T>(xs: readonly T[], key: (x: T) => string): T[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  return xs.filter((x) => {
    const k = key(x);
    if (seen.has(k)) return false;
    seen.add(k);
    return true;
  });
}

Return ReadonlySet<T> to stop callers adding values; the type is erased, so copy when you
need real protection
ts-set-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-set-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-set-unique-by. Follow-up: ts-set-literal-narrowing. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A function that returns its internal Set can be trusted not to have it modified by callers.
A returned Set<T> lets callers call add and delete on your private state. The type ReadonlySet<T> removes those
methods at compile time (TS2339 on add). The restriction is not enforced at runtime, so return new Set(internal)
when callers are untrusted.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function addBad(s: ReadonlySet<number>): void {
  s.add(1);
}
Correct:
 class Tags {
  private items = new Set<string>();
  add(t: string): void { this.items.add(t); }
  view(): ReadonlySet<string> { return this.items; }
  copy(): Set<string> { return new Set(this.items); }
}
Set<"a" | "b">.has(x) rejects a plain string; widen the Set to ReadonlySet<string> to use has
as a type guard
ts-set-literal-narrowing   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: ts-set-typing
Prerequisites: ts-set-readonly. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. ALLOWED.has(input) narrows input to the literal union.
Set.has is typed to accept only T, so a string argument is error TS2345 when T is a literal union, and has does not
narrow its argument anyway. Declare the Set as ReadonlySet<string>, then write an explicit type guard that returns
input is Role.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 const ROLES = new Set(["admin", "user"] as const);
type Role = "admin" | "user";
function isRoleBad(x: string): x is Role {
  return ROLES.has(x);
}
Correct:
 const ROLE_SET: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set(["admin", "user"]);
type Role = "admin" | "user";
function isRole(x: string): x is Role {
  return ROLE_SET.has(x);
}

Page 1
TypeScript Tuple
A training document for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It teaches the TypeScript tuple type: fixed length,
push, inference, optional and rest elements, destructuring, labels, identity and variadic tuples.
13 October 2026. Every example in this document was executed in TypeScript 5.9 (strict mode) on Node 22: 8 concept chunks and 5
exercises, with 16 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.
Built for retrieval. Each concept card is one RAG chunk (one misconception, one explanation, one failing and one
passing example) and each exercise is one more. The algorithms and strategies live in their own section (4) and are
tagged section: algorithms-and-strategies in the metadata, so the mentor can filter to them.
Contents
  1. How to use this document
 2. Overview and mental model: Tuple
 3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
 4. Typing strategies for fixed-shape data

 6. Core practice exercises with answer key

Page 2
1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.
Reader

algorithm toolkit and practice problems

 8 concept chunks, 2 in core concepts and 6 in the algorithms section.
 5 exercises, graded by exact match, rubric or judge.
 28 reference records built from the overview, traversal catalogue, strategy chooser, live outputs, gotchas and
levels.
 Answers live only in the exercise payload. The embedded text of an exercise is the prompt alone, so retrieval
cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: Tuple
A tuple is an array type with a fixed length and a type for each position, such as [number, string]. It exists only in the
type checker: at run time a tuple is an ordinary array.
The compiler checks positions and the length of literals, but it does not stop push, pop or splice on a mutable tuple.
Declare readonly tuples when the shape must not change.
Use tuples for short, ordered, heterogeneous values (pairs, coordinates, function arguments, return values). Use an
object when fields need names.
Toolbox
 const p: [number, string] = [1, "a"];
const [n, s] = p;                       // n: number, s: string
const r = [1, "a"] as const;           // readonly [1, "a"]
type Range = [start: number, end?: number];
type Cat<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]> = [...A, ...B];
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
2 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Tuple: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
A tuple has a fixed length: reading an index past the end is error TS2493
ts-tuple-fixed-length   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-tuple-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-tuple-push-hole. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A tuple behaves like an array, so t[2] on a two-element tuple is undefined and allowed.
The tuple type [number, string] knows it has exactly two elements. Reading t[2] is error TS2493 ("Tuple type of length
2 has no element at index 2"), unlike a number[] where any index is accepted. That is the main benefit of tuples:
wrong positions are caught at compile time. At run time a tuple is an ordinary array.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2493):
 function thirdBad(t: [number, string]): unknown {
  return t[2];
}
Correct:
 function second(t: [number, string]): string {
  return t[1];
}
TypeScript allows push on a tuple, so the runtime length can differ from the type; return a
new tuple instead
ts-tuple-push-hole   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-fixed-length. Follow-up: ts-tuple-inference. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A [number, number] tuple cannot grow, because its length is part of the type.
Methods such as push, pop and splice are still available on a mutable tuple and the compiler does not track them.
After t.push(3) the value has three elements while its type says two. Treat tuples as immutable: declare them
readonly, or build a new tuple with spread and an explicit return type.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function addBad(t: [number, number]): [number, number] {
  t.push(9);
  return t;
}
Correct:
 function add(t: readonly [number, number]): [number, number, number] {
  return [...t, 9];
}
4. Typing strategies for fixed-shape data
These chunks cover tuple strategies: inferring tuples, optional and rest shapes, safe destructuring, labels, hashing
coordinates and variadic composition. Every row is backed by a tested chunk.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
An array literal is inferred as an array, not a tuple; annotate it or use as const
ts-tuple-inference   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-creation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-push-hole. Follow-up: ts-tuple-optional-rest. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. const p = [1, "a"] has the tuple type [number, string].
TypeScript infers (string | number)[] for [1, "a"]. Assigning that variable to a [number, string] parameter is error
TS2322. Write the annotation (const p: [number, string] = [1, "a"]) or use as const, which gives readonly [1, "a"].
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 const pairBad = [1, "a"];
const tBad: [number, string] = pairBad;
Correct:
 const pair: [number, string] = [1, "a"];
const frozen = [1, "a"] as const;
function label(p: readonly [number, string]): string {
  return `${p[0]}:${p[1]}`;
}
Destructuring an array gives string, not string | undefined; check the length or use a tuple
ts-tuple-destructure   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-access
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-optional-rest. Follow-up: ts-tuple-labels. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. const [a, b] = xs always gives two strings when xs is a string[].
For an array type the compiler assumes every element exists, so b has type string even when the array has one
element, and the result is "undefined" at run time. A tuple type or a length check proves the shape. The compiler
option noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to array reads.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function joinBad(xs: string[]): string {
  const [a, b] = xs;
  return a + b;
}
Correct:
 function join(xs: string[]): string | null {
  if (xs.length < 2) return null;
  const [a, b] = xs as [string, string];
  return a + b;
}

TypeScript Tuple: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Tuples are arrays, so a Set or Map keyed by a tuple compares references; key by a string
ts-tuple-identity   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-equality
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-labels. Follow-up: ts-tuple-variadic. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. new Set([[1, 2]]).has([1, 2]) is true.
Two tuple literals are different objects, so Set.has and Map.get never find an equal-looking key. For grids and
coordinate pairs, build a string key such as `${x},${y}` or a numeric key, and convert back when needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function visitedBad(seen: Set<[number, number]>, x: number, y: number): boolean {
  return seen.has([x, y]);
}
Correct:
 function visited(seen: Set<string>, x: number, y: number): boolean {
  return seen.has(`${x},${y}`);
}
Optional and rest elements make a tuple flexible, but an optional element can be undefined
ts-tuple-optional-rest   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-tuple-creation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-inference. Follow-up: ts-tuple-destructure. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. In [string, number?] the second element is always a number.
The ? marks an element that may be missing, so its type is number | undefined, and arithmetic on it is error TS2532.
A rest element ([number, ...string[]]) allows any number of trailing items. Handle the optional case with ?? or a check.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2532):
 function bumpBad(t: [string, number?]): number {
  return t[1] + 1;
}
Correct:
 function bump(t: [string, number?]): number {
  return (t[1] ?? 0) + 1;
}
function head(t: [number, ...string[]]): number {
  return t[0];
}

TypeScript Tuple: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Labels document tuple positions but are not property names; destructure to use them
ts-tuple-labels   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-tuple-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-destructure. Follow-up: ts-tuple-identity. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. With [start: number, end: number], r.start reads the first element.
Labels exist only for editors and error messages. The tuple is still indexed by position, and r.start is error TS2339.
Destructure ([start, end]) or index with 0 and 1. If the data needs real names, use an object type.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function spanBad(r: [start: number, end: number]): number {
  return r.end - r.start;
}
Correct:
 function span(r: [start: number, end: number]): number {
  const [start, end] = r;
  return end - start;
}
Variadic tuple types let concat return [...A, ...B]; without them the result widens to an array
ts-tuple-variadic   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ts-tuple-transform
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-identity. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Spreading two tuples into an array literal keeps their element types.
Without an explicit return type, [...a, ...b] has type (A[number] | B[number])[], and assigning it to [number, string] is
error TS2322. A generic function with A extends unknown[] and B extends unknown[] can return [...A, ...B], which
keeps positions.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 function concatBad<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]>(a: A, b: B) {
  return [...a, ...b];
}
const tt: [number, string] = concatBad([1], ["a"]);
Correct:
 function concat<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]>(
  a: [...A],
  b: [...B],
): [...A, ...B] {
  return [...a, ...b];
}
const joined: [number, string] = concat([1], ["a"]);

Page 8

ts-tuple-identity-ex1   format: predict-output   level: L1   grading: exact   modes: practice, quiz
Prompt. What does String(new Set([[1, 2]]).has([1, 2])) return?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). false

Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). undefined
ts-tuple-labels-ex1   format: choose-the-structure   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. A function returns a start and an end position. Compare returning a tuple, an object and a two-element

silently and it is easier to extend. A plain number[] loses the length and position checks. Prefer an object when there are
more than two values or the order is not obvious.

2. Overview and mental model: WeakSet
A WeakSet is a set of objects that does not keep them alive. Membership is by identity, and members vanish when
nothing else references them.
Only add, has and delete exist. There is no size, no iteration, no clear. That is deliberate: collection timing is not
observable.
It is best at marking: objects already processed, nodes already visited, objects issued by a factory. Use a Set
whenever you need to count or list.
Toolbox
 const done = new WeakSet<object>();
const job = {};
done.add(job);
done.has(job);        // true
done.has({});         // false
// done.size          // error TS2339

 type GNode = { id: number; next: GNode[]; seen?: boolean };
function walk(n: GNode, seen: WeakSet<GNode> = new WeakSet(), out: number[] = []): number[] {
  if (seen.has(n)) return out;
  seen.add(n);
  out.push(n.id);
  for (const m of n.next) walk(m, seen, out);
  return out;

2. Overview and mental model: ArrayBuffer
An ArrayBuffer is a fixed block of raw bytes. It has no element type and no index access. You read and write it
through views: typed arrays and DataView.
Many views can sit on one buffer, so a write through one is visible through the others. Copying is explicit (slice),
moving is explicit (transfer), and sharing is the default for views.
Newer features: a buffer can be resizable (maxByteLength, resize) and can be transferred to a new owner, which
detaches the original.
Toolbox
 const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8);
const bytes = new Uint8Array(buf);        // view
const words = new Uint32Array(buf);       // second view, same memory
bytes[0] = 255; words[0];                  // 255 (little-endian)
const copy = buf.slice(0, 4);             // independent copy
const moved = buf.transfer();             // buf is now detached

Only a buffer created with maxByteLength can resize; a fixed buffer throws TypeError
ts-arraybuffer-resizable   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-arraybuffer-resize
Prerequisites: ts-arraybuffer-alignment. Follow-up: ts-arraybuffer-transfer. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Any ArrayBuffer can grow with buf.resize(n).
A normal ArrayBuffer is fixed in size. resize works only on a resizable buffer, created with new ArrayBuffer(n, {
maxByteLength }), and never beyond that maximum. A typed array created with no explicit length on a resizable
buffer tracks the length automatically. Otherwise, allocate a bigger buffer and copy.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  buf.resize(buf.byteLength * 2);
}
Correct:
 function makeGrowable(n: number, max: number): ArrayBuffer {
  return new ArrayBuffer(n, { maxByteLength: max });
}
function growTo(buf: ArrayBuffer, n: number): boolean {
  if (!buf.resizable || n > buf.maxByteLength) return false;
  buf.resize(n);
  return true;
}
Two ArrayBuffers are equal only if you compare their bytes; === checks identity
ts-arraybuffer-equal   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-arraybuffer-equality
Prerequisites: ts-arraybuffer-transfer. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a === b is true for buffers holding the same bytes.
ArrayBuffer is an object, so === and == test identity. Compare byteLength first, then every byte through a Uint8Array
view. In Node, Buffer.compare or buffer.equals does the same.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sameBad(a: ArrayBuffer, b: ArrayBuffer): boolean {
  return a === b;
}
Correct:
 function same(a: ArrayBuffer, b: ArrayBuffer): boolean {
  if (a.byteLength !== b.byteLength) return false;
  const x = new Uint8Array(a);
  const y = new Uint8Array(b);
  for (let i = 0; i < x.length; i++) if (x[i] !== y[i]) return false;
  return true;
}

A view needs the buffer length to be a multiple of its element size, or the constructor throws
RangeError
ts-arraybuffer-alignment   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-arraybuffer-views
Prerequisites: ts-arraybuffer-slice-copy. Follow-up: ts-arraybuffer-resizable. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. new Uint32Array(buf) works for any buffer length.
Each Uint32 element takes four bytes, so a six-byte buffer cannot be covered and the constructor throws RangeError.
Pass an explicit length that fits, new Uint32Array(buf, 0, buf.byteLength >> 2), and handle the leftover bytes yourself.
A non-zero byteOffset must also be a multiple of the element size.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  return new Uint32Array(buf);
}
Correct:
 function asU32(buf: ArrayBuffer): Uint32Array {
  return new Uint32Array(buf, 0, buf.byteLength >> 2);
}
transfer() moves the bytes to a new buffer and detaches the old one; its views become empty
ts-arraybuffer-transfer   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-arraybuffer-ownership
Prerequisites: ts-arraybuffer-resizable. Follow-up: ts-arraybuffer-equal. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. buf.transfer() copies the data and leaves the original usable.
transfer returns a new ArrayBuffer that owns the bytes and detaches the original: byteLength becomes 0, detached is
true, and views over it read as length 0 or undefined. Read what you need first, or build a new view on the returned
buffer. Use slice if you want a copy.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function readAfterMoveBad(buf: ArrayBuffer): number | undefined {
  const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
  buf.transfer();
  return view[0];
}
Correct:
 function moveAndRead(buf: ArrayBuffer): { moved: ArrayBuffer; first: number | undefined } {
  const moved = buf.transfer();
  return { moved, first: new Uint8Array(moved)[0] };
}

TypeScript Trie
A training document for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It teaches the trie (prefix tree) in TypeScript with
typed TrieNode and Trie classes: insert, word versus prefix search, code point iteration, delete with
pruning, autocomplete, wildcard search and longest common prefix. Mnemonist (npm) provides Trie and
TrieMap.

exercises, with 11 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.
Built for retrieval. Each concept card is one RAG chunk (one misconception, one explanation, one failing and one
passing example) and each exercise is one more. The algorithms and strategies live in their own section (4) and are

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

 7 concept chunks, 3 in core concepts and 4 in the algorithms section.
 5 exercises, graded by exact match, rubric or judge.
 29 reference records built from the overview, traversal catalogue, strategy chooser, live outputs, gotchas and
levels.
 Answers live only in the exercise payload. The embedded text of an exercise is the prompt alone, so retrieval
cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: Trie
A trie stores strings in a tree where each edge is one character and words that share a prefix share a path. A flag on
a node marks the end of a stored word.
Insert, search and prefix checks take O(L) time for a word of length L, independent of how many words are stored.
Children are kept in a Map.
Use it for autocomplete, spell checking, prefix counting, wildcard search and longest common prefix. When only exact
membership is needed, a Set is simpler.
Toolbox
 const t = new Trie();
t.insert("apple");
t.has("app");         // false, a prefix only
t.startsWith("app");  // true
complete(t, "ap");    // ["apple"]
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Trie: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Whole-word search checks the end flag; reaching the node only proves a prefix exists
ts-trie-end-flag   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-trie-access
Prerequisites: ts-trie-creation. Follow-up: ts-trie-code-points. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. If walking the word ends at a node, the word is in the trie.
A node exists for every prefix of every stored word. After inserting "apple", the path for "app" exists although "app"
was never inserted. A word search must also check that the final node is marked as the end of a word, while
startsWith only needs the path.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hasBad(t: Trie, word: string): boolean {
  return t.find(word) !== undefined;
}
Correct:
 function hasWord(t: Trie, word: string): boolean {
  const node = t.find(word);
  return node !== undefined && node.end;
}
Insert reuses an existing child node; creating a new node at every character erases earlier
words
ts-trie-creation   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ts-trie-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-trie-end-flag. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. insert can create a fresh node for each character of the word.
Words share their prefixes, which is the point of a trie. Insert must look for an existing child first and create one only
when it is missing. Replacing the child at every character overwrites the subtree that earlier words built, so inserting
"app" after "apple" removes "apple".
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertBad(t: Trie, word: string): void {
  let node = t.root;
  for (const ch of word) {
    const next = new TrieNode();
    node.children.set(ch, next);
    node = next;
  }
  node.end = true;
}

TypeScript Trie: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Correct:
 class TrieNode {
  children = new Map<string, TrieNode>();
  end = false;
}
class Trie {
  root = new TrieNode();
  insert(word: string): void {
    let node = this.root;
    for (const ch of word) {
      let next = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!next) {
        next = new TrieNode();
        node.children.set(ch, next);
      }
      node = next;
    }
    node.end = true;
  }
  find(prefix: string): TrieNode | undefined {
    let node: TrieNode | undefined = this.root;
    for (const ch of prefix) {
      node = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!node) return undefined;
    }
    return node;
  }
  has(word: string): boolean { return this.find(word)?.end === true; }
  startsWith(prefix: string): boolean { return this.find(prefix) !== undefined; }
}
Iterate a word with for...of; an index loop splits characters outside the basic plane
ts-trie-code-points   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-trie-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-trie-end-flag. Follow-up: ts-trie-delete. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. word.length and word[i] walk the characters of a word.
A string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units. Characters such as emoji take two units, so indexing or split("") cuts
them into halves and the trie stores meaningless nodes. for...of and the spread operator iterate whole code points.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function unitsBad(word: string): string[] {
  return word.split("");
}
Correct:
 function codePoints(word: string): string[] {
  return [...word];
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Autocomplete collects only nodes marked as word ends below the prefix node
ts-trie-autocomplete   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-trie-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-trie-delete. Follow-up: ts-trie-wildcard. Complexity: O(P + output).
 Common misconception. Every node below the prefix is a completion.
Interior nodes are prefixes, not words. Collect the path only when the node is marked as a word end. Emitting at
every node returns "ap" and "appl" as suggestions when only "app", "apple" and "apt" were inserted. Start from the
node found for the prefix and return an empty list when it does not exist.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function completeBad(t: Trie, prefix: string): string[] {
  const start = t.find(prefix);
  if (!start) return [];
  const out: string[] = [];
  const walk = (node: TrieNode, acc: string): void => {
    out.push(acc);
    for (const [ch, c] of node.children) walk(c, acc + ch);
  };
  walk(start, prefix);
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function complete(t: Trie, prefix: string): string[] {
  const start = t.find(prefix);
  if (!start) return [];
  const out: string[] = [];
  const walk = (node: TrieNode, acc: string): void => {
    if (node.end) out.push(acc);
    for (const [ch, c] of node.children) walk(c, acc + ch);
  };
  walk(start, prefix);
  return out;
}
Delete clears the end flag and prunes nodes that no longer lead to any word
ts-trie-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ts-trie-deletion
Prerequisites: ts-trie-code-points. Follow-up: ts-trie-autocomplete. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. Deleting a word only needs to clear its end flag.
Clearing the flag makes has() correct but leaves the path in place, so startsWith still reports the prefix and memory is
never freed. After clearing the flag, walk back up and remove each node that has no children and is not the end of
another word, stopping at the first node that is still needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function removeBad(t: Trie, word: string): boolean {
  const node = t.find(word);
  if (!node || !node.end) return false;
  node.end = false;
  return true;
}

TypeScript Trie: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Correct:
 function remove(t: Trie, word: string): boolean {
  const path: Array<[TrieNode, string]> = [];
  let node = t.root;
  for (const ch of word) {
    const next = node.children.get(ch);
    if (!next) return false;
    path.push([node, ch]);
    node = next;
  }
  if (!node.end) return false;
  node.end = false;
  for (let i = path.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const [parent, ch] = path[i] as [TrieNode, string];
    const child = parent.children.get(ch) as TrieNode;
    if (child.end || child.children.size > 0) break;
    parent.children.delete(ch);
  }
  return true;
}
The common prefix stops at the first branch or the first word end
ts-trie-lcp   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-trie-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-trie-wildcard. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. Follow single-child nodes to find the longest common prefix.
A node with one child can still be the end of a stored word, such as "app" among "app" and "apple". The common
prefix of all words stops there, because the short word has no more characters. Stop at a node that has several
children, no child, or the end flag.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function lcpBad(t: Trie): string {
  let node = t.root;
  let out = "";
  while (node.children.size === 1) {
    const [ch, next] = [...node.children][0] as [string, TrieNode];
    out += ch;
    node = next;
  }
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function lcp(t: Trie): string {
  let node = t.root;
  let out = "";
  while (node.children.size === 1 && !node.end) {
    const [ch, next] = [...node.children][0] as [string, TrieNode];
    out += ch;
    node = next;
  }
  return out;
}

TypeScript Trie: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
A wildcard search branches over all children at a dot instead of looking up the dot
ts-trie-wildcard   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-trie-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-trie-autocomplete. Follow-up: ts-trie-lcp. Complexity: O(26^d * L).
 Common misconception. A pattern with "." can be searched with the normal has().
The normal search follows one child per character, so "." is looked up as the literal character and never matches. At a
dot the search must try every child and succeed if any branch matches the rest of the pattern. All other characters
follow one child.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function searchDotBad(t: Trie, pattern: string): boolean {
  return t.has(pattern);
}
Correct:
 function searchDot(t: Trie, pattern: string): boolean {
  const go = (node: TrieNode, i: number): boolean => {
    if (i === pattern.length) return node.end;
    const ch = pattern[i] as string;
    if (ch === ".") {
      for (const c of node.children.values()) if (go(c, i + 1)) return true;
      return false;
    }
    const next = node.children.get(ch);
    return next !== undefined && go(next, i + 1);
  };
  return go(t.root, 0);
}
4.5 Practice with answers
ts-trie-delete-ex1   format: predict-output   level: L3   grading: exact   modes: practice, quiz
Prompt. Two tries each contain only "app". After remove(a, "app") and removeBad(b, "app"), what does
[a.startsWith("app"), b.startsWith("app")].join(" ") return?

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Date
A Date wraps one number: milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Everything else (year, month, weekday) is
computed from it in either UTC or the machine's local zone. Two Dates are only equal if their numbers are.
TypeScript types Date as an object, so it blocks arithmetic operators on Dates and catches wrong argument types. It
cannot see zero-based months, local versus UTC parsing, or invalid dates, which all pass the compiler.
For anything calendar-like, prefer UTC methods, copy before mutating, and validate with getTime(). For heavy date
logic consider the Temporal API or a library.
Toolbox
 const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 0, 31));   // January: month 0
d.getUTCMonth();                         // 0
const t = d.getTime();                   // number of ms
const copy = new Date(d);                // copy before mutating
d.toISOString();                         // "2024-01-31T00:00:00.000Z"
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
5 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Date: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Date months are zero-based (0 is January) while days and years are not
ts-date-month-zero   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-date-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-date-mutable-setters. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. new Date(2024, 3, 1) means March 1st.
The month argument and getMonth() run from 0 to 11, so 3 is April. Days of the month start at 1 and getDay() returns
0 for Sunday. Convert a human month with month - 1 and back with getMonth() + 1. This is the most common
off-by-one error with Date.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function makeBad(y: number, month: number, d: number): Date {
  return new Date(Date.UTC(y, month, d));
}
Correct:
 function make(y: number, month: number, d: number): Date {
  return new Date(Date.UTC(y, month - 1, d));
}
Date setters mutate the object in place; copy the Date before changing it
ts-date-mutable-setters   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-date-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-date-month-zero. Follow-up: ts-date-parse-formats. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. date.setUTCDate(n) returns a new date and leaves the original unchanged.
A Date is mutable. setDate, setMonth, setHours and their UTC versions change the object and return a number (the
new timestamp), not a Date. A helper that changes its argument corrupts the caller's value. Make a copy with new
Date(d) first.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function addDaysBad(d: Date, n: number): Date {
  d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() + n);
  return d;
}
Correct:
 function addDays(d: Date, n: number): Date {
  const r = new Date(d);
  r.setUTCDate(r.getUTCDate() + n);
  return r;
}

TypeScript Date: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Compare dates by getTime(); === compares object identity
ts-date-compare   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-date-equality
Prerequisites: ts-date-invalid. Follow-up: ts-date-sort. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. a === b is true for two Dates that hold the same moment.
Date is an object, so === and == compare references. Two Dates for the same instant are not equal that way.
Compare getTime() values, or use +a === +b. The relational operators < and > work because they convert to
numbers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sameBad(a: Date, b: Date): boolean {
  return a === b;
}
Correct:
 function same(a: Date, b: Date): boolean {
  return a.getTime() === b.getTime();
}
new Date("bad") is an Invalid Date: getTime is NaN and toISOString throws RangeError
ts-date-invalid   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-date-edge
Prerequisites: ts-date-parse-formats. Follow-up: ts-date-compare. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The Date constructor throws on a bad string.
The constructor never throws. It returns a Date whose time value is NaN. Methods like getFullYear return NaN, and
toISOString throws RangeError. Validate with Number.isNaN(d.getTime()) before using the value.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isoBad(s: string): string {
  return new Date(s).toISOString();
}
Correct:
 function iso(s: string): string | null {
  const d = new Date(s);
  return Number.isNaN(d.getTime()) ? null : d.toISOString();
}

TypeScript Date: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
A date-only ISO string is read as UTC but a date-time without a Z is read as local time
ts-date-parse-formats   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-date-creation
Prerequisites: ts-date-mutable-setters. Follow-up: ts-date-invalid. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. new Date("2024-03-10T00:00:00") and new Date("2024-03-10") are the same instant.
The ECMAScript rule is: date-only forms ("2024-03-10") are UTC, while date-time forms without an offset are local
time. The two differ by the time zone offset. Add Z or an explicit offset to a date-time to make parsing independent of
the machine's zone.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function parseDayBad(s: string): Date {
  return new Date(s + "T00:00:00");
}
Correct:
 function parseDay(s: string): Date {
  return new Date(s + "T00:00:00Z");
}

TypeScript Date: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Subtracting Dates is an error in TypeScript (TS2362, TS2363); subtract getTime() values in a
comparator
ts-date-sort   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-date-order
Prerequisites: ts-date-compare. Follow-up: ts-date-month-overflow. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. dates.sort((a, b) => a - b) works because dates convert to numbers.
JavaScript allows it, but TypeScript rejects arithmetic on Date operands with TS2362 (left side) and TS2363 (right
side). Subtract getTime() values. The default sort() converts to strings, which does not order dates correctly.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2362, TS2363):
 function sortBad(ds: Date[]): Date[] {
  return [...ds].sort((a, b) => a - b);
}
Correct:
 function sortDates(ds: readonly Date[]): Date[] {
  return [...ds].sort((a, b) => a.getTime() - b.getTime());
}
JSON turns a Date into an ISO string and parse does not turn it back; rebuild with new Date
ts-date-json   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-date-transform
Prerequisites: ts-date-dst-diff. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(d)) returns a Date.
JSON.stringify calls toISOString, so the output is a string. JSON.parse returns that string, not a Date, even when you
cast it. A cast only changes the compile-time type, so calling getTime then throws TypeError. Wrap the parsed value
in new Date(...).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function roundTripBad(d: Date): Date {
  return JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(d)) as Date;
}
Correct:
 function roundTrip(d: Date): Date {
  return new Date(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(d)) as string);
}

TypeScript Date: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Adding a month to January 31 overflows into March; clamp the day to the end of the target
month
ts-date-month-overflow   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-date-arithmetic
Prerequisites: ts-date-sort. Follow-up: ts-date-dst-diff. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. setUTCMonth(m + 1) on Jan 31 gives Feb 29 or Feb 28.
When the day does not exist in the target month, Date rolls forward: Jan 31 plus one month becomes March 2 or 3.
For billing and calendars you usually want the last day of the target month. Compute the target month length with
Date.UTC(y, m + 1, 0) and take the smaller day.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function addMonthsBad(d: Date, n: number): Date {
  const r = new Date(d);
  r.setUTCMonth(r.getUTCMonth() + n);
  return r;
}
Correct:
 function addMonths(d: Date, n: number): Date {
  const y = d.getUTCFullYear();
  const m = d.getUTCMonth() + n;
  const last = new Date(Date.UTC(y, m + 1, 0)).getUTCDate();
  return new Date(Date.UTC(y, m, Math.min(d.getUTCDate(), last)));
}
Day differences by dividing milliseconds by 86,400,000 break across daylight saving changes
ts-date-dst-diff   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ts-date-arithmetic
Prerequisites: ts-date-month-overflow. Follow-up: ts-date-json. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A day is always 24 hours, so ms / 86400000 counts days.
In zones with daylight saving, a local day can be 23 or 25 hours. Dividing the millisecond difference between two local
midnights gives fractions such as 1.96. Convert both dates to UTC midnight with Date.UTC(year, month, day) and
round the quotient.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function daysBetweenBad(a: Date, b: Date): number {
  return Math.floor((b.getTime() - a.getTime()) / 86_400_000);
}
Correct:
 function daysBetween(a: Date, b: Date): number {
  const ua = Date.UTC(a.getFullYear(), a.getMonth(), a.getDate());
  const ub = Date.UTC(b.getFullYear(), b.getMonth(), b.getDate());
  return Math.round((ub - ua) / 86_400_000);
}

ts-date-dst-diff-ex1   format: choose-the-structure   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. How do you compute the number of calendar days between two Dates so the result is correct across a
daylight saving change?

day can be 23 or 25 hours. Take the calendar parts of each date (year, month, day), build UTC midnights with Date.UTC,
subtract, divide by 86,400,000 and round. Alternatively use a date library or Temporal.

generic AvlNode class: rotations and height updates, the four imbalance cases, rebalancing insert and
delete, a recomputing checker and the Fibonacci height bound.

exercises, with 12 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.

passing example) and each exercise is one more. The algorithms and strategies live in their own section (4) and are

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

 Answers live only in the exercise payload. The embedded text of an exercise is the prompt alone, so retrieval
cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: AVL Tree
An AVL tree is a binary search tree that keeps the heights of the two subtrees of every node within one of each other.
It rebalances with rotations after every insert and delete.
The balance factor is height(left) - height(right). A factor of +2 or -2 is repaired by a single or double rotation (left-left,
left-right, right-right, right-left cases).
Search, insert and delete are O(log n) in the worst case, with height at most about 1.44 log2 n. Use AVL for
read-heavy ordered sets; no built-in sorted tree exists in JavaScript or in Mnemonist.
Toolbox

for (let k = 1; k <= 7; k++) t = insert(t, k, numCmp);
t.key;       // 4, the root of a perfect tree

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)

The worst AVL height is about 1.44 log n, set by the sparsest valid tree, not by a perfect tree
ts-avltree-height-bound   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: ts-avl-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-avltree-checker. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. An AVL tree with n nodes has height floor(log2 n) + 1.
That formula is the height of a perfect tree, the best case. The tallest AVL tree is the sparsest one, where each
subtree of height h has the fewest nodes: minNodes(h) = minNodes(h-1) + minNodes(h-2) + 1, a Fibonacci
recurrence. The maximum height for n nodes is the largest h with minNodes(h) <= n.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function maxHeightBad(n: number): number {
  return Math.floor(Math.log2(n)) + 1;
}
Correct:
 function minNodes(h: number): number {
  if (h <= 0) return 0;
  if (h === 1) return 1;
  return minNodes(h - 1) + minNodes(h - 2) + 1;
}
function maxHeight(n: number): number {
  let h = 0;
  while (minNodes(h + 1) <= n) h++;
  return h;
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
After a rotation, recompute the demoted node first and the new root second
ts-avltree-rotation-heights   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-avl-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-avltree-double-rotation. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. After a rotation the two heights can be updated in either order.
A node height is computed from its children. After rotateRight the old root y becomes a child of the new root x, so y
must be recomputed first. Computing x first reads the stale height of y and stores a wrong height that spreads to
every ancestor.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rotateRightBad<K>(y: AvlNode<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  const x = y.left as AvlNode<K>;
  y.left = x.right;
  x.right = y;
  fix(x);
  fix(y);
  return x;
}

TypeScript AVL Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
Correct:
 class AvlNode<K> {
  height = 1;
  constructor(
    public key: K,
    public left: AvlNode<K> | null = null,
    public right: AvlNode<K> | null = null,
  ) {}
}
function hOf<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null): number {
  return n === null ? 0 : n.height;
}
function fix<K>(n: AvlNode<K>): void {
  n.height = 1 + Math.max(hOf(n.left), hOf(n.right));
}
function rotateRight<K>(y: AvlNode<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  const x = y.left as AvlNode<K>;
  y.left = x.right;
  x.right = y;
  fix(y);
  fix(x);
  return x;
}
function rotateLeft<K>(x: AvlNode<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  const y = x.right as AvlNode<K>;
  x.right = y.left;
  y.left = x;
  fix(x);
  fix(y);
  return y;
}
A left-right case needs a rotation of the child first; one rotation leaves it unbalanced
ts-avltree-double-rotation   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-avl-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-avltree-rotation-heights. Follow-up: ts-avltree-insert. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any imbalance of +2 is fixed by one right rotation.
When the left child is itself right-heavy (balance factor negative), a single right rotation only moves the problem to the
other side. Rotate the left child left first, which turns the case into left-left, then rotate the node right. The mirror case
needs a right rotation of the right child, then a left rotation.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rebalanceBad<K>(n: AvlNode<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  fix(n);
  const b = hOf(n.left) - hOf(n.right);
  if (b > 1) return rotateRight(n);
  if (b < -1) return rotateLeft(n);
  return n;
}

TypeScript AVL Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Correct:
 function bf<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null): number {
  return n === null ? 0 : hOf(n.left) - hOf(n.right);
}
function rebalance<K>(n: AvlNode<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  fix(n);
  const b = bf(n);
  if (b > 1) {
    if (bf(n.left) < 0) n.left = rotateLeft(n.left as AvlNode<K>);
    return rotateRight(n);
  }
  if (b < -1) {
    if (bf(n.right) > 0) n.right = rotateRight(n.right as AvlNode<K>);
    return rotateLeft(n);
  }
  return n;
}
Insert must rebalance every ancestor on the way back, not only update heights
ts-avltree-insert   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ts-avl-insertion
Prerequisites: ts-avltree-double-rotation. Follow-up: ts-avltree-delete. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Updating heights after an insert is enough to keep the tree balanced.
Heights only describe the tree. Each ancestor of the new leaf must be checked and rotated when its balance factor
reaches 2 in absolute value. Without that, sorted input builds a chain with height n, which removes the logarithmic
guarantee.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertBad<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  if (n === null) return new AvlNode(key);
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = insertBad(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = insertBad(n.right, key, cmp);
  fix(n);
  return n;
}
Correct:
 type Cmp<K> = (a: K, b: K) => number;
const numCmp: Cmp<number> = (a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0);
function insert<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): AvlNode<K> {
  if (n === null) return new AvlNode(key);
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = insert(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = insert(n.right, key, cmp);
  else return n;
  return rebalance(n);
}
function inorder<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null): K[] {
  return n === null ? [] : [...inorder(n.left), n.key, ...inorder(n.right)];
}

TypeScript AVL Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
A balance checker must recompute heights from the shape, not trust the stored values
ts-avltree-checker   lens: testing   level: L3   family: ts-avl-testing
Prerequisites: ts-avltree-delete. Follow-up: ts-avltree-height-bound. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Comparing stored height fields proves the tree is balanced.
Stored heights are exactly what a bug corrupts, so a checker that reads them agrees with the bug. Recompute the
height of each subtree from the structure and return a sentinel such as -1 as soon as any node differs by more than
one.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isAvlBad<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null): boolean {
  if (n === null) return true;
  const diff = Math.abs(hOf(n.left) - hOf(n.right));
  return diff <= 1 && isAvlBad(n.left) && isAvlBad(n.right);
}
Correct:
 function checkAvl<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null): number {
  if (n === null) return 0;
  const l = checkAvl(n.left);
  const r = checkAvl(n.right);
  if (l < 0 || r < 0 || Math.abs(l - r) > 1) return -1;
  return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
}
Delete can unbalance an ancestor far above the removed node, so rebalance after every
recursive call
ts-avltree-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L4   family: ts-avl-deletion
Prerequisites: ts-avltree-insert. Follow-up: ts-avltree-checker. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Only inserts need rotations; a delete can only shorten a tree.
Removing a node shortens one side of its ancestors, which can make a sibling side too tall by two. After the recursive
removal (including the successor removal) every ancestor must be rebalanced. A delete may need several rotations
along the path, where an insert needs at most one.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function removeBad<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): AvlNode<K> | null {
  if (n === null) return null;
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = removeBad(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = removeBad(n.right, key, cmp);
  else {
    if (n.left === null) return n.right;
    if (n.right === null) return n.left;
    let s = n.right;
    while (s.left !== null) s = s.left;
    n.key = s.key;
    n.right = removeBad(n.right, s.key, cmp);
  }
  fix(n);
  return n;
}

TypeScript AVL Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 function remove<K>(n: AvlNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): AvlNode<K> | null {
  if (n === null) return null;
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = remove(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = remove(n.right, key, cmp);
  else {
    if (n.left === null) return n.right;
    if (n.right === null) return n.left;
    let s = n.right;
    while (s.left !== null) s = s.left;
    n.key = s.key;
    n.right = remove(n.right, s.key, cmp);
  }
  return rebalance(n);
}

This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Stack
A stack is last in, first out. In JavaScript the natural implementation is an array with push and pop at the end, both
O(1). A class wrapper hides the rest of the array API so the discipline cannot be broken.
pop and peek return T | undefined because the stack may be empty. TypeScript forces you to handle that, which is
the main benefit of a typed wrapper over a raw array.
Stacks appear in parsing (brackets, expressions), undo history, recursion removal (iterative DFS) and
monotonic-stack problems such as next greater element.
Toolbox
 class Stack<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  push(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.pop(); }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.items[this.items.length - 1]; }
}
const s = new Stack<number>(); s.push(1); s.pop();   // 1

explanation.
A stack is last in, first out: push and pop must work on the same end of the array
ts-stack-core   lens: creation   level: L0   family: ts-stack-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-stack-empty. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. shift removes the most recently added element.
pop removes the last element of an array, which is the most recent push. shift removes the first, which turns the stack
into a queue and is O(n). A Stack class around a private array exposes only push, pop, peek, size and isEmpty, so
callers cannot break the discipline. Mnemonist (npm) has Stack and FixedStack classes with the same operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class StackBad<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  push(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.shift(); }
}
Correct:
 class Stack<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  push(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.pop(); }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.items[this.items.length - 1]; }
  get size(): number { return this.items.length; }
  isEmpty(): boolean { return this.items.length === 0; }
}
pop and peek return T | undefined; assigning the result to T is error TS2322
ts-stack-empty   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-stack-access
Prerequisites: ts-stack-core. Follow-up: ts-stack-parentheses. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A stack of numbers always returns a number from pop.
The type of pop is T | undefined because the stack may be empty, and the compiler rejects assigning it to a number
(TS2322). Check isEmpty first, or handle undefined with ?? or an explicit branch. Avoid ! unless emptiness is already
proven.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 function topBad(s: Stack<number>): number {
  const top: number = s.pop();
  return top;
}
Correct:
 function top(s: Stack<number>): number | null {
  return s.isEmpty() ? null : (s.pop() as number);
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Iterative DFS pushes the right child first so the left child is visited first
ts-stack-dfs   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-stack-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-stack-monotonic. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Pushing left then right visits the left subtree first.
A stack pops the most recent push first. To visit left before right, push right first and left last. Pushing in reading order
reverses the traversal: the preorder becomes root, right subtree, left subtree.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type TNode = { val: number; left: TNode | null; right: TNode | null };
function preorderBad(root: TNode | null): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  const st: TNode[] = root ? [root] : [];
  while (st.length) {
    const n = st.pop() as TNode;
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.left) st.push(n.left);
    if (n.right) st.push(n.right);
  }
  return out;
}
Correct:
 type TNode = { val: number; left: TNode | null; right: TNode | null };
function preorder(root: TNode | null): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  const st: TNode[] = root ? [root] : [];
  while (st.length) {
    const n = st.pop() as TNode;
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.right) st.push(n.right);
    if (n.left) st.push(n.left);
  }
  return out;
}

TypeScript Stack: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Balanced brackets need a stack of expected closers; a counter cannot detect mismatched
kinds
ts-stack-parentheses   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-stack-empty. Follow-up: ts-stack-rpn. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Counting opening and closing brackets is enough to validate nesting.
A single counter accepts "([)]" because the counts match, but the nesting is wrong. A stack remembers the order of
open brackets: on a closer, the top of the stack must be the matching opener. The string is balanced only if the stack
is empty at the end.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function balancedBad(s: string): boolean {
  let n = 0;
  for (const c of s) {
    if ("([{".includes(c)) n++;
    else if (")]}".includes(c)) n--;
    if (n < 0) return false;
  }
  return n === 0;
}
Correct:
 function balanced(s: string): boolean {
  const pairs: Record<string, string> = { ")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{" };
  const stack: string[] = [];
  for (const c of s) {
    if ("([{".includes(c)) stack.push(c);
    else if (c in pairs && stack.pop() !== pairs[c]) return false;
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}
In postfix evaluation the first value popped is the right operand
ts-stack-rpn   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-stack-parentheses. Follow-up: ts-stack-min. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. For "3 1 -" pop a then b and compute a - b.
Operands are pushed left to right, so the top of the stack is the right operand. Popping the right one first and the left
one second gives left - right. Reversing them computes 1 - 3 and gets -2 instead of 2; the mistake only shows for
subtraction and division.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rpnBad(tokens: string[]): number {
  const st: number[] = [];
  for (const t of tokens) {
    if (["+", "-", "*", "/"].includes(t)) {
      const a = st.pop() as number;
      const b = st.pop() as number;
      st.push(t === "+" ? a + b : t === "-" ? a - b : t === "*" ? a * b : a / b);
    } else st.push(Number(t));
  }
  return st[0] as number;
}

TypeScript Stack: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Correct:
 function rpn(tokens: string[]): number {
  const st: number[] = [];
  for (const t of tokens) {
    if (["+", "-", "*", "/"].includes(t)) {
      const b = st.pop() as number;
      const a = st.pop() as number;
      st.push(t === "+" ? a + b : t === "-" ? a - b : t === "*" ? a * b : a / b);
    } else st.push(Number(t));
  }
  return st[0] as number;
}
A min stack keeps a parallel stack of minimums; a single min variable is wrong after a pop
ts-stack-min   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-stack-rpn. Follow-up: ts-stack-monotonic. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Storing one running minimum is enough to answer getMin after pops.
When the minimum element is popped, the previous minimum is lost if only one variable is kept. Keep a second stack
that records the minimum at every depth, or store pairs (value, minSoFar). Both give O(1) push, pop and getMin.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class MinStackBad {
  private items: number[] = [];
  private min = Infinity;
  push(x: number): void { this.items.push(x); this.min = Math.min(this.min, x); }
  pop(): number | undefined { return this.items.pop(); }
  getMin(): number { return this.min; }
}
Correct:
 class MinStack {
  private items: number[] = [];
  private mins: number[] = [];
  push(x: number): void {
    this.items.push(x);
    this.mins.push(Math.min(x, this.mins[this.mins.length - 1] ?? Infinity));
  }
  pop(): number | undefined {
    this.mins.pop();
    return this.items.pop();
  }
  getMin(): number { return this.mins[this.mins.length - 1] ?? Infinity; }
}

TypeScript Stack: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
A monotonic stack finds the next greater element; use while, not if, when popping smaller
values
ts-stack-monotonic   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-stack-min. Follow-up: ts-stack-dfs. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Popping one smaller value per new element is enough.
A new value can be greater than several stack entries, and each of them has just found its answer. Using if pops only
one, leaving unresolved entries behind and producing wrong answers. The while loop pops every smaller value, so
each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function nextGreaterBad(xs: number[]): number[] {
  const res = xs.map(() => -1);
  const st: number[] = [];
  xs.forEach((x, i) => {
    const t = st[st.length - 1];
    if (t !== undefined && (xs[t] as number) < x) res[st.pop() as number] = x;
    st.push(i);
  });
  return res;
}
Correct:
 function nextGreater(xs: number[]): number[] {
  const res = xs.map(() => -1);
  const st: number[] = [];
  xs.forEach((x, i) => {
    while (st.length && (xs[st[st.length - 1] as number] as number) < x) {
      res[st.pop() as number] = x;
    }
    st.push(i);
  });
  return res;
}

ts-stack-monotonic-ex1   format: choose-the-structure   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Explain how a monotonic stack finds the next greater element for every position in O(n), and why the inner
loop is while rather than if.
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Scan left to right keeping a stack of indexes whose next greater value is
not yet known, in decreasing order of value. For each new value, pop while the top value is smaller and record the new
value as their answer, then push the current index. A new value may resolve several entries, so a while loop is required.
Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n).

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
A disjoint set keeps a collection of elements partitioned into groups and answers two questions fast: which group is
this element in (find), and merge two groups (union).
It stores a parent array: a root is its own parent. find follows parents to the root; union attaches one root under the
other. Two optimisations make it nearly constant time: path compression and union by size.
Use it for connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs, Kruskal minimum spanning trees and
grouping equivalent items.
Toolbox
 const uf = new UnionFind(5);
uf.union(0, 1);          // true: merged two sets
uf.union(1, 0);          // false: already connected
uf.connected(0, 2);      // false
uf.count;                // 4 components
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
2 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Disjoint Set (Union-Find): Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
find must follow parents all the way to the root; returning the direct parent is only correct for
depth one
ts-disjointset-find   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-dsu-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-union-roots. Complexity: O(depth).
 Common misconception. find(x) can return parent[x], since that is the set representative.
The representative of a set is its root, the element that is its own parent. After several unions an element may be
several levels below the root, so a single hop returns an intermediate node and two members of one set compare as
different. Loop until parent[x] === x.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function findBad(parent: number[], x: number): number {
  return parent[x] as number;
}
Correct:
 function find(parent: number[], x: number): number {
  while (parent[x] !== x) x = parent[x] as number;
  return x;
}
union must link the roots of the two sets, not the two elements
ts-disjointset-union-roots   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-dsu-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-find. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-compression. Complexity: O(depth).
 Common misconception. parent[a] = b merges the sets of a and b.
Linking a to b overwrites the parent pointer of a, which may have been linking a to its own set. Elements that reached
the root through a are cut off. Find both roots first and attach one root under the other.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function unionBad(parent: number[], a: number, b: number): void {
  parent[a] = b;
}
Correct:
 function union(parent: number[], a: number, b: number): void {
  parent[find(parent, a)] = find(parent, b);
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Path compression points every visited node at the root so later finds are nearly constant
ts-disjointset-compression   lens: complexity   level: L2   family: ts-dsu-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-union-roots. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-by-size. Complexity: O(alpha(n)).
 Common misconception. Walking to the root without compression keeps find fast.
Without compression a chain of unions can leave a path of length n, and every find walks it. Compression rewrites
each node on the path to point directly at the root, flattening the tree. Combined with union by size it gives the
inverse-Ackermann bound, which is practically constant.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function findSlow(parent: number[], x: number): number {
  while (parent[x] !== x) x = parent[x] as number;
  return x;
}
Correct:
 function findCompress(parent: number[], x: number): number {
  let root = x;
  while (parent[root] !== root) root = parent[root] as number;
  while (parent[x] !== root) {
    const next = parent[x] as number;
    parent[x] = root;
    x = next;
  }
  return root;
}
Decrement the component count only when a union really merges two different sets
ts-disjointset-count   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-dsu-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-by-size. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-cycle. Complexity: O(alpha(n)).
 Common misconception. Every call to union reduces the number of components by one.
A union of two elements that are already in the same set changes nothing. Counting it makes the component total too
small. Return a boolean from union (true when a merge happened) and decrement the count only then.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class CountBad {
  parent: number[];
  count: number;
  constructor(n: number) {
    this.parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
    this.count = n;
  }
  union(a: number, b: number): void {
    this.parent[find(this.parent, a)] = find(this.parent, b);
    this.count--;
  }
}

TypeScript Disjoint Set (Union-Find): Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Correct:
 class UnionFind {
  parent: number[];
  size: number[];
  count: number;
  constructor(n: number) {
    this.parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
    this.size = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 1);
    this.count = n;
  }
  find(x: number): number {
    let root = x;
    while (this.parent[root] !== root) root = this.parent[root] as number;
    while (this.parent[x] !== root) {
      const next = this.parent[x] as number;
      this.parent[x] = root;
      x = next;
    }
    return root;
  }
  union(a: number, b: number): boolean {
    let ra = this.find(a);
    let rb = this.find(b);
    if (ra === rb) return false;
    if ((this.size[ra] as number) < (this.size[rb] as number)) [ra, rb] = [rb, ra];
    this.parent[rb] = ra;
    this.size[ra] = (this.size[ra] as number) + (this.size[rb] as number);
    this.count--;
    return true;
  }
  connected(a: number, b: number): boolean { return this.find(a) === this.find(b); }
}
Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, keeping trees shallow
ts-disjointset-by-size   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: ts-dsu-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-compression. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-count. Complexity: O(alpha(n)).
 Common misconception. Always attaching the first root under the second gives balanced trees.
If every union attaches the first root under the second, a sequence of unions can build one long chain of depth n.
Attaching the smaller tree under the larger one limits the height to log n. Track sizes at the roots and update the
larger root after merging.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function unionNaive(parent: number[], a: number, b: number): void {
  parent[findCompress(parent, a)] = findCompress(parent, b);
}

TypeScript Disjoint Set (Union-Find): Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Correct:
 class UnionFind {
  parent: number[];
  size: number[];
  count: number;
  constructor(n: number) {
    this.parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
    this.size = Array.from({ length: n }, () => 1);
    this.count = n;
  }
  find(x: number): number {
    let root = x;
    while (this.parent[root] !== root) root = this.parent[root] as number;
    while (this.parent[x] !== root) {
      const next = this.parent[x] as number;
      this.parent[x] = root;
      x = next;
    }
    return root;
  }
  union(a: number, b: number): boolean {
    let ra = this.find(a);
    let rb = this.find(b);
    if (ra === rb) return false;
    if ((this.size[ra] as number) < (this.size[rb] as number)) [ra, rb] = [rb, ra];
    this.parent[rb] = ra;
    this.size[ra] = (this.size[ra] as number) + (this.size[rb] as number);
    this.count--;
    return true;
  }
  connected(a: number, b: number): boolean { return this.find(a) === this.find(b); }
}
Detect a cycle by testing whether union merged two sets; testing connectivity after the union
is always true
ts-disjointset-cycle   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ts-dsu-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-count. Follow-up: ts-disjointset-kruskal. Complexity: O(E alpha(n)).
 Common misconception. After union(a, b), connected(a, b) tells whether the edge closed a cycle.
Immediately after union the two endpoints are connected, so the check always reports a cycle. Detect the cycle
before merging, or use the boolean returned by union: false means the endpoints were already connected, so the
edge creates a cycle.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hasCycleBad(n: number, edges: [number, number][]): boolean {
  const uf = new UnionFind(n);
  for (const [a, b] of edges) {
    uf.union(a, b);
    if (uf.connected(a, b)) return true;
  }
  return false;
}
Correct:
 function hasCycle(n: number, edges: [number, number][]): boolean {
  const uf = new UnionFind(n);
  for (const [a, b] of edges) if (!uf.union(a, b)) return true;
  return false;
}

TypeScript Disjoint Set (Union-Find): Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Kruskal sorts edges by weight with a numeric comparator; the default sort orders arrays as
strings
ts-disjointset-kruskal   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-dsu-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-disjointset-cycle. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(E log E).
 Common misconception. edges.sort() orders the edges by their last element, the weight.
Default sort converts each edge array to a string such as "0,1,10" and compares the text, so edges are ordered by
the first vertex, not by weight. Sort with (a, b) => a[2] - b[2]. Then add an edge to the tree whenever union merges two
components.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function kruskalBad(n: number, edges: [number, number, number][]): number {
  const uf = new UnionFind(n);
  let total = 0;
  for (const [a, b, w] of [...edges].sort()) if (uf.union(a, b)) total += w;
  return total;
}
Correct:
 function kruskal(n: number, edges: [number, number, number][]): number {
  const uf = new UnionFind(n);
  let total = 0;
  for (const [a, b, w] of [...edges].sort((x, y) => x[2] - y[2])) {
    if (uf.union(a, b)) total += w;
  }
  return total;
}

ts-disjointset-cycle-ex1   format: spot-the-bug   level: L3   grading: judge   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. hasCycleBad reports a cycle for every non-empty edge list. Why, and how is it fixed?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). After union(a, b) the endpoints are in the same set, so connected(a, b) is
always true. Check before merging, or use the boolean result of union: it returns false when the endpoints were already
connected, which means the edge closes a cycle.

Page 9
ts-disjointset-by-size-ex1   format: choose-the-structure   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why do path compression and union by size together make union-find nearly O(1)?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Union by size keeps every tree shallow, at most log n high, because the
smaller tree always goes under the larger one. Path compression flattens the path walked by each find so later finds on
those nodes take one step. Together the amortised cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, which is at
most 4 for any realistic n.

2. Overview and mental model: Array
A TypeScript array is a JavaScript array with an element type: number[] or Array. Everything about runtime behaviour
is unchanged: arrays are objects, they are resized dynamically, indexes past the end give undefined, and most
methods either mutate in place or return a new array. The types add a layer that can catch some mistakes and
silently allow others.
The compiler is strongest at element types, readonly arrays and generics, and weakest at length and bounds: it does
not know how many elements an array has. This document keeps the two apart: each chunk states what the compiler
reports (with the error code when there is one) and what only a runtime test can show.
Complexity is the JavaScript engine's: push and pop are O(1), shift, unshift and splice in the middle are O(n), sort is
O(n log n), and copying with spread or slice is O(n).
Toolbox
 const nums: number[] = [3, 1, 2];
const ro: readonly number[] = nums;      // read-only view of the same array
const grid: number[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
const maybe: (number | undefined)[] = [1, undefined];
const last = nums.at(-1);               // number | undefined

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
5 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Indexing an array is typed T even when the index is out of range; at() and a check give T |
undefined
ts-array-index-undefined   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-array-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-array-readonly. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. nums[i] is always a number, because the array is typed number[].
By default TypeScript types nums[i] as number, but an index past the end gives undefined at runtime, and arithmetic
on it yields NaN. The compiler only reports it if you turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Array.prototype.at(i) is typed
number | undefined, and also accepts negative indexes, so the compiler makes you handle the missing case.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function lastBad(a: number[]): number {
  return a[a.length];
}
Correct:
 function last(a: readonly number[]): number | undefined {
  return a.at(-1);
}
function lastOr(a: readonly number[], fallback: number): number {
  return a.at(-1) ?? fallback;
}
new Array(n).fill([]) puts one array in every slot; build rows with Array.from
ts-array-fill-alias   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ts-array-creation
Prerequisites: ts-array-sort-numbers. Follow-up: ts-array-spread-copy. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. new Array(3).fill([]) creates three independent empty rows.
fill stores the same value in every slot. For a primitive that is fine; for an array or object all slots point to one object, so
pushing to one row changes all rows. Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) runs the callback once per slot and creates
separate rows. Annotate the element type, because [] alone is inferred as never[].
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function gridBad(n: number): number[][] {
  return new Array<number[]>(n).fill([]);
}
Correct:
 function grid(n: number): number[][] {
  return Array.from({ length: n }, () => [] as number[]);
}

readonly number[] removes the mutating methods from the type, so a function can promise
not to change its argument
ts-array-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-array-readonly
Prerequisites: ts-array-index-undefined. Follow-up: ts-array-sort-numbers. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A function that takes number[] and does not change it is as safe as one that takes readonly
number[].
A parameter typed number[] allows push, sort and splice, so callers cannot tell whether their array survives the call.
readonly number[] (or ReadonlyArray<number>) hides the mutating methods, and the compiler rejects them. A
mutable array can be passed where readonly is expected, but not the other way round. Return a new array instead of
changing the input.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function addBad(xs: readonly number[]): void {
  xs.push(1);
}
Correct:
 function add(xs: readonly number[], x: number): number[] {
  return [...xs, x];
}
Spread and slice make a shallow copy: the outer array is new but nested arrays are shared
ts-array-spread-copy   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-array-copy
Prerequisites: ts-array-fill-alias. Follow-up: ts-array-filter-type-guard. Complexity: O(rows * cols).
 Common misconception. const copy = [...grid] gives an independent copy of a two-dimensional array.
Spread, slice and Array.from copy only the first level. The inner arrays are the same objects in both, so writing
copy[0][0] changes the original too. Copy each level you intend to change, for example grid.map(row => [...row]), or
use structuredClone for plain data. The type readonly number[][] does not protect the inner arrays; use readonly
(readonly number[])[].
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function setBad(grid: number[][]): number[][] {
  const copy = [...grid];
  copy[0]![0] = 99;
  return copy;
}
Correct:
 function setCell(grid: readonly (readonly number[])[], v: number): number[][] {
  const copy = grid.map(row => [...row]);
  copy[0]![0] = v;
  return copy;
}

Page 5
sort() compares as strings by default and sorts in place; pass a numeric comparator or use
toSorted()
ts-array-sort-numbers   lens: ordering   level: L1   family: ts-array-sort
Prerequisites: ts-array-readonly. Follow-up: ts-array-fill-alias. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. nums.sort() sorts a number[] numerically, since the compiler knows the elements are
numbers.
The default comparator converts elements to strings, so 10 sorts before 9. TypeScript accepts it without complaint.
Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers. sort mutates the array and returns it; toSorted (ES2023) returns a sorted copy and
leaves the original alone.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sortBad(nums: number[]): number[] {
  return nums.sort();
}
Correct:
 function sortNumbers(nums: readonly number[]): number[] {
  return nums.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);
}
