4.4 Algorithm chunks
Build in linear time by pushing each node into its parent; copying the array is not a tree
ts-fenwicktree-build   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ts-fen-creation
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-set. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-range-update. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A Fenwick tree can be created by copying the input array.
Each tree node holds a partial sum, so the raw array is not a valid tree. Calling add for every element costs O(n log
n). A linear build puts the values at indexes 1..n, then adds each node into its parent at i + lowbit(i) once.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function fromArrayBad(a: number[]): number[] {
  return [...a];
}
Correct:
 function fromArray(a: number[]): number[] {
  const n = a.length;
  const tree = [0, ...a];
  for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    const parent = i + (i & -i);
    if (parent <= n) tree[parent] = (tree[parent] as number) + (tree[i] as number);
  }
  return tree;
}

TypeScript Fenwick Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Setting a value means adding the difference from the stored value, not the new value
ts-fenwicktree-set   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-fen-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-range. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-build. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. set(i, v) can call add(i, v).
A Fenwick tree stores sums, so add always accumulates. To replace a value, keep a plain array of the current values
and add v minus the old value. Calling add with the new value doubles the element on a repeated set.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class SetBad extends Fenwick {
  set(i: number, v: number): void {
    this.add(i, v);
  }
}
Correct:
 class FenwickSet extends Fenwick {
  vals: number[];
  constructor(n: number) {
    super(n);
    this.vals = new Array<number>(n).fill(0);
  }
  set(i: number, v: number): void {
    this.add(i, v - (this.vals[i] as number));
    this.vals[i] = v;
  }
}
Compress values to ranks with a numeric sort before counting inversions
ts-fenwicktree-inversions   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-fen-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-range-update. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Sorting the distinct values with sort() gives their ranks.
Counting inversions uses a Fenwick tree indexed by rank. The default sort compares strings, so 10 comes before 9
and the ranks are wrong. Sort with (x, y) => x - y, map each value to its rank, and for each element count the earlier
elements with a larger rank as i minus prefix(rank).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function inversionsBad(a: number[]): number {
  const sorted = [...new Set(a)].sort();
  const rank = new Map<number, number>(sorted.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  const f = new Fenwick(sorted.length);
  let inv = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    const r = rank.get(a[i] as number) as number;
    inv += i - f.prefix(r);
    f.add(r, 1);
  }
  return inv;
}

TypeScript Fenwick Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 function inversions(a: number[]): number {
  const sorted = [...new Set(a)].sort((x, y) => x - y);
  const rank = new Map<number, number>(sorted.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  const f = new Fenwick(sorted.length);
  let inv = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    const r = rank.get(a[i] as number) as number;
    inv += i - f.prefix(r);
    f.add(r, 1);
  }
  return inv;
}
Range add with point query stores differences, so the range end must cancel the start
ts-fenwicktree-range-update   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-fen-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-build. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-inversions. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Adding d at l alone adds d to the range [l, r].
Store a difference array in the tree. A point query is the prefix sum of differences. Adding d at l raises every later
position, so a matching -d at r + 1 is needed to end the range. Without it the change leaks to the end of the array.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class RangeAddBad {
  f: Fenwick;
  constructor(n: number) { this.f = new Fenwick(n); }
  rangeAdd(l: number, r: number, d: number): void {
    this.f.add(l, d);
  }
  get(i: number): number { return this.f.prefix(i); }
}
Correct:
 class RangeAdd {
  f: Fenwick;
  constructor(n: number) { this.f = new Fenwick(n); }
  rangeAdd(l: number, r: number, d: number): void {
    this.f.add(l, d);
    this.f.add(r + 1, -d);
  }
  get(i: number): number { return this.f.prefix(i); }
}

2. Overview and mental model: Object
In TypeScript an object type describes a shape, and any object with at least those properties fits. Objects are used as
records (fixed, known keys) and as dictionaries (dynamic string keys). The two uses need different types: an interface
or type alias for records, Record or a Map for dictionaries.
The type system is structural and erased at compile time. It checks the shape of values you write, but it does not stop
extra properties travelling through variables, does not enforce readonly at runtime, and types dictionary lookups as
always present. Each chunk marks where the compiler helps and where only a runtime check does.
Runtime facts that surprise: objects inherit keys from Object.prototype, integer-like keys sort first, spread copies one
level, and Object.keys returns plain strings.
Toolbox
 type User = { id: number; name: string; email?: string };
const u: User = { id: 1, name: "Ada" };
const dict: Record<string, number> = { a: 1 };   // dynamic keys
const v = dict["missing"];                       // typed number, actually undefined
const copy = { ...u, name: "Grace" };             // shallow copy with an override

explanation.
A Record<string, number> types every key as number, but a missing key gives undefined at
runtime
ts-object-index-signature   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-object-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-object-prototype-keys. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. counts[key] is always a number when counts is Record<string, number>.
An index signature promises a value for every possible string key, which is never true. Reading a missing key returns
undefined, and arithmetic on it gives NaN. The compiler only complains if noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled.
Use ?? to give a default, or type the lookup result as number | undefined.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function countOfBad(counts: Record<string, number>, key: string): number {
  return counts[key]!;
}
Correct:
 function countOf(counts: Record<string, number>, key: string): number {
  return counts[key] ?? 0;
}
A type does not forbid extra properties: only fresh object literals are checked, so extra fields
can leak through variables
ts-object-excess-property   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-object-structural
Prerequisites: ts-object-keys-typing. Follow-up: ts-object-spread-merge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A parameter typed { x: number } guarantees that the object has only x.
TypeScript is structural: any object with at least the declared properties fits. Excess property errors (TS2353) apply
only to object literals written directly at the call. The same object passed through a variable carries extra fields along,
and JSON.stringify or spread then exposes them. Copy the fields you want explicitly before sending data out.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function toJsonBad(p: { x: number }): string {
  return JSON.stringify(p);
}
Correct:
 function toJson(p: { x: number }): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ x: p.x });
}

Page 4
A plain object inherits keys such as toString and constructor; use Object.hasOwn, a
null-prototype object, or a Map
ts-object-prototype-keys   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-object-prototype
Prerequisites: ts-object-index-signature. Follow-up: ts-object-keys-typing. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. An empty object literal has no keys, so counts[word] is undefined for a new word.
Object literals inherit from Object.prototype, so counts["constructor"] and counts["toString"] are functions, not
undefined. A word counter then computes "function Object() ..." plus 1. Check own properties with
Object.hasOwn(obj, key), create the object with Object.create(null), or use a Map, which has no inherited keys.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function countBad(words: string[]): Record<string, number> {
  const counts: Record<string, number> = {};
  for (const w of words) counts[w] = (counts[w] ?? 0) + 1;
  return counts;
}
Correct:
 function count(words: readonly string[]): Map<string, number> {
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const w of words) counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1);
  return counts;
}

mutation, checking presence, freezing, ordering and narrowing a union of object shapes. Every row is backed by a

Object.assign mutates its first argument; spread builds a new object, and the last spread
wins
ts-object-spread-merge   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-object-merge
Prerequisites: ts-object-excess-property. Follow-up: ts-object-optional-vs-undefined. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.assign(defaults, overrides) returns a merged copy and leaves defaults alone.
Object.assign copies properties onto its first argument and returns that same object, so a shared defaults object is
changed for every later caller. { ...defaults, ...overrides } creates a new object; for duplicate keys the later source
wins. Both copy only one level: nested objects stay shared.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function mergeBad<T extends object>(defaults: T, overrides: Partial<T>): T {
  return Object.assign(defaults, overrides);
}
Correct:
 function merge<T extends object>(defaults: T, overrides: Partial<T>): T {
  return { ...defaults, ...overrides };
}
Object.keys returns string[], not (keyof T)[]; indexing with those keys fails to compile unless
you narrow deliberately
ts-object-keys-typing   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: ts-object-keys
Prerequisites: ts-object-prototype-keys. Follow-up: ts-object-excess-property. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. for (const k of Object.keys(o)) o[k] type-checks, because k is a key of o.
An object of type T can have more properties than T declares, so TypeScript types Object.keys(o) as string[] and
rejects o[k] with error TS7053. When you know the object is exact, cast once in a helper: (Object.keys(o) as (keyof
T)[]). Object.entries(o) avoids indexing altogether.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS7053):
 function sumBad(o: { a: number; b: number }): number {
  let total = 0;
  for (const k of Object.keys(o)) total += o[k];
  return total;
}
Correct:
 function typedKeys<T extends object>(o: T): (keyof T)[] {
  return Object.keys(o) as (keyof T)[];
}
function sum(o: { a: number; b: number }): number {
  let total = 0;
  for (const k of typedKeys(o)) total += o[k];
  return total;
}

Page 7
readonly is erased at runtime; Object.freeze is the runtime guard and is shallow
ts-object-readonly-freeze   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-object-readonly
Prerequisites: ts-object-optional-vs-undefined. Follow-up: ts-object-key-order. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A property marked readonly cannot be changed at runtime.
readonly and Readonly<T> exist only in the type checker. A cast, an alias with a looser type, or plain JavaScript can
still change the value. Object.freeze makes the object immutable at runtime (strict-mode writes throw TypeError), but
only for its own properties: nested objects stay writable. Freeze nested levels too, or use a copy-on-write style.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function bumpBad(o: Readonly<{ n: number }>): void {
  (o as { n: number }).n += 1;
}
Correct:
 function lock<T extends object>(o: T): Readonly<T> {
  return Object.freeze(o);
}
"a" in o tells whether the key exists; o.a !== undefined tells whether it holds a value; they
differ for { a: undefined }
ts-object-optional-vs-undefined   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-object-presence
Prerequisites: ts-object-spread-merge. Follow-up: ts-object-readonly-freeze. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Checking "key" in obj is the same as checking obj.key !== undefined.
A property can exist and hold undefined, for example after spreading an object with an optional field that was
explicitly set. in reports true, while the value check reports false. Choose by intent: use in (or Object.hasOwn) for
presence, and a value check for usable data. With optional properties, TypeScript allows both a missing key and an
explicit undefined unless exactOptionalPropertyTypes is on.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hasValueBad(o: { a?: number }): boolean {
  return "a" in o;
}
Correct:
 function hasValue(o: { a?: number }): boolean {
  return o.a !== undefined;
}
function hasKey(o: object, k: string): boolean {
  return Object.hasOwn(o, k);
}

TypeScript Object: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Integer-like keys come first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order
ts-object-key-order   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-object-order
Prerequisites: ts-object-readonly-freeze. Follow-up: ts-object-in-narrowing. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.keys returns keys in the order they were added.
For ordinary objects the engine orders integer-like keys (such as "1" or "42") numerically before all other keys,
whatever the insertion order; other string keys follow in insertion order, then symbols. Code that relies on insertion
order for numeric ids breaks. A Map always iterates in insertion order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function firstKeyBad(ids: number[]): string | undefined {
  const o: Record<number, boolean> = {};
  for (const id of ids) o[id] = true;
  return Object.keys(o)[0];
}
Correct:
 function firstKey(ids: readonly number[]): number | undefined {
  const m = new Map<number, boolean>();
  for (const id of ids) m.set(id, true);
  return m.keys().next().value;
}
Use the in operator or a discriminant property to narrow a union of object types
ts-object-in-narrowing   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-object-narrowing
Prerequisites: ts-object-key-order. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading a property that exists on only one member of a union is fine if you know which one it
is.
Accessing s.radius on Circle | Square is error TS2339, because Square has no radius. The in operator narrows in the
true branch ("radius" in s). A discriminant property such as kind: "circle" is better, since it also works for members that
share property names.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 type Circle = { radius: number };
type Square = { side: number };
function areaBad(s: Circle | Square): number {
  return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
}
Correct:
 type Circle = { radius: number };
type Square = { side: number };
function area(s: Circle | Square): number {
  return "radius" in s ? Math.PI * s.radius ** 2 : s.side ** 2;
}

2. Overview and mental model: Interface
An interface names the shape of an object. It is purely a compile-time construct: it produces no JavaScript, so it
cannot be tested with instanceof or inspected at run time.
Interfaces can extend each other, merge when declared twice, describe callable objects, and be generic. A class can
implement an interface to promise its shape.
Checking is structural: any value with the right members fits. Excess-property checks apply to fresh object literals
only, and readonly is not enforced at run time.
Toolbox
 interface User { readonly id: number; name: string; email?: string }
interface Admin extends User { level: number }
interface Stack<T> { push(x: T): void; pop(): T | undefined }
interface Counter { (): number; reset(): void }
class ArrayStack<T> implements Stack<T> { /* ... */ }
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
4 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

Page 3
A readonly property cannot be assigned (TS2540), but the check is compile-time only
ts-interface-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-interface-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-interface-extends-conflict. Follow-up: ts-interface-index-signature. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. readonly in an interface prevents changes at run time.
Assigning to a readonly property is error TS2540. The modifier is erased, so a cast or plain JavaScript can still write
to it, and a mutable alias of the same object can change it. Use Object.freeze when the guarantee must hold at run
time.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2540):
 function renameBad(u: { readonly name: string }): void {
  u.name = "x";
}
Correct:
 interface User { readonly name: string }
function renamed(u: User, name: string): User {
  return { ...u, name };
}
Interfaces with the same name merge; a type alias declared twice is error TS2300
ts-interface-merging   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-interface-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-interface-extends-conflict. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Declaring the same name twice always replaces the earlier declaration.
Two interface declarations of the same name in one scope are merged into one type with all members, which is how
libraries are augmented. Two type aliases with the same name are error TS2300 (duplicate identifier). Accidental
merging can also hide a typo, so keep declarations together.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2300):
 type PointB = { x: number };
type PointB = { y: number };
Correct:
 interface Point { x: number }
interface Point { y: number }
function norm(p: Point): number {
  return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y);
}

Page 4
An interface that extends another cannot change a property to an incompatible type (TS2430)
ts-interface-extends-conflict   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-interface-inheritance
Prerequisites: ts-interface-merging. Follow-up: ts-interface-readonly. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A child interface may redefine a property with any type.
A property in the child must be assignable to the parent property of the same name, otherwise error TS2430.
Narrowing is allowed (string to "a" | "b"); widening or changing the type is not. To change a type, use Omit and add
the property back.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2430):
 interface BaseB { id: number }
interface ChildB extends BaseB { id: string }
Correct:
 interface Base { id: number }
interface Child extends Omit<Base, "id"> { id: string }
function idOf(c: Child): string {
  return c.id;
}
With a string index signature every named property must match it (TS2411); use a union
value type
ts-interface-index-signature   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-interface-edge
Prerequisites: ts-interface-readonly. Follow-up: ts-interface-callable. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. An interface can mix named properties with an index signature of a different type.
The index signature [k: string]: number promises that every property is a number, so a named property name: string
is error TS2411. Make the index value a union (number | string), or move the dynamic part to a separate object
property.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2411):

  [k: string]: number;
  name: string;
}
Correct:

  [k: string]: number | string;
  name: string;
}
function nameOf(d: Dict): string {
  return d.name;
}

An interface can describe a function with properties; a plain function is missing them
(TS2741)
ts-interface-callable   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-interface-creation
Prerequisites: ts-interface-index-signature. Follow-up: ts-interface-generic. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A function can be assigned to an interface that has a call signature and extra members.
interface Counter { (): number; reset(): void } describes a callable object. A plain arrow function is missing reset (error
TS2741). Build it with Object.assign(fn, { reset }), so the function and its members form one value.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2741):
 interface CounterB {
  (): number;
  reset(): void;
}
const cBad: CounterB = () => 1;
Correct:
 interface Counter {
  (): number;
  reset(): void;
}
function makeCounter(): Counter {
  let n = 0;
  return Object.assign(() => ++n, { reset: () => { n = 0; } });
}

TypeScript Interface: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Interfaces are erased: instanceof with an interface is error TS2693; test shapes with a type
guard
ts-interface-erased   lens: testing   level: L2   family: ts-interface-testing
Prerequisites: ts-interface-generic. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. x instanceof Shape works when Shape is an interface.
An interface exists only at compile time, so there is nothing to compare against at run time. Using it as a value is error
TS2693. Write a type guard function that checks the properties or a discriminant field, or use a class when instanceof
is required.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2693):
 interface ShapeB { area(): number }
function isShapeBad(x: unknown): boolean {
  return x instanceof ShapeB;
}
Correct:
 interface Shape { area(): number }
function isShape(x: unknown): x is Shape {
  return typeof x === "object" && x !== null && typeof (x as Shape).area === "function";
}
A generic interface describes a data structure once, and the compiler rejects wrong element
types
ts-interface-generic   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-interface-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-interface-callable. Follow-up: ts-interface-erased. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Stack<number> accepts any value that can be converted to a number.
Stack<T> fixes the element type: pushing a string into a Stack<number> is error TS2345. An interface lets several
classes implement the same contract and lets tests use a simple fake.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 interface StackB<T> {
  push(x: T): void;
  pop(): T | undefined;
}
function fillBad(s: StackB<number>): void {
  s.push("a");
}
Correct:
 interface Stack<T> {
  push(x: T): void;
  pop(): T | undefined;
}
class ArrayStack<T> implements Stack<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  push(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.pop(); }
}

2. Overview and mental model: DataView
A DataView reads and writes numbers of mixed types at arbitrary byte offsets in an ArrayBuffer, with explicit
endianness. Typed arrays are for uniform arrays; DataView is for formats and protocols.
Every accessor names its type: getUint8, getInt16, getUint32, getFloat32, getFloat64, getBigInt64 and the matching
setters. Offsets are bytes. Out-of-range access throws RangeError.
TypeScript checks the argument and return types (bigint versus number) but not offsets, bounds or endianness.
Those need runtime checks and tests.
Toolbox
 const dv = new DataView(new ArrayBuffer(8));
dv.setUint16(0, 258);           // big-endian by default
dv.setUint16(2, 258, true);     // little-endian
dv.getUint8(0);                 // 1
dv.setFloat32(4, 0.1);          // rounded to float32
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript DataView: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
DataView reads big-endian by default; typed arrays use the platform order, usually
little-endian
ts-dataview-endianness   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-dataview-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-dataview-bounds. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading two bytes through a Uint16Array and through a DataView give the same number.
Network protocols and file formats usually use big-endian. DataView methods default to big-endian and take a
littleEndian flag. A Uint16Array uses the CPU order, which is little-endian on x86 and ARM. The bytes [1, 2] are 258
big-endian and 513 little-endian.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function readU16Bad(buf: ArrayBuffer): number {
  return new Uint16Array(buf)[0] ?? 0;
}
Correct:
 function readU16(buf: ArrayBuffer): number {
  return new DataView(buf).getUint16(0);
}
Reading past the end of a DataView throws RangeError instead of returning undefined
ts-dataview-bounds   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-dataview-edge
Prerequisites: ts-dataview-endianness. Follow-up: ts-dataview-window. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dv.getUint32(offset) returns undefined past the end, like an array.
DataView methods throw RangeError when offset + size exceeds byteLength. Check the bounds first and return a
safe value. This is the main difference from a typed array, where an out-of-range index gives undefined.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function readBad(dv: DataView, off: number): number {
  return dv.getUint32(off);
}
Correct:
 function read(dv: DataView, off: number): number | undefined {
  return off >= 0 && off + 4 <= dv.byteLength ? dv.getUint32(off) : undefined;
}

getBigInt64 returns a bigint; adding a number is error TS2365, so write 1n
ts-dataview-bigint   lens: access   level: L2   family: ts-dataview-typing
Prerequisites: ts-dataview-window. Follow-up: ts-dataview-float. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A 64-bit read returns a number you can add 1 to.
A JavaScript number cannot hold every 64-bit integer, so getBigInt64 and getBigUint64 return bigint. Mixing bigint
with number in arithmetic is error TS2365 in the compiler and TypeError at run time. Use bigint literals (1n) and
convert deliberately with Number(x) when the value is small.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2365):
 function nextBad(dv: DataView): bigint {
  return dv.getBigUint64(0) + 1;
}
Correct:
 function next(dv: DataView): bigint {
  return dv.getBigUint64(0) + 1n;
}
setFloat32 rounds to single precision, so comparing the read value with the original often
fails; compare with Math.fround
ts-dataview-float   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-dataview-numbers
Prerequisites: ts-dataview-bigint. Follow-up: ts-dataview-header. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Writing 0.1 with setFloat32 and reading it back gives 0.1.
Float32 has about seven decimal digits. 0.1 reads back as 0.10000000149011612. Compare to Math.fround(x),
which rounds a number to float32, or compare with a tolerance. Use setFloat64 when you need double precision.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function roundTripBad(x: number): boolean {
  const dv = new DataView(new ArrayBuffer(4));
  dv.setFloat32(0, x);
  return dv.getFloat32(0) === x;
}
Correct:
 function roundTrip(x: number): boolean {
  const dv = new DataView(new ArrayBuffer(4));
  dv.setFloat32(0, x);
  return dv.getFloat32(0) === Math.fround(x);
}

Page 7
Strings are not bytes: use TextEncoder, because string length counts UTF-16 units, not
UTF-8 bytes
ts-dataview-strings   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-dataview-transform
Prerequisites: ts-dataview-header. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A string of length n needs n bytes, and charCodeAt gives each byte.
Non-ASCII text takes several bytes in UTF-8: "é" has length 1 but is two bytes. Allocating s.length bytes truncates the
data, and writing charCodeAt values stores UTF-16 code units. Use new TextEncoder().encode(s) to get the bytes
and TextDecoder to read them.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function packBad(s: string): Uint8Array {
  const out = new Uint8Array(s.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) out[i] = s.charCodeAt(i);
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function pack(s: string): Uint8Array {
  return new TextEncoder().encode(s);
}
function unpack(b: Uint8Array): string {
  return new TextDecoder().decode(b);
}
Encode and decode a binary header with named offsets and one endianness; mixing flags
corrupts fields
ts-dataview-header   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-dataview-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-dataview-float. Follow-up: ts-dataview-strings. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Writing little-endian and reading with the default flag round-trips correctly.
Every multi-byte read and write must use the same endianness. A good layout defines constants for each field offset
and size, plus one LITTLE flag used everywhere. Decoding a little-endian field with the default big-endian read gives
a different number.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function decodeBad(buf: ArrayBuffer): { type: number; length: number } {
  const dv = new DataView(buf);
  return { type: dv.getUint8(0), length: dv.getUint16(1) };
}
Correct:
 const LITTLE = true;
function encode(type: number, length: number): ArrayBuffer {
  const buf = new ArrayBuffer(3);
  const dv = new DataView(buf);
  dv.setUint8(0, type);
  dv.setUint16(1, length, LITTLE);
  return buf;
}
function decode(buf: ArrayBuffer): { type: number; length: number } {
  const dv = new DataView(buf);
  return { type: dv.getUint8(0), length: dv.getUint16(1, LITTLE) };
}

2. Overview and mental model: Record
Record is the type of an object whose keys are K and whose values are V. When K is a union of literals it is an
exhaustive table; when K is string it is an open dictionary.
Record is a type, not a data structure: at run time it is an ordinary object, with all the object quirks (string keys,
inherited names, key order). Use Map when keys are dynamic or not strings.
The compiler is strict about missing keys on literal-union Records, but lenient about reads on string-keyed Records,
where a missing key is still typed as V.
Toolbox
 type Color = "red" | "green";
const label: Record<Color, string> = { red: "Red", green: "Green" };
const counts: Record<string, number> = {};
const sparse: Partial<Record<Color, number>> = {};
const frozen: Readonly<Record<Color, string>> = Object.freeze({ ...label });
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Record: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Record<"a" | "b", V> requires every key of the union; a missing key is error TS2741
ts-record-missing-key   lens: creation   level: L0   family: ts-record-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-record-partial. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Record over a union of keys can leave some keys out.
Record<K, V> with a union K means every member must be present. Omitting one is error TS2741 ("property is
missing"). Use Partial<Record<K, V>> when keys are optional, or Record<string, V> when keys are dynamic.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2741):
 const scoresB: Record<"a" | "b", number> = { a: 1 };
Correct:
 const scores: Record<"a" | "b", number> = { a: 1, b: 2 };
function total(r: Record<"a" | "b", number>): number {
  return r.a + r.b;
}
Partial<Record<K, V>> reads give V | undefined, so arithmetic on them is error TS18048
ts-record-partial   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-record-access
Prerequisites: ts-record-missing-key. Follow-up: ts-record-number-keys. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading a key from a Partial<Record<K, number>> gives a number.
Optional keys may be missing, so the property type is number | undefined. Adding to it is error TS18048. Default with
?? 0, or check the key. This models "sparse" data correctly, unlike a full Record.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS18048):
 function addBad(r: Partial<Record<"a" | "b", number>>): number {
  return r.a + 1;
}
Correct:
 function add(r: Partial<Record<"a" | "b", number>>): number {
  return (r.a ?? 0) + 1;
}
Record<number, V> still has string keys at run time; Object.keys gives strings
ts-record-number-keys   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: ts-record-keys
Prerequisites: ts-record-partial. Follow-up: ts-record-dispatch. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.keys of a Record<number, string> returns numbers.
Object keys are always strings or symbols. The number key 5 is stored as "5", and Object.keys returns ["5"].
Comparing or searching with a number is error TS2345 (and false at run time). Convert with Number(k) or String(n),
or use a Map<number, V> for real numeric keys.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 function hasKeyBad(r: Record<number, string>, n: number): boolean {
  return Object.keys(r).includes(n);
}
Correct:
 function hasKey(r: Record<number, string>, n: number): boolean {
  return Object.keys(r).includes(String(n));
}

Readonly<Record<K, V>> blocks assignment at compile time (TS2540); Object.freeze

ts-record-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-record-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-record-dispatch. Follow-up: ts-record-entries. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Readonly<Record<K, V>> makes the object immutable.
Assigning to a key of a readonly record is error TS2540. The protection is compile-time only, so a cast or untyped
code can still change it. Freeze the object for run-time safety, and note that freeze is shallow.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2540):
 function setBad(r: Readonly<Record<"a", number>>): void {
  r.a = 2;
}
Correct:
 function lock(r: Record<"a", number>): Readonly<Record<"a", number>> {
  return Object.freeze({ ...r });
}

Object.entries gives [string, V][], so indexing another Record with the key is error TS7053
ts-record-entries   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-record-keys
Prerequisites: ts-record-readonly. Follow-up: ts-record-from-entries. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.entries(rec) returns keys typed as the Record key union.
The key in Object.entries is string, because an object may have extra keys. Using it to index a Record<"a" | "b", V> is
error TS7053. Cast once (k as keyof typeof table) when you control the object, or iterate over a constant key list.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS7053):
 const table: Record<"a" | "b", number> = { a: 1, b: 2 };
function sumBad(r: Record<string, number>): number {
  return Object.entries(r).reduce((t, [k, v]) => t + v * table[k], 0);

Correct:

A Record keyed by a union is an exhaustive lookup table; Record<string, V> hides typos
ts-record-dispatch   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-record-patterns

TypeScript JSON
A training document for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It teaches the built-in JSON object in TypeScript:
untyped parse results, parse errors, lossy round trips, bigint, key order, revivers, cycles, toJSON and
canonical strings.
13 October 2026. Every example in this document was executed in TypeScript 5.9 (strict mode) on Node 22: 9 concept chunks and 5
exercises, with 12 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.
Built for retrieval. Each concept card is one RAG chunk (one misconception, one explanation, one failing and one
passing example) and each exercise is one more. The algorithms and strategies live in their own section (4) and are

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

 9 concept chunks, 3 in core concepts and 6 in the algorithms section.
 5 exercises, graded by exact match, rubric or judge.
 28 reference records built from the overview, traversal catalogue, strategy chooser, live outputs, gotchas and
levels.
 Answers live only in the exercise payload. The embedded text of an exercise is the prompt alone, so retrieval
cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: JSON
JSON.parse and JSON.stringify convert between text and plain data: objects, arrays, strings, finite numbers,
booleans and null. Everything else is dropped, converted or rejected.
TypeScript types JSON.parse as any, which is the largest hole in strict code. Treat parsed data as unknown until it is
validated, and handle SyntaxError.
Use the replacer and reviver arguments, toJSON methods and structuredClone to control what is lost. Sort keys
when you need a canonical string.
Toolbox
 const v: unknown = JSON.parse('{"age":4}');          // validate before use
JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: [1, 2] }, null, 2);          // indent
JSON.stringify(obj, (k, val) => val);                   // replacer
JSON.parse(text, (k, val) => val);                      // reviver
const copy = structuredClone(obj);                      // real deep copy
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript JSON: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
JSON.parse returns any, which switches type checking off; parse into unknown and validate
ts-json-parse-unknown   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-json-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-json-parse-throws. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.parse(text) returns the type I declare, so p.age + 1 is checked.
JSON.parse is typed to return any, so the compiler accepts whatever you do with the result. A missing field gives
NaN or a TypeError at run time. Assign the result to unknown, check its shape with a type guard, and only then use it.
A cast (as User) does not check anything.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function nextAgeBad(s: string): number {
  return JSON.parse(s).age + 1;
}
Correct:
 function isAge(x: unknown): x is { age: number } {
  if (typeof x !== "object" || x === null) return false;
  return typeof (x as { age?: unknown }).age === "number";
}
function nextAge(s: string): number | null {
  const v: unknown = JSON.parse(s);
  return isAge(v) ? v.age + 1 : null;
}
JSON.parse throws SyntaxError on invalid text; wrap it and return a result
ts-json-parse-throws   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-json-edge
Prerequisites: ts-json-parse-unknown. Follow-up: ts-json-lossy. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.parse returns null or undefined for text that is not JSON.
Invalid JSON, including single quotes, trailing commas and an empty string, throws SyntaxError. Wrap the call in
try/catch and return a discriminated result so callers must handle failure. Parsing user input without a guard crashes
the request.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function parseBad(s: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(s);
}
Correct:
 type Parsed = { ok: true; value: unknown } | { ok: false; error: string };
function safeParse(s: string): Parsed {
  try {
    return { ok: true, value: JSON.parse(s) };
  } catch (e) {
    return { ok: false, error: (e as Error).message };
  }
}

TypeScript JSON: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Parsed objects list integer-like keys first; keep order-sensitive data as an array of pairs
ts-json-key-order   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-json-order
Prerequisites: ts-json-bigint. Follow-up: ts-json-reviver. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.parse preserves the order of keys in the text.
JSON objects are unordered by specification, and JavaScript objects put integer-like keys first in ascending order.
{"b":1,"2":1} parses to keys ["2","b"]. When order matters, store an array of [key, value] pairs or an array of objects.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function firstKeyBad(s: string): string | undefined {
  return Object.keys(JSON.parse(s))[0];
}
Correct:
 function firstKey(s: string): string | undefined {
  const pairs = JSON.parse(s) as [string, unknown][];
  return pairs[0]?.[0];
}

A JSON round trip drops undefined and functions, turns NaN into null and Dates into strings;
use structuredClone to copy
ts-json-lossy   lens: transformation   level: L1   family: ts-json-transform
Prerequisites: ts-json-parse-throws. Follow-up: ts-json-bigint. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is a faithful deep copy.
JSON has no undefined, function, symbol, NaN, Infinity, Date, Map or Set. Properties holding undefined or functions
are dropped, NaN and Infinity become null, a Date becomes an ISO string, and Map and Set become {}.
structuredClone copies those values correctly (but not functions).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function cloneBad<T>(x: T): T {
  return JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x));
}
Correct:
 function clone<T>(x: T): T {
  return structuredClone(x);
}

TypeScript JSON: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
A reviver that converts every string to a Date also converts non-dates; match the key or the
format
ts-json-reviver   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-json-transform
Prerequisites: ts-json-key-order. Follow-up: ts-json-circular. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Reviving all strings that look like dates is harmless.
The reviver is called for every value. new Date("hello") produces an Invalid Date, so a blanket reviver corrupts
ordinary strings. Convert only specific keys, or strings that match a strict ISO pattern, and keep everything else
unchanged.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function reviveBad(s: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(s, (_k, v) => (typeof v === "string" ? new Date(v) : v));
}
Correct:
 function revive(s: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(s, (_k, v) =>
    typeof v === "string" && /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T[\d:.]+Z$/.test(v) ? new Date(v) : v);
}
JSON.stringify throws TypeError on a bigint; convert it in a replacer
ts-json-bigint   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-json-edge
Prerequisites: ts-json-lossy. Follow-up: ts-json-key-order. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.stringify writes a bigint as a number.
JSON has no bigint type and the default behaviour is to throw TypeError. Supply a replacer that converts bigints to
strings (and a reviver that converts them back) or send them as decimal strings from the start.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function stringifyBad(o: { n: bigint }): string {
  return JSON.stringify(o);
}
Correct:
 function stringify(o: unknown): string {
  return JSON.stringify(o, (_k, v) => (typeof v === "bigint" ? v.toString() : v));
}

TypeScript JSON: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
JSON.stringify throws TypeError on a circular reference; track visited objects in a replacer
ts-json-circular   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-json-edge
Prerequisites: ts-json-reviver. Follow-up: ts-json-tojson. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.stringify skips a reference it has already seen.
A cycle makes stringify throw TypeError ("Converting circular structure to JSON"). Use a replacer with a WeakSet of
ancestors seen so far and replace repeats with a marker, or remove the back-reference before serialising.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function dumpBad(o: object): string {
  return JSON.stringify(o);
}
Correct:
 function dump(o: object): string {
  const seen = new WeakSet<object>();
  return JSON.stringify(o, (_k, v) => {
    if (typeof v === "object" && v !== null) {
      if (seen.has(v)) return "[Circular]";
      seen.add(v);
    }
    return v;
  });
}
Equal objects can stringify differently; sort keys recursively for a stable string to compare or
hash
ts-json-stable   lens: equality   level: L3   family: ts-json-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-json-tojson. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Two objects with the same fields always produce the same JSON string.
stringify writes keys in insertion order, so {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} differ. For cache keys, hashes and equality checks,
produce a canonical form: sort the keys at every level. Arrays keep their order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function keyBad(o: unknown): string {
  return JSON.stringify(o);
}
Correct:
 function sortKeys(v: unknown): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return v.map(sortKeys);
  if (typeof v === "object" && v !== null) {
    const o = v as Record<string, unknown>;
    return Object.fromEntries(Object.keys(o).sort().map((k) => [k, sortKeys(o[k])]));
  }
  return v;
}
function stableKey(o: unknown): string {
  return JSON.stringify(sortKeys(o));
}

TypeScript JSON: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Define toJSON on a class to choose exactly which fields are serialised
ts-json-tojson   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-json-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-json-circular. Follow-up: ts-json-stable. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. JSON.stringify includes only the fields that are public in the TypeScript class.
TypeScript visibility (private, protected) is erased, so every own enumerable property is serialised, including a
password. If a value has a toJSON method, stringify calls it and serialises the result instead. Return a plain object
with only the safe fields.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class UserBad {
  constructor(public name: string, private password: string) {}
}
Correct:
 class User {
  constructor(public name: string, private password: string) {}
  toJSON(): { name: string } {
    return { name: this.name };
  }
}

Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). {"c":null,"d":[null]}

Prompt. What does [keyBad({ a: 1, b: 2 }) === keyBad({ b: 2, a: 1 }), stableKey({ a: 1, b: 2 }) === stableKey({ b: 2, a:
1 })].join(" ") return?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). false true
ts-json-lossy-ex2   format: choose-the-structure   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. You need to deep copy a state object that contains Dates, Maps and undefined values. Compare
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) with structuredClone.
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, Maps and Sets into empty
objects, drops undefined and functions and turns NaN into null. structuredClone preserves Date, Map, Set, typed arrays,
undefined and cyclic references. It throws on functions. Use structuredClone, or write a custom clone when the object
holds functions or class instances whose prototype matters.

2. Overview and mental model: Enum
An enum gives names to a set of constants. A numeric enum emits an object with reverse mappings; a string enum
emits an object with only the forward mapping; a const enum emits nothing.
Enums are one of the few TypeScript features that produce run-time code, so they behave differently from types. The
common alternative is an as const object with a derived union type.
The risks are numeric values flowing in unchecked, iteration that sees the reverse mappings, and switches that
silently ignore new members.
Toolbox
 enum Color { Red, Green }              // Color.Red === 0, Color[0] === "Red"
enum Dir { Up = "UP" }                   // no reverse mapping
const MODE = { Read: 0, Write: 1 } as const;
type Mode = (typeof MODE)[keyof typeof MODE];
enum Perm { Read = 1, Write = 2 }        // flags: Perm.Read | Perm.Write
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

A numeric enum compiles to an object with reverse mappings, so Object.keys lists the
numbers too
ts-enum-reverse-mapping   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-enum-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-enum-string-lookup. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.keys(Color) returns only the member names.
For a numeric enum TypeScript emits both Color.Red = 0 and Color[0] = "Red". Object.keys, Object.values and
for...in therefore see twice as many entries. Filter out the numeric keys, or use a string enum or an as const object,
which have no reverse mapping.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 enum ColorB { Red, Green }
function namesBad(): string[] {
  return Object.keys(ColorB);
}
Correct:
 enum Color { Red, Green }
function names(): string[] {
  return Object.keys(Color).filter((k) => Number.isNaN(Number(k)));
}
A string enum has no reverse mapping; looking up a member by its value needs a search, not
Dir[value]
ts-enum-string-lookup   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-enum-access
Prerequisites: ts-enum-reverse-mapping. Follow-up: ts-enum-number-assign. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Dir["UP"] returns the member name for the value "UP".
Only numeric members get a reverse mapping. Indexing a string enum with a value string is error TS7053. To find the
member name of a value, search Object.entries, or build the reverse map once.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS7053):

function nameOfBad(v: string): string {
  return DirB[v];
}
Correct:
 enum Dir { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN" }
function nameOf(v: string): string | undefined {
  return Object.entries(Dir).find(([, val]) => val === v)?.[0];
}

trusting it

 Common misconception. A variable of numeric enum type always holds one of its members.
A literal like 99 is rejected for the enum type, but a value typed number is accepted by a cast or a loose helper, and
the enum then holds a value that is not a member. Check input with Object.values or an explicit list before using it as
the enum.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

Correct:

Prerequisites: ts-enum-const. Follow-up: ts-enum-flags. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any string can be assigned to a type derived from an as const object.
type Dir = (typeof DIR)[keyof typeof DIR] is the union "UP" | "DOWN". Assigning "LEFT" is error TS2322, and no extra
runtime code is generated beyond the object. This style works with erasable-syntax-only settings and with plain
JavaScript tooling.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):

type DirTypeB = (typeof DIRB)[keyof typeof DIRB];
const badDir: DirTypeB = "LEFT";
Correct:

type DirType = (typeof DIR)[keyof typeof DIR];
function move(d: DirType): string {

A const enum leaves no object at run time, so it cannot be iterated or passed around as a
value
ts-enum-const   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: ts-enum-fit
Prerequisites: ts-enum-number-assign. Follow-up: ts-enum-as-const. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A const enum is a normal enum with a speed benefit, so Object.keys(Mode) works.
const enum members are replaced by their values at compile time and the enum object is not emitted. Using the
enum as a value (Object.keys(Mode), passing it as an argument) is error TS2475. Use a regular enum, or an as const
object, when the set of members must exist at run time.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2475):
 const enum Mode { Read, Write }
const keysBad = Object.keys(Mode);
Correct:
 const MODE = { Read: 0, Write: 1 } as const;
type Mode = (typeof MODE)[keyof typeof MODE];
function modeNames(): string[] {
  return Object.keys(MODE);
}
Bit-flag enums combine with |, and a combined value must be tested with & rather than ===
ts-enum-flags   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-enum-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-enum-as-const. Follow-up: ts-enum-exhaustive. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. p === Perm.Write is true whenever the Write permission is among the flags.
Powers of two let one number hold several flags: Read | Write is 3. Equality with a single flag is false for any
combination. Test a flag with (p & flag) === flag, add with |, and remove with & ~flag.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hasBad(p: number, flag: number): boolean {
  return p === flag;
}
Correct:
 enum Perm { Read = 1, Write = 2, Exec = 4 }
function has(p: Perm, flag: Perm): boolean {
  return (p & flag) === flag;
}

Add an assertNever default so a new enum member turns a forgotten case into a compile
error
ts-enum-exhaustive   lens: testing   level: L3   family: ts-enum-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-enum-flags. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A switch over an enum with no default is checked for missing members.
The compiler accepts a switch that handles only some members and returns undefined for the rest. Adding a default
branch that passes the value to a function taking never turns a missing case into error TS2345 as soon as the enum
gains a member.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 enum ShapeB { Circle, Square }
function assertNeverB(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(String(x));
}
function sidesBad(s: ShapeB): number {
  switch (s) {
    case ShapeB.Circle: return 0;
    default: return assertNeverB(s);
  }
}
Correct:
 enum Shape { Circle, Square }
function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(String(x));
}
function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case Shape.Circle: return 0;
    case Shape.Square: return 4;
    default: return assertNever(s);
  }
}

TypeScript B-Tree
A training document for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It teaches the B-tree in TypeScript with a BNode
class and a BTree class of minimum degree t: node limits, search, split, root growth, in-order traversal,
range scans, an invariant checker and the logarithmic height bound. This document covers insertion and
search; deletion is not covered by tested chunks.
13 October 2026. Every example in this document was executed in TypeScript 5.9 (strict mode) on Node 22: 8 concept chunks and 7
exercises, with 14 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: B-Tree
A B-tree is a balanced search tree whose nodes hold many keys. With minimum degree t every non-root node has
between t-1 and 2t-1 keys, and all leaves are at the same depth.
Insertion splits full nodes on the way down, moving the median key to the parent. Only splitting the root increases the
height, so the tree stays perfectly balanced.
Use B-trees where a node maps to a disk page or a network request: databases and file systems. In memory a Map
or a balanced binary tree is usually simpler. No built-in B-tree exists in JavaScript or Mnemonist.
Toolbox
 const t = new BTree(2);
for (let k = 10; k >= 1; k--) t.insert(k);
t.has(7);                // true
inorder(t.root);         // [1, 2, ..., 10]
range(t.root, 3, 6);     // [3, 4, 5, 6]
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
4 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript B-Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
With minimum degree t a node holds t-1 to 2t-1 keys; a node with 2t keys cannot split evenly
ts-btree-capacity   lens: mental-model   level: L1   family: ts-btree-mental-model
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-btree-node-search. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A node may hold up to 2t keys.
A full node holds 2t-1 keys. Splitting it moves the median key up and leaves two nodes of t-1 keys each, because
2(t-1) + 1 = 2t-1. A node of 2t keys has no single median, so the split would be uneven. Non-root nodes keep at least
t-1 keys and internal nodes have between t and 2t children.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function limitsBad(t: number): { min: number; max: number; maxChildren: number } {
  return { min: t - 1, max: 2 * t, maxChildren: 2 * t + 1 };
}
Correct:
 function limits(t: number): { min: number; max: number; maxChildren: number } {
  return { min: t - 1, max: 2 * t - 1, maxChildren: 2 * t };
}
Search checks for an equal key in every node, because keys live in internal nodes too
ts-btree-node-search   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-btree-access
Prerequisites: ts-btree-capacity. Follow-up: ts-btree-split. Complexity: O(t log_t n).
 Common misconception. Search can always descend to a leaf.
Unlike a B+ tree, a B-tree stores keys in internal nodes. After finding the first key that is not smaller than the target,
check whether it is equal and stop; otherwise the search descends into the child left of that key and misses the key.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function searchBad(x: BNode, k: number): boolean {
  let i = 0;
  while (i < x.keys.length && k > (x.keys[i] as number)) i++;
  if (x.leaf) return i < x.keys.length && x.keys[i] === k;
  return searchBad(x.children[i] as BNode, k);
}
Correct:
 class BNode {
  keys: number[] = [];
  children: BNode[] = [];
  constructor(public leaf: boolean) {}
}
function search(x: BNode, k: number): boolean {
  let i = 0;
  while (i < x.keys.length && k > (x.keys[i] as number)) i++;
  if (i < x.keys.length && x.keys[i] === k) return true;
  if (x.leaf) return false;
  return search(x.children[i] as BNode, k);
}

TypeScript B-Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
A full root is split under a new root; this is the only way the tree gets taller
ts-btree-root-growth   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-btree-insertion
Prerequisites: ts-btree-split. Follow-up: ts-btree-inorder. Complexity: O(t log_t n).
 Common misconception. Insert into the root even when it is full.
A full root has no parent to receive its median. Create a new empty root, make the old root its only child, split that
child, and then insert. Skipping this step lets the root grow past 2t-1 keys. Height increases only here, at the top, so
all leaves stay at the same depth.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertNoGrow(tree: BTree, k: number): void {
  tree.insertNonFull(tree.root, k);
}
Correct:
 class BTree {
  root = new BNode(true);
  constructor(readonly t: number) {}
  has(k: number): boolean { return search(this.root, k); }
  insert(k: number): void {
    if (this.has(k)) return;
    if (this.root.keys.length === 2 * this.t - 1) {
      const s = new BNode(false);
      s.children.push(this.root);
      splitChild(s, 0, this.t);
      this.root = s;
    }
    this.insertNonFull(this.root, k);
  }
  insertNonFull(x: BNode, k: number): void {
    let i = x.keys.length - 1;
    while (i >= 0 && k < (x.keys[i] as number)) i--;
    if (x.leaf) {
      x.keys.splice(i + 1, 0, k);
      return;
    }
    i++;
    if ((x.children[i] as BNode).keys.length === 2 * this.t - 1) {
      splitChild(x, i, this.t);
      if (k > (x.keys[i] as number)) i++;
    }
    this.insertNonFull(x.children[i] as BNode, k);
  }
}

TypeScript B-Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
A split moves the median up and removes it from the child so it appears once
ts-btree-split   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-btree-insertion
Prerequisites: ts-btree-node-search. Follow-up: ts-btree-root-growth. Complexity: O(t).
 Common misconception. Copy the median key into the parent and keep the child as is.
The median becomes the separator in the parent, so it must leave the child. Copying it and keeping a copy in the left
half stores the key twice and breaks the sorted order. Give the upper keys (and upper children) to a new right sibling,
truncate the child to t-1 keys, and insert the median and the sibling in the parent.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function splitChildBad(p: BNode, i: number, t: number): void {
  const y = p.children[i] as BNode;
  const z = new BNode(y.leaf);
  z.keys = y.keys.splice(t);
  if (!y.leaf) z.children = y.children.splice(t);
  p.keys.splice(i, 0, y.keys[t - 1] as number);
  p.children.splice(i + 1, 0, z);
}
Correct:
 function splitChild(p: BNode, i: number, t: number): void {
  const y = p.children[i] as BNode;
  const z = new BNode(y.leaf);
  const median = y.keys[t - 1] as number;
  z.keys = y.keys.splice(t);
  y.keys.length = t - 1;
  if (!y.leaf) z.children = y.children.splice(t);
  p.keys.splice(i, 0, median);
  p.children.splice(i + 1, 0, z);
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
The height is about log base t of n, so a wide node keeps the tree very shallow
ts-btree-height   lens: complexity   level: L1   family: ts-btree-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-btree-checker. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A search tree with n keys has height about log2 n.
A node with at least t children divides the keys by t at each level, so the height is at most log base t of (n + 1) / 2. With
t = 50 and a million keys the height is 3 edges, not 19. Fewer levels means fewer disk reads, which is why databases
use B-trees.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function maxHeightBad(n: number, t: number): number {
  return Math.floor(Math.log2(n));
}
Correct:
 function maxHeight(n: number, t: number): number {
  return Math.floor(Math.log((n + 1) / 2) / Math.log(t) + 1e-9);
}

TypeScript B-Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
An internal node with k keys has k+1 children, so in-order traversal visits one more child after
the last key
ts-btree-inorder   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-btree-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-btree-root-growth. Follow-up: ts-btree-range. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Visit child i, then key i, for every key.
A node with k keys has k+1 children. A loop over the keys visits the first k children; the last child is to the right of the
last key and needs a separate visit after the loop. Forgetting it drops the largest keys of every internal node.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function inorderBad(x: BNode): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < x.keys.length; i++) {
    if (!x.leaf) out.push(...inorderBad(x.children[i] as BNode));
    out.push(x.keys[i] as number);
  }
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function inorder(x: BNode): number[] {
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < x.keys.length; i++) {
    if (!x.leaf) out.push(...inorder(x.children[i] as BNode));
    out.push(x.keys[i] as number);
  }
  if (!x.leaf) out.push(...inorder(x.children[x.keys.length] as BNode));
  return out;
}
A range scan visits the child before the first key above the upper bound before it stops
ts-btree-range   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ts-btree-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-btree-inorder. Follow-up: ts-btree-checker. Complexity: O(log n + m).
 Common misconception. Stop as soon as a key is above the upper bound.
The child to the left of a key holds values smaller than that key, and some of them can still be inside the range. Visit
that child first, then stop at the key. Child subtrees whose keys are all below the lower bound are skipped without a
visit.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rangeBad(x: BNode, lo: number, hi: number, out: number[] = []): number[] {
  for (let i = 0; i < x.keys.length; i++) {
    const k = x.keys[i] as number;
    if (k < lo) continue;
    if (k > hi) return out;
    if (!x.leaf) rangeBad(x.children[i] as BNode, lo, hi, out);
    out.push(k);
  }
  if (!x.leaf) rangeBad(x.children[x.keys.length] as BNode, lo, hi, out);
  return out;
}

TypeScript B-Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 function range(x: BNode, lo: number, hi: number, out: number[] = []): number[] {
  for (let i = 0; i < x.keys.length; i++) {
    const k = x.keys[i] as number;
    if (k < lo) continue;
    if (!x.leaf) range(x.children[i] as BNode, lo, hi, out);
    if (k > hi) return out;
    out.push(k);
  }
  if (!x.leaf) range(x.children[x.keys.length] as BNode, lo, hi, out);
  return out;
}
A B-tree checker verifies key counts, order and equal leaf depth, not only sortedness
ts-btree-checker   lens: testing   level: L3   family: ts-btree-testing
Prerequisites: ts-btree-range. Follow-up: ts-btree-height. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. If the keys of every node are sorted, the tree is a valid B-tree.
A B-tree also needs every non-root node to hold between t-1 and 2t-1 keys, every internal node to have one more
child than keys, and all leaves to be at the same depth. Return the leaf depth from each subtree or -1 when any rule
fails.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sortedOnlyBad(x: BNode): boolean {
  for (let i = 1; i < x.keys.length; i++) {
    if ((x.keys[i - 1] as number) >= (x.keys[i] as number)) return false;
  }
  return x.children.every(sortedOnlyBad);
}
Correct:
 function checkB(x: BNode, t: number, isRoot = true): number {
  const n = x.keys.length;
  if (n > 2 * t - 1 || (!isRoot && n < t - 1)) return -1;
  for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
    if ((x.keys[i - 1] as number) >= (x.keys[i] as number)) return -1;
  }
  if (x.leaf) return 0;
  if (x.children.length !== n + 1) return -1;
  let depth = -2;
  for (const c of x.children) {
    const d = checkB(c, t, false);
    if (d < 0) return -1;
    if (depth === -2) depth = d;
    else if (d !== depth) return -1;
  }
  return depth + 1;
}

Prompt. A root with key [5] has a leaf child [1, 2] and an internal child [7] whose children are leaves [6] and [8]. For t =

Prompt. What does [maxHeight(1000000, 50), maxHeightBad(1000000, 50)].join(" ") return?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). 3 19
ts-btree-height-ex2   format: choose-the-structure   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why do databases and file systems use B-trees instead of binary search trees?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Disk and network reads move whole pages, so the cost of a lookup is the
number of pages read. A B-tree node is sized to fill one page and holds many keys, so the tree is very shallow (three or
four levels for millions of keys) and a lookup reads few pages. A binary tree needs about log2 n levels and each is a
separate read.

2. Overview and mental model: WeakMap
A WeakMap associates data with objects without keeping those objects alive. When the key object is no longer
reachable anywhere else, the entry can be garbage collected.
That design removes size, keys, values and forEach: the program cannot observe when collection happens. The type
K extends WeakKey allows objects, functions and non-registered symbols; primitives are rejected at compile time.
Use it for metadata attached to objects you do not own, private fields, and caches whose lifetime follows the key. Use
a Map for anything you must list or count.
Toolbox
 const meta = new WeakMap<object, string>();
const el = {};
meta.set(el, "note");
meta.get(el);       // "note"
meta.has({});       // false: different identity
// meta.size        // error TS2339

explanation.
WeakMap keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols); a string key is error TS2345
ts-weakmap-key-types   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-weakmap-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-weakmap-no-iteration. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A WeakMap works like a Map, so a string can be used as a key.
WeakMap<K, V> requires K to be a WeakKey: an object, function or non-registered symbol. A primitive key is
rejected by the compiler (TS2345) and throws TypeError at runtime, because primitives cannot be garbage collected
independently. Use a Map when keys are strings or numbers.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):

  wm.set("a", 1);
}
Correct:

A WeakMap has no size, keys or forEach; track counts yourself or use a Map
ts-weakmap-no-iteration   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: ts-weakmap-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-weakmap-key-types. Follow-up: ts-weakmap-key-identity. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A WeakMap can be listed and counted like a Map.
Entries can disappear whenever the garbage collector runs, so the API hides them: only get, set, has and delete
exist. Reading size is error TS2339 and undefined at runtime. If you need to list or count entries, use a Map and
manage removal yourself.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):

  return wm.size;
}
Correct:

  return m.size;
}

A copy of an object is a different WeakMap key; the data stays with the original
ts-weakmap-key-identity   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-weakmap-equality
Prerequisites: ts-weakmap-no-iteration. Follow-up: ts-weakmap-private-data. Complexity: O(1).

Pass the original reference, or store the data on the copy when you create it.

Keep private per-object data in a WeakMap instead of adding a property that shows up in
keys and JSON
ts-weakmap-private-data   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-weakmap-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-weakmap-key-identity. Follow-up: ts-weakmap-memoize. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Adding a hidden field to an object keeps it out of serialised output.
A property added to an object is enumerable: it appears in Object.keys, spread copies and JSON.stringify, so it can
leak. A module-level WeakMap keyed by the object stores the secret outside the object, is dropped with it when
collected, and works on frozen objects.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function setSecretBad<T extends object>(o: T, s: string): T {
  return Object.assign(o, { secret: s });
}
Correct:
 const secrets = new WeakMap<object, string>();
function setSecret(o: object, s: string): void {
  secrets.set(o, s);
}
function getSecret(o: object): string | undefined {
  return secrets.get(o);
}
Cache results per object in a WeakMap so cached entries do not keep the objects alive
ts-weakmap-memoize   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: ts-weakmap-cache
Prerequisites: ts-weakmap-private-data. Follow-up: ts-weakmap-symbol-keys. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Map keyed by object is an equivalent cache.
A Map holds strong references to its keys, so every object ever cached stays in memory for the life of the cache. A
WeakMap holds keys weakly: when the object is otherwise unreachable, its entry can be collected. The trade-off is
that a WeakMap cannot be listed, counted or cleared.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function memoBad<T extends object, R>(fn: (x: T) => R): ((x: T) => R) & { size(): number } {
  const cache = new Map<T, R>();
  const f = (x: T): R => {
    if (!cache.has(x)) cache.set(x, fn(x));
    return cache.get(x) as R;
  };
  return Object.assign(f, { size: () => cache.size });
}
Correct:
 function memo<T extends object, R>(fn: (x: T) => R): (x: T) => R {
  const cache = new WeakMap<T, R>();
  return (x: T): R => {
    if (!cache.has(x)) cache.set(x, fn(x));
    return cache.get(x) as R;
  };
}

Page 7
Symbol.for symbols are registered and cannot be WeakMap keys; Symbol() symbols can
ts-weakmap-symbol-keys   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ts-weakmap-keys
Prerequisites: ts-weakmap-memoize. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any symbol is allowed as a WeakMap key.
Since ES2023 a WeakMap accepts symbols that are not in the global registry. Symbol("x") is fine, but Symbol.for("x")
can never be collected, so using it as a key throws TypeError. The compiler types both as symbol, so this error only
appears at runtime.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function setRegisteredBad(wm: WeakMap<symbol, number>, n: number): void {
  wm.set(Symbol.for("k"), n);
}
Correct:
 function setLocal(wm: WeakMap<symbol, number>, n: number): symbol {
  const key = Symbol("k");
  wm.set(key, n);
  return key;
}

2. Overview and mental model: Priority Queue
A priority queue returns the element with the best priority first. The standard implementation is a binary heap stored in
an array: push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1).
JavaScript has no built-in heap, so you write one or use a library. In TypeScript the class takes a comparator (a, b) =>
number, and the compiler checks that it returns a number and that peek and pop are handled as T | undefined.
Priority queues drive Dijkstra, top-k selection, merging sorted streams, scheduling and event simulation.
Toolbox
 const pq = new PriorityQueue<number>((a, b) => a - b);   // min first
pq.push(5); pq.push(1); pq.push(3);
pq.pop();      // 1
pq.peek();     // 3
const maxFirst = new PriorityQueue<number>((a, b) => b - a);

A priority queue is a binary heap with a comparator; sorting with the default sort orders
numbers as strings
ts-priorityqueue-core   lens: creation   level: L0   family: ts-pq-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-comparator. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Keeping an array sorted with items.sort() always puts the smallest number first.
Array.sort without a comparator converts values to strings, so 10 sorts before 9. Re-sorting on every push is also O(n
log n) per insert. A binary heap keeps the smallest (by comparator) element at index 0, with O(log n) push and pop.
The comparator returns negative, zero or positive, like Array.sort. Mnemonist (npm) has Heap, MinHeap and
MaxHeap for the same job.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class PqBad {
  private items: number[] = [];
  push(x: number): void {
    this.items.push(x);
    this.items.sort();
  }
  pop(): number | undefined {
    return this.items.shift();
  }
}
Correct:
 class PriorityQueue<T> {
  private heap: T[] = [];
  constructor(private cmp: (a: T, b: T) => number) {}
  get size(): number { return this.heap.length; }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.heap[0]; }
  push(x: T): void {
    const h = this.heap;
    h.push(x);
    let i = h.length - 1;
    while (i > 0) {
      const p = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (this.cmp(h[i] as T, h[p] as T) >= 0) break;
      [h[i], h[p]] = [h[p] as T, h[i] as T];
      i = p;
    }
  }
  pop(): T | undefined {
    const h = this.heap;
    if (h.length === 0) return undefined;
    const top = h[0] as T;
    const last = h.pop() as T;
    if (h.length > 0) {
      h[0] = last;
      let i = 0;
      for (;;) {
        const l = 2 * i + 1;
        const r = l + 1;
        let m = i;
        if (l < h.length && this.cmp(h[l] as T, h[m] as T) < 0) m = l;
        if (r < h.length && this.cmp(h[r] as T, h[m] as T) < 0) m = r;
        if (m === i) break;
        [h[i], h[m]] = [h[m] as T, h[i] as T];
        i = m;
      }
    }
    return top;
  }
}

A comparator must return a number; returning a boolean is error TS2322 and breaks the
order at run time

Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-core. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-empty. Complexity: O(1).

The comparator type is (a, b) => number. A boolean is not a number, so the compiler rejects it (TS2322). In plain
JavaScript true and false convert to 1 and 0, so negative results never occur and the order is wrong. Use a - b for
numbers, b - a for a max-first queue, and localeCompare for strings.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):

Correct:

peek returns T | undefined; reading a property of it is error TS2532

Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-comparator. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-ties. Complexity: O(1).

The queue may be empty, so the type includes undefined and reading peek().p is error TS2532. Check size or use

  return q.peek()?.name;

4.4 Algorithm chunks
A heap is not stable; break ties with an insertion counter to keep first-in order
ts-priorityqueue-ties   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-pq-order
Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-empty. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-update. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Equal-priority items come out in the order they were pushed.
A binary heap makes no promise about equal keys: sift operations reorder them. For tasks of the same priority add a
sequence number and compare by priority first and sequence second. That gives FIFO among equals.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type Task = { p: number; id: number };
function drainBad(ids: number[]): number[] {
  const q = new PriorityQueue<Task>((a, b) => a.p - b.p);
  for (const id of ids) q.push({ p: 1, id });
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let t = q.pop(); t; t = q.pop()) out.push(t.id);
  return out;
}
Correct:
 type Task = { p: number; id: number };
function drain(ids: number[]): number[] {
  let seq = 0;
  const q = new PriorityQueue<Task & { seq: number }>((a, b) => a.p - b.p || a.seq - b.seq);
  for (const id of ids) q.push({ p: 1, id, seq: seq++ });
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let t = q.pop(); t; t = q.pop()) out.push(t.id);
  return out;
}
Top k largest uses a min-heap of size k; a max-heap discards the wrong end
ts-priorityqueue-top-k   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-pq-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-update. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-merge-k. Complexity: O(n log k).
 Common misconception. Keeping a bounded heap with a max-first comparator keeps the largest values.
To keep the k largest values, evict the smallest of the kept set, which requires a min-heap whose root is the smallest
kept item. With a max-heap the eviction removes the largest, so the result is the k smallest. The bounded min-heap
costs O(n log k).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function topKBad(xs: number[], k: number): number[] {
  const q = new PriorityQueue<number>((a, b) => b - a);
  for (const x of xs) {
    q.push(x);
    if (q.size > k) q.pop();
  }
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let v = q.pop(); v !== undefined; v = q.pop()) out.push(v);
  return out.reverse();
}

Correct:
 function topK(xs: number[], k: number): number[] {
  const q = new PriorityQueue<number>((a, b) => a - b);
  for (const x of xs) {
    q.push(x);
    if (q.size > k) q.pop();
  }
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let v = q.pop(); v !== undefined; v = q.pop()) out.push(v);
  return out.reverse();
}
Changing an item priority in place does not reorder the heap; push a new entry and skip stale
ones
ts-priorityqueue-update   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-pq-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-ties. Follow-up: ts-priorityqueue-top-k. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Updating an object priority field moves it to the right place in the queue.
The heap does not watch its elements. Mutating the field leaves the item where it was, so pop returns the wrong item.
The common fix is lazy deletion: push a new entry with the new priority, remember the best priority per key, and
discard popped entries that are out of date. Dijkstra with a binary heap uses exactly this.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type Item = { p: number };
function popAfterMutateBad(): number | undefined {
  const a: Item = { p: 5 };
  const b: Item = { p: 3 };
  const q = new PriorityQueue<Item>((x, y) => x.p - y.p);
  q.push(a);
  q.push(b);
  a.p = 1;
  return q.pop()?.p;
}
Correct:
 class UpdatablePq<K> {
  private q = new PriorityQueue<{ key: K; p: number }>((a, b) => a.p - b.p);
  private best = new Map<K, number>();
  set(key: K, p: number): void {
    this.best.set(key, p);
    this.q.push({ key, p });
  }
  pop(): [K, number] | undefined {
    for (let e = this.q.pop(); e; e = this.q.pop()) {
      if (this.best.get(e.key) === e.p) {
        this.best.delete(e.key);
        return [e.key, e.p];
      }
    }
    return undefined;
  }
}
