Page 8
Merging k sorted lists pushes the successor of each popped item, or the result is truncated
ts-priorityqueue-merge-k   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-pq-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-priorityqueue-top-k. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(N log k).
 Common misconception. Pushing the first element of every list once is enough to merge them.
The heap holds one candidate per list. After popping a value, the next value from the same list becomes the new
candidate and must be pushed. Without it the output has only the first elements. Store (value, list index, position) in
the heap entries.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function mergeKBad(lists: number[][]): number[] {
  const q = new PriorityQueue<[number, number, number]>((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
  lists.forEach((l, i) => { if (l.length) q.push([l[0] as number, i, 0]); });
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let e = q.pop(); e; e = q.pop()) out.push(e[0]);
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function mergeK(lists: number[][]): number[] {
  const q = new PriorityQueue<[number, number, number]>((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
  lists.forEach((l, i) => { if (l.length) q.push([l[0] as number, i, 0]); });
  const out: number[] = [];
  for (let e = q.pop(); e; e = q.pop()) {
    out.push(e[0]);
    const next = (lists[e[1]] as number[])[e[2] + 1];
    if (next !== undefined) q.push([next, e[1], e[2] + 1]);
  }
  return out;
}

Prompt. A shortest-path algorithm needs to lower the priority of a node that is already in the queue. A binary heap
has no decrease-key. What do you do?

known priority per node in a map, and when popping skip entries whose priority is worse than the recorded one. The
heap grows by at most the number of edges, so the algorithm stays O((V + E) log V). Alternatively use an indexed heap
that tracks positions, or a Fibonacci heap.

2. Overview and mental model: RegExp
A RegExp describes a pattern over strings. The type system knows the method signatures and the nullable results,
but it does not read the pattern or the flags, so most regex bugs are found at run time.
Three habits prevent most defects: handle null from match and exec, avoid shared regexes with the g or y flag, and
escape any text that becomes part of a pattern.
For untrusted input also bound the pattern: avoid nested quantifiers that can backtrack catastrophically and prefer
anchored, specific patterns.

const m = re.exec("2024-05");        // RegExpExecArray | null
const y = m?.groups?.year;           // string | undefined
const all = [..."a1b2".matchAll(/\d/g)];

is error TS2531 ("Object is possibly null"). Use optional chaining with a default, or test the result first. Do not silence it
with !, which fails at runtime on the first non-matching input.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2531):
 function firstDigitBad(s: string): string {
  return s.match(/\d/)[0];
}
Correct:

  return s.match(/\d/)?.[0] ?? null;
}
Named groups are in match.groups, which TypeScript types as possibly undefined
ts-regexp-named-groups   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-regexp-access
Prerequisites: ts-regexp-global-lastindex. Follow-up: ts-regexp-matchall. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. match.groups.year is always defined once the pattern has a (?<year>...) group.
exec returns an array whose groups property is typed as optional, because a pattern without named groups has
none. Reading m.groups.year is error TS18048. Use m?.groups?.year, or destructure with a default. Check the
match for null first.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS18048):

  const m = /(?<year>\d{4})/.exec(s);
  return m?.groups.year;
}
Correct:

  return /(?<year>\d{4})/.exec(s)?.groups?.year;
}

A regex with the g or y flag keeps lastIndex between test() calls, so repeated calls can
alternate
ts-regexp-global-lastindex   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-regexp-state
Prerequisites: ts-regexp-match-null. Follow-up: ts-regexp-named-groups. Complexity: O(n).

With the g flag, test and exec start at lastIndex and update it after a match. The same regex tested twice against the
same string returns true then false. Use a regex without g for plain tests, create it inside the function, or reset

JavaScript strings are UTF-16. A character outside the basic plane, such as an emoji, is two code units, and .
matches each half separately. The u flag makes . match a whole code point. Use /\p{L}/u for letters in any language.
Even with u, a combined emoji sequence can contain several code points.

A training document for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It teaches the Bloom filter in TypeScript: double
hashing for k positions, one-sided errors, sizing, counting filters for deletion, bit packing and merging.
Mnemonist (npm) provides a BloomFilter class; the parameters and pitfalls below apply to any
implementation.

exercises, with 9 test runs and 0 failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.

Page 2
1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

 6 concept chunks, 2 in core concepts and 4 in the algorithms section.
 5 exercises, graded by exact match, rubric or judge.

levels.
 Answers live only in the exercise payload. The embedded text of an exercise is the prompt alone, so retrieval
cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: Bloom Filter
A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions. add sets k bits; has checks them. A false answer is certain (no false
negatives); a true answer may be wrong (false positives) with a probability that depends on m, n and k.
The filter uses a few bits per item instead of the item itself, which is why large systems use it as a pre-filter before a
disk or network lookup. It cannot enumerate its members and cannot delete, except in the counting variant.
TypeScript types the API but not the maths: the choice of m and k, the independence of the hashes and the bit
arithmetic must be tested.
Toolbox
 const { m, k } = params(1000, 0.01);        // 9586 bits, 7 hashes
const f = new BloomFilter(m, k);
f.add("alice");
f.has("alice");     // true
f.has("bob");       // false (certain) or true (false positive)
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
2 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Bloom Filter: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
A Bloom filter says "possibly present" or "definitely absent"; a true answer must be
confirmed
ts-bloomfilter-false-positive   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-bloom-access
Prerequisites: ts-bloomfilter-hashes. Follow-up: ts-bloomfilter-sizing. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. has(x) returning true proves that x was added.
Bits set by other items can cover every position of an item that was never added, which is a false positive. A false
answer is always correct (no false negatives) but a true answer is only probable. Use the filter as a cheap pre-check
in front of an authoritative lookup, such as a Set or a database.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isMemberBad(f: BloomFilter, x: string): boolean {
  return f.has(x);
}
Correct:
 function isMember(f: BloomFilter, truth: ReadonlySet<string>, x: string): boolean {
  return f.has(x) && truth.has(x);
}
A Bloom filter needs k different bit positions per item; repeating one hash makes k
meaningless
ts-bloomfilter-hashes   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-bloom-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-bloomfilter-false-positive. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. Calling the same hash function k times gives k probes.
Each item sets k bits. If all k positions come from the same hash value they collapse to one bit, so the filter behaves
as if k = 1 and its false positive rate is much higher than designed. Derive k positions from two independent hashes:
index_i = (h1 + i * h2) mod m, with h2 made odd so that it is never zero.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function fnv1a(s: string, seed = 0x811c9dc5): number {
  let h = seed >>> 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
    h ^= s.charCodeAt(i);
    h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193) >>> 0;
  }
  return h;
}
function indexes(item: string, m: number, k: number): number[] {
  const h1 = fnv1a(item);
  const h2 = (fnv1a(item, 0x9747b28c) | 1) >>> 0;
  return Array.from({ length: k }, (_, i) => (h1 + i * h2) % m);
}
class BloomOneHash {
  bits: Uint8Array;
  constructor(readonly m: number, readonly k: number) { this.bits = new Uint8Array(m); }
  private idx(item: string): number[] {
    return Array.from({ length: this.k }, () => fnv1a(item) % this.m);
  }
  add(item: string): void { for (const i of this.idx(item)) this.bits[i] = 1; }
  bitsSet(): number { return this.bits.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }
}

TypeScript Bloom Filter: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Correct:
 function fnv1a(s: string, seed = 0x811c9dc5): number {
  let h = seed >>> 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
    h ^= s.charCodeAt(i);
    h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193) >>> 0;
  }
  return h;
}
function indexes(item: string, m: number, k: number): number[] {
  const h1 = fnv1a(item);
  const h2 = (fnv1a(item, 0x9747b28c) | 1) >>> 0;
  return Array.from({ length: k }, (_, i) => (h1 + i * h2) % m);
}
class BloomFilter {
  bits: Uint8Array;
  constructor(readonly m: number, readonly k: number) { this.bits = new Uint8Array(m); }
  add(item: string): void {
    for (const i of indexes(item, this.m, this.k)) this.bits[i] = 1;
  }
  has(item: string): boolean {
    return indexes(item, this.m, this.k).every((i) => this.bits[i] === 1);
  }
  bitsSet(): number { return this.bits.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }
}

When packing bits into bytes, shift by i & 7; shifting by i loses bits above the byte
ts-bloomfilter-bit-packing   lens: access   level: L2   family: ts-bloom-access
Prerequisites: ts-bloomfilter-delete. Follow-up: ts-bloomfilter-merge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. bytes[i >> 3] |= 1 << i packs bit i into its byte.
A byte holds bits 0 to 7. The shift 1 << i is taken modulo 32, so for i = 9 it is 512, which does not fit in a Uint8Array
element and is stored as 0, silently dropping the bit. Use 1 << (i & 7) for the position inside the byte and i >> 3 for the
byte index. Packing divides memory by 8.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function setBitBad(bits: Uint8Array, i: number): void {
  bits[i >> 3] |= 1 << i;
}
Correct:
 function setBit(bits: Uint8Array, i: number): void {
  bits[i >> 3] |= 1 << (i & 7);
}
function getBit(bits: Uint8Array, i: number): boolean {
  return ((bits[i >> 3] as number) & (1 << (i & 7))) !== 0;
}
Clearing bits to delete an item can break other items; use a counting Bloom filter
ts-bloomfilter-delete   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-bloom-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-bloomfilter-sizing. Follow-up: ts-bloomfilter-bit-packing. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. Setting an item bits back to 0 removes it from the filter.
Other items may share those bits, and clearing them makes those items disappear, which is a false negative, the one
error a Bloom filter must never make. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter per position: add increments,
remove decrements, and a position counts as set while its counter is above zero.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function removeBad(f: BloomFilter, item: string): void {
  for (const i of indexes(item, f.m, f.k)) f.bits[i] = 0;
}
Correct:
 class CountingBloom {
  counts: Uint8Array;
  constructor(readonly m: number, readonly k: number) { this.counts = new Uint8Array(m); }
  add(item: string): void {
    for (const i of indexes(item, this.m, this.k)) this.counts[i]!++;
  }
  remove(item: string): void {
    if (!this.has(item)) return;
    for (const i of indexes(item, this.m, this.k)) this.counts[i]!--;
  }
  has(item: string): boolean {
    return indexes(item, this.m, this.k).every((i) => (this.counts[i] as number) > 0);
  }
}

Size the filter with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 and k = (m / n) ln 2
ts-bloomfilter-sizing   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: ts-bloom-fit
Prerequisites: ts-bloomfilter-false-positive. Follow-up: ts-bloomfilter-delete. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. m = -n ln p / ln 2 gives the right bit count.
The optimal number of bits for n items and false positive rate p is m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2, and the optimal number of
hashes is k = (m / n) ln 2. Dropping the square under ln 2 gives a filter about 30 percent too small, with a worse false
positive rate than requested. For n = 1000 and p = 0.01 the formulas give m = 9586 and k = 7.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function paramsBad(n: number, p: number): { m: number; k: number } {
  const m = Math.ceil((-n * Math.log(p)) / Math.LN2);
  return { m, k: Math.round((m / n) * Math.LN2) };
}
Correct:
 function params(n: number, p: number): { m: number; k: number } {
  const m = Math.ceil((-n * Math.log(p)) / (Math.LN2 * Math.LN2));
  return { m, k: Math.max(1, Math.round((m / n) * Math.LN2)) };
}
Merge two filters of the same size with bitwise OR; AND would drop members
ts-bloomfilter-merge   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-bloom-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-bloomfilter-bit-packing. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(m).
 Common misconception. The union of two filters is the bitwise AND of their bit arrays.
An item is in the union if it is in either filter, so a position must be set when it is set in either: OR. AND keeps only
positions set in both, so items that were in just one filter become false negatives. Both filters must use the same m, k
and hash functions.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function mergeBad(a: BloomFilter, b: BloomFilter): BloomFilter {
  const out = new BloomFilter(a.m, a.k);
  out.bits = a.bits.map((v, i) => v & (b.bits[i] as number));
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function merge(a: BloomFilter, b: BloomFilter): BloomFilter {
  if (a.m !== b.m || a.k !== b.k) throw new Error("incompatible filters");
  const out = new BloomFilter(a.m, a.k);
  out.bits = a.bits.map((v, i) => v | (b.bits[i] as number));
  return out;
}

Embedded C - Volatile Shared State · 3. Canonical C implementation pattern
3. Canonical C implementation pattern
// Canonical embedded-C pattern// 1) validate preconditions// 2) update only owned state/register fields// 3) keep bounded execution time// 4) return explicit status rather than hiding failureint operation(context_t *ctx) {    if (ctx == NULL) return ERR_ARG;    /* hardware/platform-specific work */    return OK;}
Implementation rules
Use <stdint.h> widths for registers, wire formats, counters, and masks.
Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.
Separate mechanism (register/HAL transport) from policy (retries, parsing, scheduling, application behavior).
Make buffer ownership transitions visible in names, state, or API contracts.
Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

record.document:
Embedded C - Volatile Shared State · 5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
Questions the learner must answer
Can this code run from foreground, ISR, DMA completion, RTOS task, or multiple contexts?
Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?
Safe design pattern
Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

3. Canonical C implementation pattern
// Canonical embedded-C pattern// 1) validate preconditions// 2) update only owned state/register fields// 3) keep bounded execution time// 4) return explicit status rather than hiding failureint operation(context_t *ctx) {    if (ctx == NULL) return ERR_ARG;    /* hardware/platform-specific work */    return OK;}
Implementation rules
Use <stdint.h> widths for registers, wire formats, counters, and masks.
Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.
Separate mechanism (register/HAL transport) from policy (retries, parsing, scheduling, application behavior).
Make buffer ownership transitions visible in names, state, or API contracts.
Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

record.document:
Embedded C - Nonblocking State Machines · 5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
Questions the learner must answer
Can this code run from foreground, ISR, DMA completion, RTOS task, or multiple contexts?
Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?
Safe design pattern
Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

Python on hardware, Pin interrupts · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks) (continued)
from machine import Pin
hits_bad = []
pins_bad = [Pin(20 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
pins_bad[i].irq(lambda p: hits_bad.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
from machine import Pin
hits = []
pins = [Pin(30 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
pins[i].irq(lambda p, i=i: hits.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Read and clear a shared counter with interrupts disabled, or an event can arrive between the
two steps
py-emb-irq-atomic   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-irq-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-closure. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-gate. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. Reading the counter and then setting it to zero is safe.
An interrupt can fire between reading n = count and writing count = 0. The event it counted is then erased and never
processed. Wrap the pair in machine.disable_irq() and enable_irq(state) so it cannot be interrupted, and keep the
protected section as short as possible.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
count_bad = [0]
def take_bad(between=None):
n = count_bad[0]
if between:
between()
count_bad[0] = 0
return n
Correct:
from machine import disable_irq, enable_irq
count_ok = [0]
def take_ok():
state = disable_irq()
n = count_ok[0]
count_ok[0] = 0
enable_irq(state)
return n

Why
Fix / rule

Do not memorize a single Big-O label for Protocol. Analyze each primitive operation, the number of times each element/state can be touched, auxiliary allocations, recursion depth, and the cost of Python-level operations used inside loops.
Question
What to inspect
Good explanation
Red flag
Time
Loop/state transitions
Count total state changes, not just nesting
Hidden linear operation inside a loop
Space
Containers + recursion
Separate output space from auxiliary space
Ignoring copies/slices/visited sets
Invariant
What remains true
State it before and after each iteration
Only describing code mechanically
Termination
What strictly progresses
Bounded pointer/frontier/state space
Update can leave state unchanged
Python cost

Python / Flask Protocol · 5. Recognition signals, best fit, and alternatives
5. Recognition signals, best fit, and alternatives
Recognition signals
The problem naturally preserves the information represented by Protocol.
The required operations align with its efficient primitives.
The constraints reward its characteristic access/update/traversal pattern.
A simpler structure/algorithm would lose ordering, identity, range, priority, connectivity, or state information needed by the problem.
Avoid or reconsider when
The input is tiny and a direct scan is clearer.
A different Python builtin provides the needed operation with less code and the same or better complexity.
The representation causes unnecessary copying, hashing, pointer chasing, or memory growth.
For Flask, CPU-heavy work occupies the worker handling the request; architecture may matter more than the micro-optimization.

record.document:
Python / Flask Protocol · 6. Python-specific gotcha catalogue
6. Python-specific gotcha catalogue
Gotcha
Why
Fix / rule
Aliasing
Two names may reference the same mutable object
Copy only when independent state is required.
Mutable defaults
Default list/dict/set arguments persist across calls
Use None and create inside the function.
Hashability
Mutable containers cannot be dict/set keys
Use immutable/hashable representations such as tuple/frozenset when semantically correct.
Recursion depth
Deep recursion can raise RecursionError
Prefer iterative stacks/queues for adversarial depth.
Slicing/copying
Slices allocate new sequences
Use indices/iterators when repeated copying changes complexity.
pop(0)
List front removal is O(n)
Use collections.deque for queues.
heapq ordering
Tuples compare lexicographically; equal priority may compare payloads
Add a monotonic tie-break counter if payloads are not comparable.
Async misconception
async def does not make CPU-bound DSA non-blocking
Offload CPU-heavy work or redesign the endpoint.
Topic-specific drill: identify which of the generic Python gotchas can actually affect Protocol, then add at least two topic-specific counterexamples during corpus expansion.

Rust Bfs · 1. Rust representation and invariants
1. Rust representation and invariants
State the representation invariant before coding. For containers, identify which values are owned and which are borrowed; for graph/tree nodes, identify the single owner or reference-counted owner; for algorithms, identify the loop/recursion invariant.
Prefer indices into Vec-backed storage for interview graphs and mutable topology when node identity matters but pointer sharing does not. This often avoids Rc<RefCell<T>> entirely.
Use Option rather than sentinel/null states. Use Result when invalid input or operation failure should be reported rather than panicked.
Question
Rust-specific answer
Failure if ignored
Who owns each value?
Name owner, borrowers, and drop point.
moves, dangling design assumptions, clone-heavy code
Where can mutation occur?
One active &mut, or controlled interior mutability.
borrow conflicts or runtime RefCell panic
What represents absence/failure?
Option / Result, not magic sentinels.
invalid state and panics
What is identity?
Index, key, pointer identity, or value equality.
incorrect graph/list behavior
What must remain invariant?
Bfs structural/algorithmic invariant.

record.document:
Rust Selection Sort · 2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.
3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
fn sort<T: Ord>(a: &mut [T]) {    // Implement using indices/slice operations; avoid unnecessary Clone bounds.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?
4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Space. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

Rust Btreeset · 2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.
3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
// Canonical Rust 2021 sketch for btreesetfn demo<T>(input: &[T]) {    let _n = input.len();    // Preserve ownership and borrowing invariants explicitly.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?
4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(log N) operations. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

record.document:
Rust Multi Source Bfs · 2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.
3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
fn solve(graph: &[Vec<usize>], start: usize) {    let _ = (graph, start);    // Maintain algorithm-specific state in Vec/VecDeque/BinaryHeap.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?
4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(V+E) Time, O(V) Space. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

record.document:
Rust Zero One Bfs · 2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
2. Ownership and borrow-checker playbook
Shorten borrow scopes: read what you need, let the borrow end, then mutate. Entry APIs, split_at_mut, slice pattern matching, Option::take, mem::replace, and local temporaries are common tools.
Do not reach for clone() as the first borrow-checker fix. Decide whether the algorithm needs ownership, a shared borrow, a mutable borrow, or a structural redesign using indices.
Recursive functions usually borrow the structure (&Node / &mut Node) while owning only small state. Returning references requires explicit lifetime relationships only when elision cannot express them.
3. Canonical Rust 2021 pattern
fn solve(graph: &[Vec<usize>], start: usize) {    let _ = (graph, start);    // Maintain algorithm-specific state in Vec/VecDeque/BinaryHeap.}
Line-by-line reasoning checklist
Which line moves ownership?
Which lines only borrow?
Where does a mutable borrow begin and end?
What allocation happens?
Which operation can panic?
What does the type system rule out before runtime?
4. Complexity, allocation, and performance
Baseline complexity: O(V+E) Time, O(V) Space. Distinguish algorithmic Big-O from ownership costs such as allocation, cloning, hashing, refcount traffic, and UTF-8 decoding.
Vec/slice traversal is usually cache-friendly. Rc/RefCell node graphs add pointer chasing, refcount updates, runtime borrow checks, and fragmented allocation.
Iterator chains are lazy and commonly optimize well, but repeated collect(), clone(), String allocation, or HashMap construction can dominate small inputs.

## 14. Obsolete and non-conforming features

Level **R**: read in full from §16 on 2026-10-16. These feed `gotcha`, `diagnosis` and `repair` exercises in topics `robust-structure`, `robust-antipatterns` and `text-semantics`.

### 14.1 Obsolete but conforming (validators warn but don't fail)

| Feature | What the spec says to do instead |
|---|---|
| `border` on `img` (allowed value is only `"0"`) | Use CSS |
| `charset` on `script` (allowed value is only `utf-8`) | Omit it; it has no effect in a UTF-8 document |
| `language` on `script` (allowed value is only `JavaScript`) | Omit it, or use `type` |
| `type` on `script` when empty or a JavaScript MIME type | Omit it; same effect |
| `type` on `style` (allowed value is only `text/css`) | Omit it |
| `name` on `a` (non-empty, unique, must equal the `id` if present) | Use `id` for fragment targets |
| `maxlength`/`size` on `input type=number` | Discouraged; tolerated so legacy UAs render a sensible width |

The spec states that conformance checkers must distinguish pages that have no conformance errors **and** none of these features from pages that have no errors **but do** use them. Its example is "Valid HTML" versus "Valid HTML with warnings." Graders should therefore treat these as warnings, not failures.

Each exercise's ≥6 checks draw from these types. No single type, and in particular no string or screenshot comparison, is allowed to be the sole correctness rule.

| CK-LABEL | clicking a label focuses or activates its control; the name contains the visible label text | interaction plus snapshot |

| CK-FOCUS | `activeElement` after open/close/navigation | DOM read |
| CK-PAYLOAD | the submitted name/value pairs equal the expected **multiset** (order-insensitive unless order matters) | interception / `formdata` |

| CK-GEOM | bounding boxes are stable before and after load within a stated tolerance | geometry |

| CK-AXE | automated rule violations = 0 for the scoped rules | axe report (evidence only) |

**Rubric (three separated scores):**
1. **Objective behavior** (pass/fail per check; required to pass).

3. **Optional style** (never blocks a pass).

Each rubric also lists accepted alternatives and known limitations.

**Hint tiers (one question each; no solutions, pseudocode or next-line instructions):**

HTML RAG Candidate Corpus — Batch 00b: Reference Inventory (continuation of Batch 00) · 14.1 Obsolete but conforming (validators warn but don't fail)
### 14.1 Obsolete but conforming (validators warn but don't fail)
| Feature | What the spec says to do instead |
|---|---|
| `border` on `img` (allowed value is only `"0"`) | Use CSS |
| `charset` on `script` (allowed value is only `utf-8`) | Omit it; it has no effect in a UTF-8 document |
| `language` on `script` (allowed value is only `JavaScript`) | Omit it, or use `type` |
| `type` on `script` when empty or a JavaScript MIME type | Omit it; same effect |
| `type` on `style` (allowed value is only `text/css`) | Omit it |
| `name` on `a` (non-empty, unique, must equal the `id` if present) | Use `id` for fragment targets |
| `maxlength`/`size` on `input type=number` | Discouraged; tolerated so legacy UAs render a sensible width |
The spec states that conformance checkers must distinguish pages that have no conformance errors **and** none of these features from pages that have no errors **but do** use them. Its example is "Valid HTML" versus "Valid HTML with warnings." Graders should therefore treat these as warnings, not failures.

## 20. Reusable check catalogue (operator only)
Each exercise's ≥6 checks draw from these types. No single type, and in particular no string or screenshot comparison, is allowed to be the sole correctness rule.
| Check type | What it asserts | Typical evidence |
|---|---|---|
| CK-DOM | element/attribute presence in the **parsed DOM** (structural, not a source-string match) | DOM query |
| CK-ROLE | role plus accessible name of a control or landmark | accessibility snapshot or role locator |
| CK-LABEL | clicking a label focuses or activates its control; the name contains the visible label text | interaction plus snapshot |
| CK-KEY | the Tab sequence equals the expected order; Enter/Space activate controls; Escape closes a modal | keyboard automation |
| CK-FOCUS | `activeElement` after open/close/navigation | DOM read |
| CK-PAYLOAD | the submitted name/value pairs equal the expected **multiset** (order-insensitive unless order matters) | interception / `formdata` |
| CK-VALID | submission blocked or allowed; `validity` flags | DOM read |
| CK-GEOM | bounding boxes are stable before and after load within a stated tolerance | geometry |
| CK-SRC | `currentSrc` at a controlled viewport and DPR | DOM read |
| CK-VALIDATOR | validator returns no errors; warnings recorded separately | validator log |
| CK-AXE | automated rule violations = 0 for the scoped rules | axe report (evidence only) |
| CK-MANUAL | screen-reader / zoom / mobile keyboard observation recorded by a human | manual log |
| CK-NEG | a named broken variant **fails** at least one specific check | mutation run |
